title: Nvidia GTC 2026 — Biggest Takeaways
transcription: I'm Katie Tarasov, here at Nvidia's annual GTC Developer Conference in San Jose, California, where CNBC will have live coverage throughout the event. I'm on the showroom floor where hundreds of companies are showing off products powered by Nvidia's chips and technologies, including a lot of robotics. 110 robots here, almost every single company in the world, I can't think of one that are building robots, is working with Nvidia. Humanoid robots from companies like Unitree, Booster, and LimX greeted me on the way in today. But the star event was, of course, CEO Jensen Huang's keynote. I just want to remind you, this is a tech conference. Nvidia's graphics processing units, GPUs, have proven absolutely crucial for powering generative AI, making the Silicon Valley giant the first ever to reach a $5 trillion market value last year. But now, agentic AI is shifting compute needs, and Nvidia is shifting strategy to match. It showed off a rack filled only with its central processing units, CPUs, at GTC this week. The more modest host chips usually act in a supporting role for GPUs but have suddenly found themselves in the limelight, creating an industry-wide renaissance as Nvidia says CPUs could be the next bottleneck for AI. Huang unveiled a new Groq language processing unit in his keynote Monday, built on technology acquired with Nvidia's largest purchase to date, $20 billion for Groq's assets in December. The new LPU has a single core, purpose-built for speeding up the GPU. It's expected to ship in the third quarter of 2026 and be integrated into a brand new rack dedicated to housing 256 of the new chips, increasing the token-per-watt performance of Rubin GPUs in the neighboring Vera Rubin rack 35 times. We united, unified two processors of extreme differences: one for high throughput, one for low latency. It still doesn't change the fact that we need a lot of memory. And so, Groq, we're just going to add a whole bunch of Groq chips, which expands the amount of memory it has. He also gave a sneak peek of this: Nvidia's Hyper architecture that will be available in the next Vera Rubin Ultra rack-scale system shipping in 2027. It totally changes the game for rack-scale systems by flipping the compute trays on their side to allow extreme density and much lower latency. Huang also met with reporters for a private Q&A session Tuesday. We've been, um, licensed for many customers in China for H200. That's right. Uh, we have received purchase orders, um, from many customers, and we're in the process of, uh, restarting our manufacturing. And so, so that's new news for all of you. And, um, uh, it's different than it was two weeks ago or three weeks ago. Uh, but that's our condition today. And, and, um, our supply chain is is getting fired up, uh, and so you'll you'll like, all of you will likely start to hear about that.

The one big shift that I'm seeing in education is that more and more of our young people are asking for education to be relevant, meaningful, significant, and challenging. I think WACP has played a very important role in our going ahead with the IBCP program. We had a very small cohort to start with, and they have benefited immensely. title: Highlights | 21st European Spectrum Management Conference
transcription:
It's so convenient to be at the Spectrum Conference this year because we just issued our MSS regulation proposal and that's of course also in the context of our digital networks act proposal and they have in common that they really have a different kind of approach on spectrum and satellites.

It's been a very interesting conference because people are preparing for the WRC-27 that is happening next year. So, the various positions on the key agenda items are being discussed. The fact that we have a variety of stakeholders enriches the discussion and makes us see the perspectives from the different sectors of the industry, which is very useful.

Reconnecting with people, the discussion face-to-face, talking to brilliant minds, and exchanging ideas. That is the real value.

Lots of discussions about the Digital Networks Act with visions from the Commission, from the Member States, from the stakeholders. Satellite, of course, is a key area. And for the broadcast community, I think we had a lot of presentations and discussions about 5G broadcast.

I think this year has been quite special for the 21st EU Spectrum Management Conference here in Brussels. Satellite has become one of the trendy topics, one of the most valuable topics also to discuss. And I think the key takeaway that I get is that we all agree on the objectives and the goals that we have. We want to connect everyone, we want to connect Europe and make Europe relevant again in the digital conversation. And for that, satellite is a key component of the ecosystem.

We need to be prepared for the improvements in EU regulation to foster competitiveness and to promote innovation in Europe. We need to be prepared for the WRC-27 and 31 in order to address the best positions for EU interests and we need to be prepared as well with our open mind to converge on the best approach for Europe.

Two things that these conferences are very good at: one is that they try to put together a neutral panel that encompass all the players, so that we can see the discussion from the various points of view, and the other one is the convening power of Forum Global that they can bring together everybody to discuss openly and not to push any agenda forward, so I'm very happy to participate in this kind of events.

transcription:
Spectrum is a complex issue. Spectrum is a scarce resource. Our spectrum needs should be clearly defined well in advance. This would have a significant impact on people on the ground. We have to accommodate and understand each other. Move towards harmonization collectively.

I think this was a fantastic event, which brought different perspectives, like 5G, 6G, innovation, and the digital divide. This was a, a significant and important step to prepare for WRC-27, because this will have a significant impact on people on the ground, right? So, I think that will help us harmonize, or move towards harmonization collectively.

Yeah, there are three key takeaways: the first one is the contentious WRC-27; the second one is the direct-to-device progress and regulation; and the last one is the spectrum roadmap that is vital for the investment and the digital growth.

I'm very glad that we were able to share the Philippine case, our developments in the country, especially now that we have a new act, the Konektadong Pinoy Act. Of course, we know that spectrum is a scarce resource, so it's important to learn from the industry and other administrations.

We have already a clear roadmap defined, first 6 GHz, 7 GHz, we call it golden band, and our spectrum needs should be clearly defined well in advance.

Spectrum is a complex issue. It involves a wide range of stakeholders with varying viewpoints, and in order to balance those viewpoints and come up with a, a solution, the only way really to get there is to put them all in the same room. If you put everybody in the same room without any structure, um, we have chaos. So, Forum Global bring to that discussion the structure within which we, as representatives of industry, can work out solutions, or work out ways forward.

So, I'd like to thank Forum Global for hosting the 12th APSMC. The timing would have not been better than this, because all the APT countries are actually preparing for the WRC now, and we are preparing to have a good harmonized view for the conference. These will help us to deliver what we are looking forward from 6G use cases like AI or XR and sensing. We need to have a harmonized contiguous band.

As usual, I think Forum Global has done an amazing job. This event is particularly important for the industry, because we have the opportunity to discuss with regulators, and with other members and different sectors. And I think it's very important for everyone to discuss and understand the point of view of each other, and in order to, uh, to move forward, we have to accommodate and understand each other.

title: RSAC 2026 Conference Quick Look: Cyber Family Feud: Generational Clashes in Cybersecurity and Fixes
transcription: Hi everyone. I am Anand Singh, Chief Security and Strategy Officer at Symmetry Systems, and this is my daughter, Aarushi Singh, undergraduate researcher and security practitioner. And honestly, we're not here to give you a standard, dry lecture. We're actually just here to finish an argument we started last Tuesday. It wasn't an argument, Aarushi. It was a spirited debate. Alright, well, that's why our session is called Cyber Family Feud, but this isn't about old versus young. It's about the clash between builders and accelerators. Exactly. And I represent the builders. We dig into the logs, optimize for failure modes, and frankly, we know where all the bodies are buried. And I represent the accelerators. I treat LLMs like junior engineers because I want to build security directly into the pipeline and move fast. Which is great until the automation is wrong. We can't forget how to actually reason through a problem when the quick fixes fail, which is why I am right, Aarushi. No, I'm right. See, this is the problem that most security teams are facing right now. The builders and the accelerators are speaking two entirely different languages. In our session, we are going to show you how to manage these two mindsets into what we call the Centaur model. We'll talk about how builders need to own the "why," the trust boundaries, and blast radius. And accelerators own the "how," the scaling, the automation, and the enforcement. If your security team feels disconnected, come join us. We'll give you a three-to-six months roadmap to get them operating on the same mission. So Aarushi, top answers on the board. Name the best way to get your builders and accelerators to stop fighting and actually secure your architecture. Well, they just need to come to our session at the RSA Conference. transcription: We work a lot with multi-agent factories, and we wanted to show you visually a lot of this stuff is happening, like, at the same time, in parallel and concurrently. And factory is a demo that Hannah and I put together in two days. Currently, what we've done is we've submitted three campaigns to run in parallel. Uh, we wanted to show you that this can happen over time and then there's a bunch of agents that have been assigned to work sequentially. As you can see, campaign synthesis, wherever that's sort of waiting, it has started its work, but it's waiting for the research to complete. When the research completes, it'll get passed on to another agent that goes through the different steps of context that you provided to me about what it takes to build a campaign. So, there is a 10-step process in building campaigns, and the agents are assigned to building out the different components of that 10-step process. And that is the basis for this agent's training. We have a number of specialist agents. They look at the slide deck and one of the agents, for example, will say, "Based on all of the research that's been gathered on this particular campaign, let me write up a series of email templates for this campaign to use in order to apply pressure or use different tactics." It takes around 20 minutes for three campaigns to run. Individually, it takes about 15 minutes. It's quite a lot of agents. You could also do this with less agents, but we did really want to show you, like, this is the future in my industry right now and I wanted you to get a taste of it as well. And this will output a campaign brief for each campaign. That campaign brief includes a, uh, power map, a planning, a strategy pack, a digital assets pack, a local media pack. There's 10 documents with suggested content from each one.

title: RSAC 2026 Conference Quick Look: The Impact of Security Usability Challenges in Cloud Environments
transcription: Hi everyone, my name is Alex Sierra and on behalf of myself and Alex Pinto, my co-presenter, I want to talk to you about a session CLS W09: The Impact of Security Usability Challenges in Cloud Environments. The point of this talk is we're going to be looking at a dataset that involves security posture checks on a variety of cloud providers, especially the hyperscalers: AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure). And we're going to correlate the UX decisions that they have made in the way that users can set up infrastructure, can set up credentials, can set up storage, with security outcomes. We're going to see how much, and if and how much, the way that the cloud providers decided to design their UI and their architecture are leading users to make more or less security mistakes. We feel like this is important for cloud providers and for people designing systems in general to understand the impact of their user experience design in security. Plus, we provide a series of practical recommendations for organizations, for companies, in the way that they use those cloud providers to minimize the impacts that those UX decisions have on their security posture. Hope to see you all there.

title: Kevin Baum - Next Generation in AI Research IJCAI-ECAI 2026
transcription: Hi, I'm Dr. Kevin Baum and I lead the research group for Responsible AI and Machine Ethics at the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence. Being a philosopher and computer scientist, I work on a problem that sounds simple, but that might be one of the most important ones in our lifetimes. The alignment problem. Put simply, it is about getting AI to do what we want in ways we find acceptable. But that framing actually hides the hard part. We live in a pluralist society and we do not agree on what we want or on what counts as acceptable. So aligning AI with human values is more than a technical challenge, it's a sociotechnical one under deep normative uncertainty. At bottom of it, it's a political problem. Whose values, decided by whom, and why? My group works on that challenge from a philosophical and a computer science point of view. We build architectures that make AI reason explicitly about norms and values, resulting in normatively competent systems that can act for the right reasons, state those reasons, and let human challenge and refine them, and we ground all that in philosophical theory. Here's why it matters. AI systems are becoming agents, making decisions in hospitals, courtrooms, and classrooms. The answer is not smarter machines, it is normatively more competent ones. Doing the right things for the right reasons, guided by real humans and keeping responsibility where it belongs.

He explains his group's work in building normatively competent systems that can reason about values and states that the goal is not just "smarter machines," but systems that act for the right reasons under human guidance. There are many facets of the conference in addition to the workshops and sessions. So, one of the highlights is always the Expo Floor, and this is really interesting. It can be overwhelming to first-timers because there's so much to see, which is understanding, but it is really exciting to have all of the edtech companies all in one place, and you could actually try things hands-on. One of the biggest takeaways this year was students. Students were everywhere from creating the amazing drone show at night. It was great seeing them on the showroom floor and actually sharing how they did it as well. The other place you really saw it is on the actual keynote stage. I love how Alana Winnick invited her students on stage to share their experience. It made it much more powerful, and I got to actually present with Alana and her students in the session, and they were so much fun. And now it's recording you. Howdy. I've seen students present before, but they've never been such a big part of the conference. The next big takeaway is about immersive technologies. We're talking about AR, VR, MR, XR. You know, virtual reality was very big at one point, and then we start seeing augmented reality really take over in education, but it was really interesting to see how it's being used in practical ways. There was a wealth of information from a VR classroom to an immersive lab on the Expo Floor and tons of sessions. The next big push was digital wellness, which is funny for a technology conference, but we saw different ways to actually balance your classroom and help students find ways to actually be more mindful about their screen time. Next is the one everyone expects, which is artificial intelligence. Now, it was a little bit different this year because it was more on now that we've had AI in schools, ways people are using it in innovative or interesting ways along with the tools and kind of where it's going next. And last but not least is community. So, this is the thing I love the most about this conference, just like my favorite conferences, is you're meeting a lot of people, you're connecting with new teachers, you're seeing old friends, and then there's an interesting thing happening because of the new FETC Affiliates Network. All of the NYSCATE board was there and lots of the other affiliates, so there was just a nice family vibe. So, FETC was a terrific experience and it never disappoints. I hope to see you there next year. So, thanks to Jen Womble for making me a featured speaker and thanks to Amy DelCorvo for bringing the whole NYSCATE crew down there. Hope to see you there next year, January 26th through 29th, 2027.

title: Innovation and AI Lab Presentation at College of Business and Economic - CSUF
transcription: Welcome to the Innovation and AI Lab video, an initiative of the College of Business at CSUF. We are focused on empowering faculty and staff through AI professional development. The Innovation and AI Lab is a dedicated space for professional development equipping educators and administrators to integrate AI into teaching, research, and operations. The space includes a boardroom with a capacity of 20 and a workstation lab with four stations for hands-on practice, located at SGMH 4240. Our mission is built around faculty and staff development. This is supported by six pillars, including curriculum and workforce development, student AI literacy, AI research, community engagement, and regional innovation. The lab is a modern space for hands-on AI work. It features a boardroom for conferences, a workshop lounge for collaboration, a workstation lab for training and research, and a clear entrance at SGMH 4240. The facility is purpose-built to facilitate quick progression from idea to working AI capability. The Innovation and AI Lab is at the intersection of four communities. We engage students with practical AI skills, faculty with research leadership and mentorship, local businesses with real-world problems, and AI companies with cutting-edge tools and industry linkages. Our spring 2026 initiatives include AI Foundations workshops for faculty and staff, an AI literacy course for business students, and active research into local AI models. We are also focused on community SBDC engagement through small business outreach. The impact of the AI Lab extends from campus to the region. We prepare faculty and staff to lead AI integration and equip students for the AI economy. This strengthens the region by providing local businesses access to AI talent and innovation capacity. We welcome collaboration from advisors, donors, and community partners. You can engage by sponsoring a program, sharing a real business challenge, or connecting us with AI companies and industry partners. Thank you for viewing this video.

title: Simon Parkinson, MSN, ARNP, FNP-C, CNRN | March 5, 2026 Successful Aging AZ Conference | Clip 12
transcription: ...and then get the PET scan, get the MRI to rule out other causes. But most importantly, there is a specific test for Lewy body dementia where we actually do a synuclein, um, skin biopsy. So, we take a punch of skin from the back of the neck, and we stain it, and we look at it under a microscope, and we can actually see these alpha-synuclein proteins deposited within the skin. And if we see an elevation of these and a negative DaTscan—which the DaTscan is the diagnostic test for Parkinson's disease—we can now know that we're leaning much more to a, to a Lewy body dementia diagnosis, as opposed to the Parkinsonian features. Um, so again, cholinesterase, the, the memantine, they do help. We have to be careful though because treating Parkinson's when you don't have Parkinson's causes trouble in itself. We try to unfreeze muscles, so putting you on medication that you don't need is, is actually problematic. And again, you've got to avoid the atypical antipsychotics in Lewy body disease. The agitation, the hallucinations we see commonly in Alzheimer's and use medications such as Rexulti or, um, quetiapine, which is Seroquel, is actually contraindicated in Lewy body disease because it will actually make you worse. And then, the non-pharmacological, um, components: support sleep—people who don't sleep are more confused—um, physical, occupational therapy—if you're shuffling, if you're falling, we don't want to add to a problem. So, in summary, um, Alzheimer's disease: hippocampal-predominant neurodegeneration, we can see it on an MRI scan, we have treatments for this. Um, vascular dementia: cerebrovascular, um, injury, strokes—prevent the strokes, prevent dementia. Um, frontotemporal dementia is atrophy within the behavioral and language areas, so instead of looking for memory problems, look for behaviors, look for problems with speech. And then alpha-synuclein pathology within the Lewy body dementia: cognitive fluctuations and very early onset, um, hallucinations—that is, that is sort of the key factor. Um, dementia is not a normal part of aging. We don't have to get more forgetful as we get older. We get slower, it takes longer to recall a fact, it takes longer to, you know, come up with a solution, but dementia is not normal. And then early diagnosis is the cornerstone of treatment. At the moment, we cannot undo the damage that dementia has done. We can't undo the loss of memory. And certainly with the findings that we're seeing now, we've got this 15-year window of this preclinical, um, time. This is where we need to be getting in with the medications. This is where we need to be preventing, you know, worsening of disease in our 40s, 50s, before those symptoms come on in our 60s.

title: Simon Parkinson, MSN, ARNP, FNP-C, CNRN | “The Longest Day” Presentation | Video Clip 4
transcription: It is very important to keep routine because if every day you have to wake up and think of doing something new, it takes a lot of energy. And you're already, as a patient with dementia and cognitive dysfunction, you're already struggling to keep going normal, you don't want to keep new tasks every day. So, keeping things a very good routine. We have breakfast at this time, we do lunch, we do this and keeping that um very straightforward. Um, provide reminders. I always tell my patients, get a a white board, write down today's date, am I going to the doctors? Put that down because those repetitive questions, the person with dementia doesn't know they are repeating. What time is my doctor's appointment? 10:00. Ten minutes later, what time is my doctor's appointment? 10:00. That's a frustration for the person caring for the patient with dementia. So, I tell my patients, what time's my doctor's appointment? 10:00. Write it on the board. Next time you're there, what time's my doctor's appointment? Go check your board. If it says 10:00, you don't have to ask your wife or your husband for the 47th time what time's my doctor's appointment. Um, watch the frustration and provide reassurance to the patient. Um, the patient is going to not want to ask, they're going to be worried, um but avoid testing memories. One things that people will try to do is, well do you remember such and such? Do you remember such and such? Trying to see to help the patient and show them, "Look you can you can remember." But also, if they can't, it it it can upset the patient. So, you know, we we try to keep everything relaxed. And if depression does come on, we can get it treated. Um, there is a depression related to chronic illness that we see across multiple diseases, but again, we will see the grieving process come through throughout this. is if depression is there, treat it because to the point of the gentleman was saying about um, fractiousness and things, the more depressed you are, the more likely you are to do something silly and hurt yourself, so and and suicide is a problem in dementia patients, so to that point. Um, moderate stage behaviors, this is where we start to see patients more likely to be wandering. Um, they argue, they'll become more combative. We start to see sleep disturbances because of REM behavior problems, they get up, they wander. Um, agitation, hitting, biting, this is when they're having much more problems forming thoughts, keeping things um straight in their mind, but also their startle reflex. One of the things that patients will find is that they will, because they have the sleep disturbance, they will sleep more during the day, they will take naps. You startle a patient who's sleeping who has dementia, they are much more likely to come out and wake up fighting. Um, so they have lost that inhibition of patience and calm.

transcription: 50 odd years old, I can't remember as well, as quick as I was when I was 20. That's not dementia, that's just it gets slower over time. Poor judgment, again, that's a safety issue. Um, we have a lot of problems with shrinkage of the frontal portions of our brain. Those are our developmental, why children do silly things, why young men do silly things, we become mature into our mid-20s, we start to make sensible decisions. As we age, the frontal portions of our brain, and there is a subsection of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, where we actually lose inhibition. title: Beyond Physiology: Dr. Fearon Discusses CathWorks FFRangio's Robust Clinical Evidence
transcription: As you've also heard, uh, coronary physiology continues to be underutilized, and there's probably a number of reasons. It can take extra time, there are issues with the wire-handling characteristics, pressure drift, and other, uh, factors associated with the measurement can be frustrating. If you're measuring FFR, the side effects of adenosine, uh, it's expensive, and there is a small risk anytime you put a wire in a vessel. And as you can see, all of these issues are related to the need for a coronary pressure wire, as well as the use of hyperemic agent like adenosine. And so that raises the question, well, what if we could get all of this information just with the angiogram alone and no need of a pressure wire or adenosine? And that's where angiography-derived, uh, physiology comes into play. Now, six years ago, we published, uh, these data comparing, uh, FFR Angio to wire-based, uh, FFR in a blinded fashion, 10 centers, over 300 patients. And you see that there was a very high, uh, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy, all above 90% with FFR Angio. And, well, what we found even more impressive was if you look at the gray zone or around the cut point of the FFR cutoff of 0.80, this is where most tests have a, uh, accuracy of 50%, kind of like a coin flip. You see that FFR Angio continued to have excellent diagnostic characteristics in that gray-zone area. We also looked at how FFR Angio compares with the non-hyperemic pressure ratios with regard to its correlation with, uh, wire-based FFR. And you see that the accuracy of FFR Angio was actually higher, uh, than the resting indices, uh, when compared with pressure-wire-based FFR. So, what data do we have with FFR Angio? Well, we have a real-world registry looking at the safety of deferring lesions in almost 900 patients, and showing a very low event rate, uh, at one year in those patients where PCI was deferred based on FFR Angio, so reassuring that you can safely defer if you get a negative FFR Angio. And we also now have randomized clinical trial data from Japan. 400 patients in the provisional trial across 13 Japanese sites looking at intermediate lesions. The primary endpoint of this study was non-inferiority of revascularization rate of FFR Angio compared with wire-based FFR. And the investigators met the primary endpoint. Uh, FFR Angio, uh, was non-inferior and had a similar, uh, revascularization rate. They also saw a significantly lower, uh, radiation exposure, 20% reduction with FFR Angio compared with wire-based. And they followed the patients now out to one year, and have shown that major adverse cardiac events, both with and without procedural MI, were, uh, equivalent, if not numerically lower, uh, with the FFR Angio group, so very reassuring data.

title: PulseCast: Highlights in Leukemias From the 2025 ASH Annual Meeting
transcription: Amir Fathi, a leukemia specialist at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts. I was fortunate to attend the American Society of Hematology meeting this last December in Orlando, Florida, where multiple presentations covering a series of topics in myeloid malignancies were provided. It was an exciting meeting. There were multiple exciting presentations. Among them, we presented the results of PARADIGM, a phase 2 randomized study that compared intensive induction chemotherapy to less intensive azacitidine and venetoclax in fit, traditionally induction-eligible patients. The study met its primary endpoint: event-free survival was better for patients who received azacitidine and venetoclax. There were also multiple secondary endpoints that were important. The rate of overall response, composite remission, was significantly higher in patients who received azacitidine and venetoclax. Patients who received azacitidine and venetoclax also tolerated treatment better, with less incidence, with lower incidence of grade 3 or higher bleeding or infectious complications, decreased time in the hospital, as well as decreased admission during their initial course to the intensive care unit. There was also better quality of life and better patient-reported outcomes. This opens the field to potentially introducing less intensive therapies for patients that are traditionally thought to receive intensive chemotherapy, the long-term standard of care in AML, which allows tolerability, safety, but also allows them to move on to curative modalities such as stem cell transplant. There was also a series of presentations on the combination of azacitidine and venetoclax and targeted therapies, such as gilteritinib, the FLT3 inhibitor, as well as multiple menin inhibitors, such as ziftomenib. These data, although early, show significant promise also in patients with acute myeloid leukemia. I look forward to future meetings and ongoing progress in myeloid malignancies. Thank you.

transcription: and they pump so much stuff into those beautiful little babies, it's a disgrace. I don't see it. I don't I think it has, I think it's very bad. Do you agree with this? I think you have to see what they recommend. Well, I think every country is different, so I think there's certainly some truth to that, but at the same time, we're also different in the fact that we're not as healthy as places like Denmark and we have lower, uh, we have higher rates of chronic disease and and they have much lower rates of chronic disease, so I think we should look to countries that are doing some things better than us and have better outcomes than we seem to have that are at least somewhat similar. title: Terence Tao on How AI Is Changing Mathematics
transcription: I'm Terence Tao, I'm director of special projects here at IPAM, the Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics. AI has really been, um, improving very rapidly. It allows me to experiment. I will try crazier things. We can vibe on the blackboard and then if there's a computation that neither of us wants to do, we can just get our AI tool to finish that. I can search literature much more accurately and effectively than I could before, so I'm doing way more AI-assisted mathematics and collaborative projects. And now, I think it's ready for prime time. Fundamentally, at OpenAI, we care about being at the frontier in terms of automating science, the economy, and ourselves. We care less about winning a Nobel Prize or a Fields Medal and more about enabling a hundred mathematicians out there to do that for themselves. We lived in a world of cognitive friction until very recently, where every task required us to use our brain. And so we didn't really think about it, we just thought this was the cost of doing something intellectual. But now we have AI and the other technologies that can bring these frictions down to zero. I hope when AI usage becomes more commonplace, people will also post not just their final product but all the different paths they used to get there, because that's also very useful information. I think we can find some way to have the best of both worlds.

transcription: My name is Prajval Moza, I'm a senior researcher at the DFKI in Kaiserslautern, Germany, and I finished my PhD last year in AI-driven image restoration as well as meta learning. And my research interest lies in teaching AI to reconstruct fine details that were never part of the image, and to do this as faithfully and efficiently as possible, and these might be blurry photos, medical scans, or even satellite images. And when AI fills in fine details that were never part of the image, then it can either stay true to reality or it can make stuff up that looks real but isn't. And in medical scans, this can mean a shape that was never part of a patient, or in natural science, it could mean a spot in a microscopic image that was never there. And my job is to keep those models honest and to tie what they add to the image so close to reality that we can actually trust what we see and not only hope it is right. Why does it matter? Well, more and more images we take nowadays is changed by AI, for instance, at the doctor, in climate sciences, in the news, or on your mobile phone even. And if we use those images to make decisions, truth has to come first, not only pretty. Um, that's what I'm working on, and thanks for stopping by, and thanks for listening.

title: Theo Vincent - Next Generation in AI Research IJCAI-ECAI 2026
transcription: Have you ever wondered if it is possible to reproduce human intelligence inside a computer? Hi everyone, I'm Théo Vincent, a PhD student at the German Research Center for AI, called the DFKI. Recent breakthroughs in generative AI are impressive, but they remain far from human intelligence, mainly because they are limited to imitating human data, and they rely on vast computational resources. My research tackles these challenges by developing algorithms that learn from experience. Learning from experience is the field of reinforcement learning, where a sequence of optimization problems needs to be solved. I proposed algorithms that solve those problems in parallel, thereby speeding up the learning process. This framework is called Iterated Temporal Difference Learning. Regarding resources, a lot of energy is spent tuning hyperparameters of learning agents. I proposed methods that adjust the agent's hyperparameters to its learning pace, thereby eliminating the need to tune hyperparameters and therefore saving resources. I'm excited about future learning algorithms that will learn from experience just as humans do. If you're interested, feel free to check my website.

title: How to Create a Journal System in Joplin | Quick Guide 2026
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to create a journal system in Joplin. Joplin is a fantastic open source note-taking app that offers a lot of flexibility and customization for keeping track of your thoughts, goals, and reflections. Whether you're an avid journaler or looking to start this beneficial habit, Joplin can help you organize your entries in a way that makes them easy to manage and review. Let's start by setting up your journal notebook. To begin, you'll need to open Joplin desktop. Once you have the application up and running, take a look at the left sidebar. You'll find a button labeled "New notebook." Go ahead and click on that. A prompt will appear asking you to enter a name for your new notebook. In this case, you should name it simply "Journal." Naming your notebook distinctly helps maintain clarity and keeps everything organized as your digital journal grows. Now that you have your journal notebook created, you can start thinking about how to organize your entries effectively. A well-structured journal system can provide insights and make reference easier over time. One effective way to structure your journal notebook is to create subnotebooks for different aspects of your journaling practice. To do this, look at the file above your journal notebook. There, you will see an option to create a "new subnotebook." For starters, you might want to create a subnotebook titled "Daily entries." This section will be where you jot down your thoughts and reflections every day. It's a space for freeform writing, capturing everything from daily events to personal reflections. Next, consider adding a subnotebook for "Weekly reviews." This section is great for reflecting on the week that just passed. It offers a valuable opportunity to see how your thoughts and experiences have evolved over the past seven days, and help set intentions for the following week. Finally, there's the "Monthly reviews" subnotebook. Monthly reviews are vital for looking at the bigger picture. They allow you to track longer-term goals and assess progress over time. Reflecting monthly provides a macro perspective of your life, habits, and achievements. When you envision this structure in Joplin, it might look like a tree, with "Journal" as the trunk, "Daily entries," "Weekly reviews," and "Monthly reviews" act as the branches extending from it, providing a clear pathway for your thoughts to spread. By organizing your journal in this manner, you create a harmonious and systematic approach that enhances your journaling practice. This customized structure caters to different aspects of life reflection, and makes it simpler for you to navigate through your thoughts and feelings. Once everything is set up, you can start using Joplin to capture your life's details, review your growth, and make journaling an enriching experience.

title: Diary Entry I Wanted To Share With ALL Footballers...
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I wanted to share with you guys a diary entry that I wrote during a time that felt like nothing was going smoothly. And you might want to save this video for later because someday you're going to need it. Recently, I've been questioning why nothing in my life seems to be going smoothly. I've been playing football at a high level for years, training harder than everybody else, taking it more seriously than ever before. And still, I'm sitting here with no confirmed answer about where I'm playing next season. Football is competitive, I understand. I have been trying to get my European visa for the past year. I made three different applications and eventually left the country hopeless. And just two days after leaving, they called me for the acceptance meeting. Just two days after I'm out of the country, probably just bad timing, right? I graduated school with a top 1% mark, went to the best university in my country, signed with a professional club, and made a system so strong it changed the lives of 300 players remotely worldwide. And yet, parents are still skeptical to work with me and delay for months just to say no. Probably just a bad coincidence, right? This might be unrelated, but I even approached a trusted brand of dental braces, and halfway through the treatment, I was the first client in company history who had manufacturing issues, so I had to restart the process. And when they sent me the new one, the package got held at customs, and now I have no idea where the $4,000 worth of dental braces are. Just simple procedures that were initially planned to run smoothly and take a few months to complete are now becoming a headache because it's taking a few years to overcome. This is the side of football, the side of life that nobody ever talks about. Every single year without fail, I go through a season like this, a stretch where nothing seems to click, where it feels like the universe itself has turned against me. And here's the lesson I learned from this and what I wanted to share with you guys today. The toughest battles in life are given to the strongest warriors, not because life is cruel but because life is precise. The moment you decide to achieve something amazing, the moment you decide to become a professional footballer, the universe will place you in difficult situations to see what you're made of, to see whether you'll push through to the other side or whether you'll make excuses, blame the system, and quietly walk away from your dream like most people do. Most footballers quit before the breakout even happens, not because they weren't talented enough but because they stopped one season too early. And here's a harsh truth: for the majority of your life, you're going to be in the fight, you're going to be grinding, uncertain if it's going to work out, waiting for the right moment, pushing through the season when nothing feels fair. And then all of a sudden, for a small percentage of your life, everything is going to start to click. You're going to be playing your best football, your confidence is going to be untouchable, the doors are going to start opening up. And that moment right there, that moment is only beautiful because of everything that came before it. The goal in football or in life is not to avoid the hard season. The goal is to refuse to leave before the season ends. You will only fail the moment you decide to quit, and that's a guarantee. So, do not stop and keep pushing till the end.

title: How to Create a Line of Credit Account in QuickBooks Online (Step-By-Step) [2026 guide]
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to create a line of credit account in QuickBooks Online. Having a line of credit account set up in QuickBooks is essential for tracking borrowed funds and repayments accurately within your financial records. Whether you're managing a small business or keeping personal finances in order, this process will help you stay organized and ensure your books are complete and up to date. If you don't already have a QuickBooks Online account, you can use the link in the description to sign up and get started. Now, let's dive into the steps. First, start by logging into your QuickBooks Online account and navigating to your dashboard. Look to the top right corner of the screen where you'll see a small gear icon. This is your settings menu. Go ahead and click on it to open the options. From the dropdown menu that appears, you'll need to scroll down and select the option labeled "Chart of accounts." This is where all your accounts are managed and organized within QuickBooks. Once you're on the chart of accounts page, look towards the upper right corner of the screen again and click the button labeled "New." This will allow you to create a new account. Next, you'll need to enter a name for the account you're setting up. You can choose something straightforward like "Line of Credit," or use a name that better suits your specific needs. It's helpful to pick a name that makes the account easily recognizable when you're reviewing your records later. After naming the account, it's time to assign the correct account type. In the dropdown menu for account type, select "Long-term Liabilities." This category is appropriate because a line of credit typically represents a financial obligation that spans longer than a year. Once you've set the account type, move to the detail type field. From this list, choose "Notes Payable." This detail type is the most accurate for a line of credit, as it represents loans or borrowings that need to be repaid. Finally, click the "Save" button to complete the process and create your new line of credit account. Once saved, the account will appear in your chart of accounts list, and you'll be able to use it to track transactions related to your line of credit. And that's it! You've successfully created a line of credit account in QuickBooks Online. If you found this video helpful, please like and subscribe.

title: Video 3: Why is sharing your radiotherapy treatment story important to you?
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: It's been really important to me all along to share my story of my treatment, my diagnosis, my treatment and my recovery, to whoever will listen, to be perfectly honest. My first desire was to tell fellow patients, and I was interviewed by a radiation oncologist. My answers to my, her questions were recorded, and those videos have been shared by doctors and other cancer team members to thousands of people who've been diagnosed with a head and neck cancer. And I'm just so grateful that clinicians have seen the value of sharing a patient's story. I think there's no substitute for a patient who's about to have radiotherapy to hear the story of a fellow patient, not only just describe what the treatment's like and the recovery's like, but just to see a patient who's survived, who's survived cancer. Because I think so many of us when we get that cancer diagnosis, we're just full of anxiety and fear, and there's nothing as reassuring as seeing a patient who's gone through it and come out the other side. But I also think it's good for cancer team members to see these videos because it, it exposes them to the emotional and psychological impact of a cancer diagnosis and the treatment. And if they can hear the patient's story, empathize, uh, understand emotionally, feel some of those feelings, I think they're much more likely to do research and make an effort to help us psychologically, which I think is as important as survival.
caption: In this audio recording, a mature female speaker with a clear Australian accent speaks passionately about the importance of sharing her experience with cancer diagnosis, treatment, and recovery. Her tone is warm, empathetic, and deeply reassuring as she describes her desire to help fellow patients overcome their anxiety and fear by seeing a survivor. She also highlights how sharing these stories can benefit cancer care teams by helping them understand the emotional and psychological impacts of the disease, potentially driving further research in psychological support. A gentle, uplifting instrumental track plays in the background, complementing her hopeful and encouraging message.

transcription: I've been coming to Integrative Acupuncture for 6 years now, I think. And, I've come for a variety of reasons, from injuries to anxiety to insomnia. And, it's been an amazing place. Um, I think the practitioners here are really great. I see Jen Ethridge. And, to have developed a relationship with her over the time that I've been working with her is really awesome. I think it's rare that you get to have those experiences, sort of, in the medical field um, to see somebody who has seen you for years, who you see on a regular basis, and really knows, sort of what you need to work on, what you want to work on. So, I really appreciate having a long-term um, partnership, I guess, with the practitioners here in the practice. Um, and, I mean, it's it's a very inviting environment. It's calm, it's really pleasant, everyone who works here is so lovely and helpful. And, those are things that, you know, you don't always find in the medical world, or the, you know, alternative medicine. So, that's been very appealing to me, as well. And, I kind of emerge from each session having, you get to think about what's happening because you're there, it's sort of a meditative experience. And, I think that is, is also interesting, and, and, and helpful in healing of all kinds. So, I appreciate that time, sort of, take to myself while this, the acupuncture is actually working on me, and helping solve the issues that I face. Um, yeah, I mean, I would recommend it. I think I just tried it because I'd heard many good things over the years, and read studies about how effective acupuncture could be. And, then coming here and seeing how it's helped, you know, from knee injuries and foot injuries from climbing, to me just having a lot of trouble with insomnia. Like, it's a kind of an amazing thing that it can work in so many different ways. Um, so, it was, I'm glad that I tried it, and I would recommend that other people try it, too. Yeah, I mean, as I said, I've been coming for 6 years, and would definitely continue as long as they are here. title: I Called My Parents and Said "I Need Help" | Logan's Story
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Before treatment, I was I was broken. I had a lot of depression, anxiety and was using drugs and alcohol to mask all that, to cope with it. I just remember feeling so hopeless. I just broke down and I called my mom and I called my dad and I said, "I need help." I remember at that moment I I still didn't feel great but I felt for the first time that I might be headed in the right direction. In terms of choosing this treatment center, I remember there was a family friend that we had. She said, "If I had a family member going through what Logan's going through, there's only one place I would send them and that was Providence." I think walking around the center and talking to different staff, you know, a lot of the clinicians made me feel like I was understood for the first time in a in almost forever. It was also fun, too. I think that's something I didn't expect is the idea that I can work on myself and I can do the tough things and I can have the groups where I tear up and I can go into individual session and talk about things I haven't talked about but at the same time with all my peers and and even a lot of the staff I was just laughing and I was having a good time. Life now is great. I don't worry people anymore. Soon after graduating Providence, I got hired and I really just started to find my purpose and find my life. The advice I would give someone that's still struggling is stop digging. Find the people in your life who care about you and ask them for help. The answers to the questions that people might have of what happens after treatment, answer themselves when you just give into the experience. So, ask for help. Uh stop digging. I promise you that you're going to be surprised with the outcome.

transcription: Let's talk about anxiety. There was a time where I wasn't just scared of food. I was terrified of it. The fear would build, turn into anxiety, and sometimes end in full panic attacks. My heart would race, my heart would spiral, and at this point, eating felt impossible for me. Even though that I knew that my body needed the food, I just couldn't because of the panic attack. This is something I have been struggle with for a long time. And at this point, I was exhausted, exhausted about living in that constant fear. Fear of food, like, normal people could eat, but why couldn't I? Why was I so scared of it? Starting medication was a big turning point for me. Of course, it didn't turn everything around overnight, but it helped quiet the panic enough for me to actually fight for my recovery. And I think I'm sharing this with you guys because I know how scared and lonely it can feel when food triggers anxiety and panic. And I just want you guys to know that you're not alone and you're not a broken human. So, for those of you who don't know where to start, just ask for the help because there is help out there. And I promise you that it can get better. And if you don't believe me, then I'm a living proof of that.

That's wonderful that I'm not missing things anymore. I do try to confirm those things with my client during the next session to make sure that there wasn't a problem. title: Just a little flower and talk therapy for my fellow moms... #Shorts #lindseybosway
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: My two boys are napping. I have my coffee and I'm going to use just Trader Joe's flowers and make a little arrangement. Let's chat motherhood. After I had my first baby, I think looking back on it, I had more postpartum anxiety than I even knew at the time. And I did not feel like myself for like 15 months. And part of that was just like no creative drive, no desire to really do anything outside of motherhood. And when I had my second, it was definitely better, but I just remember one day he was like 12 months old and I was like, "Oh, I want to make a flower arrangement." And I was like, "Oh gosh, I'm coming back." But it is wild. So, if you're not there yet, if you just had a baby and you feel like you're not yourself, I promise it gets better. And one day you'll feel like doing something again that requires energy. But it's okay if right now you just want to nap when your baby naps. So, I just made a little grid here. That'll make it easier to stick our flowers in. And once I started doing flowers when they were napping, I feel like I have so much more energy on the days that I do it. I think it's just like using your brain for something other than motherhood, and it gives me like a jolt of energy. And often times, when we're dealing with our babies or toddlers, it's such chaos. And I just find arranging flowers to be so peaceful and meditative once you really get into it. I always think about that one creator who talks about getting her pink back. And, you know, it went viral or whatever, but it's so true. And when you're a first time mom, you have no perspective on the fact that it does come back. Your second time around is a little easier because you know what's going on, and you know that it's okay to feel that way. But it can be really jarring when you have your first baby, and you don't understand that it's temporary. It really is. Like my biggest piece of advice that I give friends is just to try to remember in motherhood that everything is temporary. It's looking really pretty, but we have a lot of space to fill in. A few finishing touches here. I also think, in motherhood, it is okay if one day you want to make this huge, amazing arrangement, and the next day you don't want to. You put your kids to bed, and you spend the next hour in your bed. It's just okay. That's how it goes. And you know what I've stopped doing? Bullying myself for that. Just let myself relax. I don't ever go to a space of shame. Because you know what's not relaxing? Sitting down, trying to relax, and worrying about the fact that you're relaxing. Here she is. She's whimsical. She's fall. I love her.

title: When My Therapist Showed Up Late .... It Made Me Notice Something About Internalizing
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hey family, just wanted to share this real quick. This may be more so a message for those who internalize. And it's something that I'm picking up on in my continuous healing work, in my own personal um journey, and just growth in general, um for people who do internalize, who could relate to this. So what I'm noticing is, is that sometimes when you internalize, it could happen very subtly. You may not even realize it. And I know I wasn't, per se, and I'll share an example, like, for instance. I had a therapist that they only have a 50-minute session when you sign up with them. And I like this therapist a lot, like I feel like I'm definitely getting work done with them, right? But I noticed that they show up late on the sessions, but they do end on time. That's a thought process, right? And it's internalizing it when I'm not willing to have the conversation with that therapist, even though I think it's something I could deal with, or maybe I think it's small, or maybe I'm trying to observe it a little bit more. To not internalize that looks like having a conversation, even if you don't think that it's a big deal, or maybe you think it is, or maybe it could be a potential problem. Not internalizing that would look like having an actual conversation. And maybe that looks like me saying, "Hey, you know, I notice that our sessions, you do um come in late. You usually start late, but you end on time, and I I feel like I'm not getting the full, you know, time." And I have a few options, right? I could even ask, "Hey, could I expect that you're going to show up late during every session? And if so, if that's something that I could expect, that you normally don't come on the sessions on time, am I going to get my full 50 minutes?" That's a part of what it would look like to not internalizing it. Instead of me just thinking it, allowing it to fester without having a conversation and allowing it to potentially become a problem where I start to feel a way inside instead of having a conversation. All right? So, just just sharing that with y'all. And maybe, you know, you'll find value in that if you are somebody who internalizes.

transcription: Self-awareness helps us better understand the thoughts, emotions, and patterns that shape our lives. Here are three simple ways to deepen your self-awareness. Number one, journaling your thoughts. Sometimes clarity begins when you finally see your thoughts on paper. Number two, sitting quietly with your emotions, not avoiding them, not distracting yourself, just noticing them. Number three, asking yourself difficult but honest questions: "What triggers my stress?", "What patterns keep repeating in my life?" At American Behavioral Clinics, we believe self-awareness is one of the most important steps toward emotional wellness and personal growth. Because self-awareness isn't about perfection. It's about noticing, understanding, growing. American Behavioral Clinics, helping people better understand themselves, one step at a time.

title: The Bright Side of AI
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: With all the AI gloom and doom, I often forget how cool AI actually is. Like, what a technology, what a time to be alive. You know, like, I often have this heaviness about it, and more of this, "I gotta use this. I gotta make this work. I need to catch up with with the trends and everything, not to fall behind." And what I lose sight of sometimes is how amazing this technology is, and I just, today, I had this case of, hey, you can, you can use AI to analyze your thought patterns, like your personal thought patterns, and not only can you understand how you think, but obviously also where your blind spots are, and and how you can improve your thinking, and how, what are, what the patterns are, and this, getting this awareness about yourself, in all kinds of areas, obviously professionally, how you make decisions, but but also in private, it's such an amazing feat, to be honest. This technology didn't exist. Like, how would you else, like, get to this? Like, of course, if you do therapy for 10 years, which nobody wants, and and I'm not really a fan of it, still, there's this other person processing it, and you probably not get to the root of it. Now, you can upload hours, hundreds of hours of you interacting in in Zoom calls, whatever it is, and you can have AI analyze, find out your thought patterns, even like making your thoughts visible to yourself. And I just thought, how amazing, and this is just one use case, obviously. There's so much to be had also with this technology. It's scary. It's It puts a pressure on myself, and I guess on you as well, but it's also fabulous, and this is my, my little reminder to myself, and maybe to you, that if you, if you set aside this, this pressure, this, this fear maybe even, and and let in the, the possibilities and the opportunity a little bit more, it could be tremendously fun to interact with this technology, and and all the, the beautiful things that can come from that. See you in the next video.

title: DEPRESSION
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You really fail. Grabe ang nadudulot ng depression sa mga tao ngayon 'no? You think I care about that? Kaya minsan hindi ko maiwasang tanungin ang sarili ko. Don't you care what people think? Doesn't it bother you that people are making you out to be a joke and that I'm being included in that? Ano nga bang pakay ko? Kasi kadalasan gusto ko lahat may aakay sa'kin. Di namamalayan sa mga tanong laging sagot, ano bang malay ko? You want to be really great? Then have the courage to fail big and stick around. Lahat 'to saan papunta? Tangina sa totoo lang hindi ko rin alam kung saan ako pupunta. Babe, that's right. Do you? Nawawalang kamalayan, ayaw maiwan, ayaw ring mauna. Ayaw kong magsimula kasi huli na ang lahat. You're better than that. You really fail. Paano pa ako papalag kung sa utak ko talo na agad? You fail, you fail, you fail, you fail, you fail. Haay. Sa bugtong hininga nalipat ang pahina. Paano pa ako magpapahinga kung 'di ko naramdaman sa bawat paghinga? Now, if you know what you're worth, then go out and get what you're worth. But you gotta be willing to take the hits. Pwede ba akong magreklamo? Saan naman ako magsusumbong? Kanino ko naman ikukuwento ang lungkot na umaalulong? Wala, 'wag na baka matawag pang mahina. Lalo na't 'di pa nakikita mga dapat kong ipakita. Try again. Fail again. Fail better. Let me tell you something you already know. The world ain't all sunshine and rainbows. It's a very mean and nasty place, and I don't care how tough you are, it will beat you to your knees and keep you there permanently if you let it. You, me, or nobody is gonna hit as hard as life. But it ain't about how hard you hit. It's about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward; how much you can take and keep moving forward. That's how winning is done!

transcription: When I was alone. When I was alone, I drank everyday, so deeply depressed with so much to say. Suppressing my feelings for you, my dear, I drank and smoked and cried many tears. When I was alone, I fought all my fears. With so much to say, I had many cheers. Though I was depressed, but still on my own, I would drink and smoke and still feel alone. When I was alone, I lived with this pain. My feelings for you would cause me disdain. I drank and smoked and tried to be strong, though I love you so much, I didn't belong. When I was alone, I cried to myself, I drank and smoked and neglected my health. With tears on my face, with tears in my eyes, with so much to say you'd have me surprised. When I was alone.

The way how I feel, the way how it be, I wish I was happy, I wish I was free. Addicted to sadness, addicted to pain, I wish I was happy, I wish I was sane. I'm drinking, I'm smoking, I'm feeling depressed, though deep down inside, I'm not at my best. Chaos in the storm.

title: Are You Okay... Really?
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We ask it out of habit every single day, but we rarely listen for the truth. "How are you? Are you okay?" "Yeah, I'm fine." It's the ultimate American defense mechanism. We live in a culture that glorifies the grind, praises independence, and tells us to "fake it till we make it." So when things get heavy, our language shrinks. We reduce an entire ocean of burnout, anxiety, and quiet exhaustion into a single automatic wall. "Have you been crying?" "No, just tired." "Just tired." It's the perfect cover-up. Because nobody questions it. In a world where everyone is exhausted, it's easy to hide. But there's a massive difference between needing sleep and being tired of waking up feeling empty. Depression doesn't always look like tears or dramatic breakdowns. In reality, it looks like complete isolation. It's sitting in a crowded room in New York or a quiet suburb in Ohio, surrounded by people, yet feeling entirely invisible. It's building walls so high that even the people who love you can't reach you. "Do you want to talk about it? You can tell me anything." "No, there's nothing to talk about." When someone pushes you away, it's rarely a rejection. Most of the time, they literally just don't have the words. How do you explain a profound sadness that has no specific cause? How do you tell your family or your friends that your life looks great on paper, but feels completely hollow inside? So they say "No," hoping you'll leave them alone, but secretly praying that you won't. They don't need a lecture, they don't need a motivational speech, toxic positivity, or a 10-step plan on how to fix their life. "Do you want a hug?" "Yeah." Sometimes saving a life doesn't take a hero, it doesn't take the perfect words. It just takes the willingness to sit in the dark with someone. The most powerful thing you can say to someone who is drowning isn't "I understand." It's simply, "I'm here, and you don't have to carry this alone." Right now, millions of people are fighting battles they don't talk about. And ironically, the people who spend all their energy checking on everyone else are often the ones drowning the fastest. Do me a favor today. Don't just send a casual text asking "How's it going?" Call someone, look them in the eyes, break through the automatic answers. Because you never truly know how heavy a burden is until you offer to help hold it. Check on your people today.

The speaker discusses how common phrases like "I'm fine" and "just tired" are often used as defense mechanisms to hide deep-seated anxiety, depression, and exhaustion. He encourages listeners to move beyond casual check-ins, call their loved ones, and offer genuine presence and support, noting that sometimes saving a life simply requires sitting with someone in their darkness. title: I Won't Be Weak 💪🏽(Spoken Word Poem). #giannigrippo #spokenwordpoetry #lyricalpoetry #bjj
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I won't be weak. You gave me a voice, and yet I was weak. You taught me to stand, and taught me to speak. Though I was depressed, and though I was sad, you pushed me and loved me enough to be glad. With you by my side, the heavens would stand. My pain and my anger, my feelings command. You've been there for me and taught me enough, though there would be days I went through some stuff. The things that I saw and things that I've seen, I've struggled in silence, and that's what I mean. You stood by my side and gave me a voice, though I'm writing these words, you know it's my choice. So deeply depressed and deeply in pain, I wrote you these words with feelings I gained. You pushed me enough to fight through the shame. I took back my power and gained back my name. I won't be weak.

transcription: Crazy. You thought I was crazy for loving you much. For so many years, I would dream of your touch. My body would ooze with feelings of love. Though my feelings for you, they say is enough. But then you would lie and slander my name. They laughed and they laughed and put me to shame. You gave me a voice when I didn't feel heard. I'm deeply depressed that I wrote you these words. The things that you said that caused me to break. So misunderstood that my body would shake. You thought I was crazy for loving you well. I heard what you said, that's a story you tell. My heart and my soul were destroyed on that day. Yet my feelings for you would never go away. You slandered my name and made me look weak. So I wrote you these words with things that would speak. Crazy.

transcription: Little Robin. Our baby boy just died in his sleep. So precious and sweet, my heart it will weep. I'm aching and shaking and feeling this loss, though God has the answers, He still is the boss. Our baby was sleeping and didn't wake up. My heart has been shattered, I drank a few cups. The way that he died, so precious and sweet, I broke down and cried while feeling the heat. Our baby was tender and yet he was sweet. I cried and I cried and had to repeat. So deeply depressed and deeply in pain, though God has the answers, I just went insane. Our baby boy had magic and soul. When he passed in his sleep, I was losing control. This loss that we feeling is hard to explain. It hurt me so bad to go through this pain. Little Robin.

You make me feel happy when I was depressed, but you stood by my side and make me feel blessed. Deep in my soul.

transcription: No longer. No longer silent, I'm taking a stand. My pain, my struggles, I wish you understand. For so many years, I struggled alone. I was scared of the losses and being disowned. By turning my weakness to something to gain, no longer I'm silent, I'm fighting the pain. The years of the trauma and years of the shame, I took back my power and took back my name. Though I've been depressed and though I've been weak, I took back my power the day I would speak. The sadness, the shame, and anger I lived, by me speaking my pain, I will learn to forgive. No longer.

title: Inside the Mind of Someone Who Feels Alone | Deep Narration About Loneliness
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Sometimes the loneliest feeling isn't when you're alone, it's when you're surrounded by people and still feel like you don't belong. The room is full of voices, laughter, conversations, noise, but somehow, none of it reaches you. You smile when they look at you, you nod like you're listening, you say you're fine, because it's easier than explaining what's going on inside your head. Sometimes you hold your phone, staring at the screen, wanting to text someone, but not knowing who would understand. You start typing, then delete everything, because how do you explain a feeling you don't even understand yourself? Outside, the world keeps moving. People walk with purpose, cars pass by. Everyone seems to be going somewhere. And you wonder why you feel stuck in the same place, every single day. Loneliness isn't always silence. Sometimes it's noise that doesn't include you. Sometimes it's laughing with people, but feeling nothing inside. Sometimes it's going home and realizing, no one really knows how you feel. You sit in your room, the lights are off. The only sound is your own thoughts, and they don't stop. You ask yourself questions: Why do I feel like this? Why can't I connect? Why does everything feel so far away? But even on days like this, when the silence feels too loud, a small part of you is still there. Still breathing, still trying, still hoping. And sometimes, that's enough. Sometimes, making it through the day while feeling alone is already a victory. And maybe tomorrow feels lighter. Maybe not easier, but a little less heavy. And that small difference can keep you going. You can follow for more simple psychology explained.

title: Why Smaller Gifts Mean Big Potential
transcription: Over 50 million transactions were analyzed across 1,000 non-profit organizations globally in 2025. So that means that what we're seeing is actual donor behavior, and that's what we're going to talk about today. So what we found in all of this data is this big paradox. The average one-time gift size actually declined by 1% and the average monthly gift size in the US declined by almost 5.5%. Now that can set off some alarm bells, but here's the paradox. Uh conversion rates are rising. Uh recurring enrollment is growing up to 9% and mobile donations crossed uh 50% threshold. Social to recurring conversion doubled in email. Um what does all this mean? Well, I wanted to start by just kind of researching what other paradoxes are out there and are there any similar ones? Uh and forgive the like little history lesson here, but I found this super interesting. Uh there's this thing called the Jevons paradox. Uh back in the 1800s, this guy William Jevons, he noticed that when steam engines were getting much more efficient, right? We like crossed this threshold where steam engines were getting super super efficient. So the hypothesis was, hey, we're going to use less coal. Well, what happened was people didn't use less coal, the tech was so good that there were more and more steam engines. So everybody got a steam engine and total coal use exploded, right? So how does that relate to this? Well, we're seeing the exact same thing in fundraising right now. As the friction of giving goes down, the initial cost of entry is smaller. The volume of committed donors is really booming. And so donors aren't pulling back, they're moving faster, committing a little bit differently. Smaller upfront gifts don't necessarily mean lower donor value. Organizations that are winning in 2026 will build their revenue architecture around how donors are actually giving today. And from what we've seen in this data, it's mobile-first, it's social-driven, and also commitment-led.

title: 2026 Student Pitch Competition
transcription: Since January, these students have invested a tremendous amount of time and effort and courage in preparing for this competition. They didn't simply come up with ideas, they committed themselves to developing their concepts, refining their respective approaches, and standing before all of you here tonight to present their personal visions of a brighter future. My name is Elsa Baland and I'm the founder of Treisong. I grew up in the humanitarian field and I witnessed a lot of compassion as well as a lot of inefficiencies, which inspired me this year to take charge and change the way we deliver aid and make an impact in the world. My name is Devin Alexander and I'm the founder of OTLR. Growing up seeing athletes perform at the highest levels and suffering outside of it made me recognize the gap within athletics. With all of the tracking, the data, and the science built around the sport, at OTLR we focus on life first, performance follows. My name is Joseph Diaz and I'm the founder of Pantomime. I grew up playing mobile video games and I've always had the dream of one day developing my own video games. Over the years, I've noticed that the video game industry has turned away from its players and many video games have become half-baked. I want to bring back the meaning of quality in video games and prove that educational games can compete with the industry norm. My name is Jake Discount and I'm the founder of Athlete Insight. During my senior year of high school, all of my teammates were committing to colleges for baseball, and I was stressed because no schools were interested in me. So I built a recruiting website and it helped me land five college offers. Thousands of talented athletes each year don't get recruited for college sports, not because they aren't good enough, but because they're invisible and they don't know how to run the process. I'm excited to present Athlete Insight so we can help those thousands of talented athletes each year. My name is Marshall Mbau and I'm the founder of Vitabond. Growing up as an obese kid, I struggled with body image, confidence, and overall health. Weight loss is very difficult and the average person is often misled online with no clear instructions on how to lose weight consistently. Vitabond simplifies weight loss and automatically tracks your calories and provides clear, actionable data for continuous weight loss. I'm excited to share Vitabond with the world and help people who dream of a better body and better overall health. And finally, in first place, we have Vitabond's Marshall Mbau.
caption:
The audio begins with an inspiring, upbeat electronic musical track playing in the background as an enthusiastic male narrator introduces a student competition, noting the immense time and effort the participants have invested to present their personal visions for a brighter future. 

Next, Elsa Balland, a young woman speaking with a confident and clear tone, introduces herself as the founder of "Tray Song," sharing how her background in the humanitarian field inspired her to improve the delivery of aid. 

She is followed by Devin Alexander, a young man who speaks with a professional and direct delivery, introducing his venture "OTLR," which aims to address gaps in athletic training by focusing on life first and performance second. 

Then, Joseph Diaz speaks in a calm, thoughtful manner, explaining his passion for video games and his startup "Pantomime," which aims to bring quality back to educational gaming. 

Following him, Jake Discount delivers his pitch with high energy and persuasiveness, sharing his personal struggle with college recruiting and how it led him to create "Athlete Insight" to help other student-athletes become visible to recruiters. 

Finally, Marshall Mallow speaks with sincere empathy, opening up about his childhood struggles with obesity to introduce "Vitabond," a venture designed to simplify weight loss with clear, actionable data. 

As the presentations conclude, the music swells, and an energetic male announcer enthusiastically declares "Vitabond's Marshall Mallow" as the first-place winner, which is immediately met with loud, celebratory cheering, clapping, and applause from the crowd.

title: UNC Student Startups Pitch for Funding at the 2026 Luby Pitch Competition
transcription: So this is a really exciting day and having to work with the student startups leading up to this day makes me feel very proud of these students. They are so committed, so passionate and really bright and working on some big, complex problems in the world right now. The Lubie Pitch Competition is an annual Shark Tank style of event where student ventures compete for up to $35,000 in cash prizes to move their idea forward and put it to use for the public good. Our venture is CARES, and we are developing a smart AI-powered knee sleeve that tracks range of motion as well as other gait data to then assist with at home rehabilitation and recovery so patients can recover smarter, faster, and stronger. So, these student ventures range from science, technology, to the music and the arts. They are all across industry and beyond the funding, these students really learn skills like problem-solving, creativity, working with others, they certainly learn how to deal with working under stress and tight deadlines as well as public speaking and preparation for the pitch competition, too. We're excited about competing in this because this is just such an important event in the entrepreneurship community. We're honestly honored to be selected, and we're looking forward to networking with some of the other teams and also meeting the judges, as well. Our next steps are going to be to finalize our minimum viable product, as well as get our device out into local physical therapy clinics. And so, I love seeing them grow. I love to see them develop an idea and not only are they building skills to help themselves, but they're also moving forward with something that's going to help society at large.
