title: Taylor Frankie Paul responds to alleged domestic violence incident with ex-boyfriend
transcription: We want to turn to our new bachelorette, the breakout star of MomTok and "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives", Taylor Frankie Paul is with us. Good morning to you. Good morning, thank you. I want to hear all about your bachelorette journey, but first I want to give you the opportunity to respond to recent headlines about the alleged domestic violence incident with your ex-boyfriend. What do you want to share with us about this? Honestly, I... It's been a heavy time to see the headlines, especially during this time of the show being released and it's supposed to be really exciting time. Um, I'm a person that will always speak my truth and, you know, that's what I'm known for. And so, when the time is right, I will be. Um, but right now, just trying to be in the present moment and focus on this, and... But the thing is, my... my kids do come first. My kids come first, and so it's been like just a back-and-forth process. Trying to be here in the present moment, worrying about, you know, home and headlines. Um, it's been stressful, to be honest. We did reach out to Dakota um and he did not... We did not hear... For a statement, we did not get a response from him. Um, now we have reports that "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" has paused production on the next season. I know there's a season on right now and then season 2 was in production. Reports say it's been... It's paused. Is... Is that true? Um, honestly, I... I don't call the shots with production. So, as of now, I have gotten word that it also has been paused, but I do not call those shots, so as far as I know, it... It was, but I don't know for how long and why. And I... I know you're one of the executive producers on the show. Yeah, yeah. I got told that this... this year, and so I... I didn't know. And I was like, "What does that mean?" you know? I was like, "Um like, I think just because we share our lives and we produce like our own, you know, lives, but I don't know if that necessarily, what that... what that means, right?" And what... How do you envision your future on that show? Ah, hard to say now, right? Just because of, you know, everything going on. It's hard to see past this, I'm not going to lie. In this moment, it's just so heavy. And when your life is broadcasted out there in these headlines, it's like the end of the world. That's what it feels like, I'm not going to lie. Um, but I will say, I've... I've been here before and I got through it, and...

title: DISTURBING: Nancy Guthrie note warns to ‘be prepared to go international’
transcription:
Let's bring in my next guest who, along with other local news outlets, has been receiving letters allegedly, uh, coming from, uh, someone who knows the kidnapper, even the kidnapper potentially. Let's bring in TMZ founder, Harvey Levin. Harvey, boy, this gets weirder and weirder day by day, and this morning we wake up and we find out nobody's been arrested, nobody's in custody. We had a ton of police activity just 2 miles away from Nancy Guthrie's house, potentially within this 2-mile radius that the police have been asking, uh, for doorbell, dash cam, uh, video. First, give me your quick observation on where you think we are this morning. Is this- does this feel like a letdown?
Well, it's a letdown because, uh, they haven't caught the kidnapper and they haven't found Nancy Guthrie. Uh,
I, um, was in touch with law enforcement involved in this, uh, early this morning, um, and I asked them, uh, is- is this in any way tied to the information that we have given, uh, the sheriff and the FBI? And I was told no. Um, and, you know, as for, you know, what happened, it doesn't seem like they've kind of connected the dots. It was interesting, yesterday morning, I sensed something was going on, um, with law enforcement, that there were meetings, they have these kind of morning briefings, uh, that were going way longer, um, I just happened to find out about one of them, uh, way longer than, uh, they normally did. Um, and, you know, I figured something was up, and they were also playing everything really close to the vest. It may have been this, I don't know. What I can tell you is that the FBI is keenly interested in the ransom note that we received. Um, and, uh, I know this to be a fact. They are keenly interested because obviously, I mean, we're- we- we supplied them with it. And, um, you can kind of connect the dots if you will, but I am 100% they are extremely interested in this ransom note. And they're also interested in the person who has now sent us three, uh, emails saying in return for money, they will lead, uh, authorities to the kidnapper and Nancy. Let's dig into that for a second, because this- this is fascinating. This person claims to know where she is or at least who the kidnapper is.

title: How to protect your investments from an AI bubble | The Economist
transcription: Why is investor confidence in AI now wobbling? In recent weeks, we've seen big companies announce that they're going to spend absolutely jaw-dropping amounts of money investing in AI. And whereas previously, investors were cheering those announcements, actually lately, we've seen the stock market wobble in response. It seems like they're getting a bit worried about whether they're going to get returns on all of this money that companies are spending on this new technology. So what exactly is it that's making the stock markets jittery? Well, it's not just that investors are worried about the amounts that companies are spending, although those amounts are vast. It's kind of this feeling that we've been here before. So there are lots of times throughout history where you've had a new technology emerge and it looks like it's going to transform the world. So take railways or canals or electricity or the internet. And in all of those cases, the new technology actually did transform the world. But in the early stages, when it was just coming out, investors got overexcited. They ended up bidding up companies' share prices out of all proportion with their underlying profits. Um, and they also ended up picking the wrong firms, you know, not buying the companies that would actually benefit from this. And then even when the new technology was really successful, a lot of investors lost an enormous amount of money. And there's kind of this worry that something similar is happening again, that AI might be this transformative technology, but share prices have been bid up out of all proportion with underlying profits. So we're at a very nervous moment. What is it then that investors can do to avoid getting stuck? This is something of a puzzle because you might think the obvious answer is, "Okay, shares are too pricey, so I'm going to sell my shares." Professional investors often don't have that as an option. For example, if I manage a stock fund and I tell clients, "invest in my fund and I'm going to invest in stocks," I can't just suddenly sell them and sit on a pile of cash. I, I might actually not be allowed to, even if I am, my clients are going to ring me up and say, "What are you doing? This isn't what I'm paying you for."

title: ASRA 2026 Conference Highlights
transcription: Everybody, welcome to the 2026 ASRA conference! So, just coming back from the keynote address by Sean Wallace, I thought it was just really inspirational. Yeah, really. A nice introduction to the conference and kind of gets you thinking. It was fantastic. I think what I will take away from it is do not let anyone limit you, and as Sean said, education and knowledge can be your own destiny. I hope that when people heard my story, what they can take away is that you can achieve anything. The sky should always be the limit. Don't be frightened to dream. More importantly, if you do have success, it's always about trying to actually go to the next level. This is my first time attending. This is our first time at ASRA. It is my first time and is very much enjoyed so far. I've been coming to ASRA, so my first was about 2015. And as a company, we've been here for 25 years. But I have been about 10 or so, really enjoy it each time, it's fantastic. I think ASRA is a great network. I think having so many different universities but also different people working in the industry means that you can keep up to date with everything. Fundamentally, just seeing that we're all basically dealing with the same challenges but at the same time there's like a multitude of solutions out there, so this is just a key space in which you can kind of see what works and what's best fit for where you're going back to. I really like the fact that you can pretty much chat to anyone. This morning really good opportunities for discussion. I really like the round tables because you really kind of got into the depth of things. So today, I've been talking about AI in the media, what it is, how people can exploit it, people talking to me about how they use it in their personal lives, how they use it in their professional lives, sort of accepting that we're still in the foothills of it all yet. I really liked the session on AI and technology, that's just so current, and something that I definitely want to learn more about. Interesting topics about living black, AI, residential life team, absolutely everything, fantastic, yeah. Really well organised, people very engaged, very willing to share conversations, share ideas, and overall great experience. We're in a spectacular building in uh, well, the best city in the world, but then I'm, you know, biased. Really looking forward to tonight, we're going to the Cavern Club, you know, one of the key venues in the history of the Beatles. I've not really had much experience of Liverpool, to be honest, but I've heard good things. Can't wait to get down there and see Liverpool, we've not been here for a long time. Taking a little bite out of history. Yeah, let's see what it brings.

Further south, our Purple Line is going to make suburb-to-suburb connections easier in Prince George's and Montgomery Counties, and we're more than 90% complete on that project. This new light rail system will serve as a vital, long-awaited connector for tens of thousands of area residents, help decrease congestion, and drive economic development. In addition to light rail, commuter rail, and metro rail, the MTA also provides bus and commuter bus services, mobility para-transit services. The list goes on and on, and MTA does it all. Your teamwork has literally built the transit system that has put butts in seats, arms in waves, and oohs and aahs. title: OPT In Highlights: 2026 ICAN Women's Leadership Conference
transcription: Positive leadership is not a luxury for calm times. It is a discipline for uncertain ones. It's not a soft skill, but a strategic imperative. Today, leaders are here to learn about the power of positivity and the power that positivity can have on both our personal and professional lives. I CAN is positive. I CAN is powerful. I CAN is a way to opt into the hope that we all need for the world. Because a lot of us think about having a vision for our lives, but that vision just doesn't materialize out of nothing. We have to create it. So a great vision plan gives you clear direction. It's going to help you to define your goals, it's going to increase your motivation. Motivation, folks, doesn't come from just effort. It comes from having that meaning. One of my favorite things about I CAN is just its pure mission to help develop individuals within our communities, women primarily, but also to just reinforce that we are important and making sure that we are invested in those individuals. Because at some point we are taught and we believe that to be in charge means to have the answers, and that might get you promoted one day, but it will make you less valuable every day. The only way that we overcome blind spots is that we operate in a frame of curiosity. I think women leadership conferences like this makes us pause and really be able to get up on the balcony and be strategic about wow, I'm doing all this work, but what am I doing to take care of myself? What am I doing to mentor or support other women in my life? It's an intentional way to pause and really, really connect. And we find that optimism is a fuel for nearly every aspect of our lives. You're more likely to survive a cancer diagnosis if you're optimistic, your children will do better in school, it runs the whole gamut. And when we broadcast this kind of mindset to other people, it changes them for the better as well. Technology is a tool that we can use to enhance our humanity. To not get too caught up, like I CAN, in the latest release from Claude or some technology or this is going to be the thing that fixes my team that we use, don't ever forget, the most important competitive advantage each and every one of you has is your humanity.

title: Gen AI in Libraries Conference Poster on AI Tools for Literature Reviews: A Rubric for Evaluation
transcription: Our poster presentation documents the creation of a rubric by a group of librarians at American University to evaluate which AI tools, if any, made sense for us to subscribe to and promote. We ended up creating this rubric ourselves because we couldn't find an already extant tool that fit our needs, and we thought detailing our process might be helpful to other institutions currently considering the adoption of AI tools. Our university librarian asked our department to pilot an AI research tool. This group then decided to review AI tools focused on the literature review process. Literature review tools were selected for a few reasons. One, they're discipline agnostic. We're a social science heavy institution, which tends to be pretty interdisciplinary. Two, faculty, students, and staff all do literature reviews. And three, there are a number of AI tools with literature reviews built specifically in mind. In order to determine how we would evaluate these tools, we met as a group and discussed what we would want a rubric to measure. We reviewed some of the literature related to this, there wasn't much, and determined the questions by consensus. We then created a survey in Qualtrics. We divided up the list evenly between group members, with some claiming tools in which they were particularly interested or had experience with. Then, each member analyzed three to four tools and recorded the results in Qualtrics. Ithaka, the nonprofit behind JSTOR, has created the Ithaka Generative AI Product Tracker that lists generative AI tools that can be used for postsecondary teaching, learning, or research activities. The tracker includes roughly 150 AI tools and counting, many of which support key stages of the research lifecycle, including discovery, understanding, and creation. We went through the entire list and identified 18 AI tools that could help in the literature review process in subject areas within the curriculum at AU. We then developed a shared evaluation framework based on eight criteria. They include, one, access model, whether the tool is free or subscription-based...

title: CVPR 2026 : CrowdGen
transcription: Let's talk about this paper titled Generative Adversarial Perturbation with Cross-Paradigm Transferability on Localized Crowd Counting. We have seen evasion attacks on all kinds of vision tasks, classification, face recognition to name a few, but crowd models are relatively less explored. They are more complex than the classification task, but they inherit the same weakness that other deep vision models suffer. And most importantly, they are widely deployed in real life scenarios such as public safety, retail analytics and so on. So an undercounting attack could be a safety risk. As we can see a clean example on the right, while passed by a model it outputs 428 people and their locations. However, if small adversarial perturbation is added, it slashes this prediction by over 40% and we get 285 people. So, the previous studies on crowd models are mostly patch-based attacks and they are limited to only density map-based models. So naturally, the question emerges is that can adversarial perturbations transfer across heterogeneous localized crowd counting paradigms such as density map and point regression models? So, to accomplish this attack, we design a perturbation generator that takes clean image as input and outputs the perturbation noise, and this noise is added to the clean image to produce the adversarial image. For black-box transferability, we design a loss function keeping the transferability, imperceptibility and effectiveness goal in mind. Our hypothesis is that even though these models vary by outputs, they share similar backbone architecture such as VGG, ResNet and same weights. So, we our, we hypothesis that this drives the transferability. On the other hand, the crowd scenes are low-frequency dominated, so we suppress the high-frequency and magnitude of the noise for, for subtle perturbation. And lastly, the effectiveness between two paradigms of models come from model-specific loss. So, density map models do the density suppression, and point regression-based models perform logit suppression. Together, this combined loss govern the training. So, this is a sample instance of adversarial examples, where adversarial perturbations are added to the clean images for various lighting conditions.

Her presentation is structured, formal, and clear, with no background noise, indicating a professional recording environment. She introduces her team's methodology, which involves a perturbation generator designed with a loss function that balances transferability, imperceptibility, and effectiveness. The speaker details how the shared backbone architectures of different models facilitate transferability, how they suppress high-frequency noise to maintain subtlety, and how model-specific losses (density and logit suppression) are combined to govern training. She concludes by showing sample adversarial examples under various lighting conditions.

title: VeriSHAP 5min Summary Presentation
transcription: Hi there, I'm David, and in the next few minutes, I present a short summary of our paper VerifySHAP, or VerySHAP for short, on computing provable bounds for the exact Shapley values of neural networks. SHAP is a popular feature importance technique that can help us explain deep neural networks. The goal is, for example, to find out what influence an input feature, such as the arrow in this image, has on the prediction a neural network makes. SHAP provides such importance scores by computing what is called the Shapley value of each input feature. So, for example, for this arrow feature, we look at a combination of the other features, once with the arrow present, here in yellow, and once with the arrow absent, here in pink. We then use a value function V to mask out the missing features and evaluate the network on that new input with the masked-out features. We then subtract the network output we get when the arrow is absent from the output we get when the arrow is present to compute what is called the contribution delta of this arrow feature. However, SHAP does not only look at one such combination of input features, but looks at all of the combinations of the other input features that we can have. This means that computing Shapley values requires enumerating an exponential number of these feature combinations that are also called coalitions. Because this clearly does not scale very well, previous work has investigated different statistical estimators that only sample a certain number of coalitions. While this is a lot more scalable, these techniques don't necessarily tell us how far off they are with an individual estimate, which can be problematic in sensitive applications. Additionally, for empirically evaluating these SHAP estimators, we need to know the ground-truth exact Shapley values. For these reasons, we introduce VerySHAP, a new algorithm for computing the exact Shapley values of neural networks faster on higher-dimensional feature spaces, and computing guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Shapley values using ideas from neural network verification. The key idea from neural network verification that we leverage is bound propagation. Bound propagation allows us to propagate an entire set of input features, such as this entire coalition space, through the contribution function. And then we obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the contribution. We can then plug these bounds into the SHAP equation, and obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the Shapley value itself.

The recording environment is highly controlled and quiet, with no noticeable background noise or distractions, ensuring excellent audio quality. He explains the concepts of feature importance, Shapley values, and the computational challenges involved, introducing his method as a solution that leverages neural network verification and bound propagation to establish guaranteed lower and upper bounds.

title: Short Introduction of NeighborMAE (CVPR 2026)
transcription: Hello everyone, I'm Liangcong from KU Leuven. I'm glad to present our work, Neighbor MAE: Exploiting Spatial Dependencies between Neighboring Earth Observation Images in Masked Autoencoder Pre-training. The main idea of this work is simple. In Earth observation, images are not isolated samples. They are observations of the continuous Earth's surface. So instead of training masked autoencoder on each image independently, we ask whether neighboring images can provide useful spatial context for masked autoencoder pre-training. Masked image modeling has become a popular self-supervised learning strategy for Earth observation. The model masks parts of an image and learns to reconstruct the missing region. However, most existing MIM methods reconstruct a single image tile independently. This is a simplification of Earth observation data because satellite and aerial images are naturally spatially connected. Neighboring images often share useful information, such as terrain structure, land use, continuity, roads, buildings, and infrastructure patterns. At the same time, neighboring views may also differ in acquisition time, viewpoints, or sensor conditions. This means neighboring images provide varied signals, shared spatial context, and natural variations. Therefore, we ask: can neighboring images provide useful context for masked image modeling? To answer this question, we propose Neighbor MAE, which extends MAE from single image reconstruction to joint reconstruction of neighboring Earth observation images. The method has five main components. First, neighbor sampling: we use geospatial metadata to sample neighboring Earth observation images based on the intersection over union of the spatial footprints.

He is presenting a paper titled "Neighbor MAE: Exploiting spatial dependencies between neighboring Earth observation images in masked autoencoder pretraining." His speech is clear, measured, and formal, suitable for an academic presentation. The recording quality is high, with no background noise, allowing his voice to come through clearly as he explains the core ideas and methodology of his research. He highlights the spatial connection between neighboring Earth observation images and explains how Neighbor MAE extends masked autoencoder pretraining through techniques like neighbor sampling based on geospatial metadata.

title: Dr. Mani Menon Receives the 2026 AUA Ramon Guiteras Award
transcription: The final award of the evening is the Ramon Guiteras Award, our highest honor, recognizing outstanding contribution to both the art and science of urology. For pioneering contributions in robotics resulting in a paradigm shift to the surgical treatment of prostate cancer, Dr. Mani Menon. President Palmer, President-elect Reed, past and future presidents, fellow awardees, and guests. Thank you. Shira Ruben, my official AUA handler, tells me that the Guiteras Award has been given since 1970, but that only three people in its history have swept all three AUA awards: the Gold Cystoscope, the Hugh Hampton Young, and the Guiteras. Pat Walsh, who hired me as his first resident and regretted it ever since, Darracott Vaughan, who hired me as his first faculty member and withdrew the offer after a disastrous interview, and Bill Catalona, my chief resident, who for 50 years has been telling me how wrong I am. Now we're four. That is humbling company. Shira also says that the only reason that I can say this with a straight face is that until 1975, the Gold Cystoscope Award was given to the best golfer in the AUA, which would have ruled out all four of us, except maybe Bill. Before I go further, I have been nominated four times for the Guiteras Award. The North Central Section, where I did the bulk of my work on robotic surgery, nominated me three times. The New York Section, my new home, made it stick. Lane Palmer and Steve Kaplan saw it through.

He speaks slowly and deliberately, with a touch of humor and humility, clearing his throat occasionally. He expresses gratitude to the urology community, acknowledges the AUA leadership, and shares lighthearted anecdotes about the award's history and his mentors who supported his journey.

title: 2026 SAI Conference Speaker: Marlon Styles, Jr
transcription: How are you, everybody? This is Marlon Styles coming to you from the great state of Ohio. Big fan of Iowa sports, just for the record, go Hawkeyes. I will also share that I'm a product of Geraldine Watson, my grandmother. She taught me the importance of caring for people and pouring into community that I find myself in, so I'm excited to be part of the SAI community and pour into you as educators and leaders. A little bit of background about me, I'm an old-school math teacher at heart, love all things middle school. I've ventured into middle school administration, been a curriculum and instruction director at a big urban system here in Southwest Ohio. One of my favorite jobs was dreaming up experiences with kids, not for kids, but with kids. Transition into a superintendent role in Middletown City School District here in Southwest Ohio, was there for six years. Had a great run there, did some amazing things with the staff and the community for kids. Past several years, I've been out working with school districts across the country, just being a little source of inspiration for the staff, but also helping them dream up big visions and big experiences for kids that they're serving. So, excited to be part of the family, excited to be part of the community, and looking forward to our time here in August. What I'm really excited about with this first session around strategic decision-making in an AI-enabled world is very simple, right? We are responsible for thinking about our students and helping to build futures alongside them that they will be able to find themselves experiencing a great deal of success. With that comes a responsibility as executive directors to be able to make very important, critical decisions at key strategic moments so that our students can find immediate success, and the initiatives and the big moves that we make, they deliver the impact that we're looking for. So, my passion around this work comes from just serving a diverse group of kids. Our students have aspirations and are showing us every day who they want to become. This session is purely about making sure that we convene the right expertise to help dream up the right types of experiences that will align with the aspirations of our students. This session here around career connectedness, right, this is a hot topic across the country. One of the most emerging topics alongside AI is CTE for all. For me, it's not just an emerging topic, but this is a personal conversation, something I'm really passionate about. When I was younger, I never had anyone in a K-12 education environment ever ask me what I wanted to be when I grow up. I mean, think about the baggage that I carried with me

title: Dr Prashant Mishra on Trust, AI & Healthcare | AI Media Conference 2026
transcription: Look for me specifically, and I'll wear my professional hat to answer this question. Obviously, I tend to think in the context of AI and healthcare, right? So the information that we see flowing in the healthcare domain is how I would relate to AI. And considering the fact that AI obviously could offer you the speed, could give you information, but at the same time if it is misinformation, then the velocity with which AI could amplify, could disseminate things, that's also something to think about, especially in the context of health. I think it's very different, right? A simple typo doesn't mean an error, a simple typo could actually mean an effect on patient, could do with the life and death of the patient. Think about the consequences of that misinformation on a particular patient, their caregivers, families, and say, for example, the population at large. So, I tend to look at AI from that particular lens, considering that I come from the medical publishing background. So, I think that's how I look at it. I think our responsibility has always been there since ages, and if I think about my organization, our legacy goes back to almost 180 years back, and we've we are known for the trustworthy information that we produce. What happens in the real world settings, in order for you and your audience to understand, there is the research which happens, right? Now, research, many times is being done so as to improve the patient outcomes. So, there has to be a translation of that research into clinical practice, but ultimately, keeping at the center of it, the patient outcomes. How does it benefit or harm the patient? That's what you are really trying to do. So, our role had has always been very important since ages, but I think with the current times, and I would not even say with the current times, world has been evolving

title: #impressions: emergenCITY Week 2026 | Reflections, Outlooks & Research Findings
transcription: It's really my pleasure to welcome you all to our Emergent City Week 2026. The focus this year is going to be on what we achieved mostly over the last year. I would want to start with this famous quote by Martin Luther King, "We may have all come on different ships, but we're in the same boat now." So we have quite a number of different disciplines, so we are rather interdisciplinary in Emergent City. We have quite a number of international researchers that came to Darmstadt to work on Emergent City. And this is really something where I'm, I'm proud of, that this boat, that Emergent City, is basically sailing on a very nice trajectory. This LOEWE Center is an absolute success story. Funded by the state of Hesse since 2020, TU Darmstadt has been working together with its partners to find solutions for making our cities safe in times of crisis. Well, resilient systems today is a very hot topic. If you see what happened one year back, with the blackout in Spain, there were about nine hours without electricity, so it was really chaotic at the system at this point, as people want to commute, and said, "Yes, we need something which is resilient." Well, then, you had the COVID before, the supply chain did not work anymore, and you see, "Okay, you cannot really rely on everything." And just recently, with the terrible war there, and the Strait of Hormuz, which is closed, also means to be resilient is something which we have to take much more into account today than even 20 years back. We see that we have more and more technology, information technology, we have better data, we have also better models, we have a better understanding, we saw. But at the same time, of course, we also see that the number of disasters and their impact continue to grow. If you then look at Emergent City and what this means, well, it is an established center that contributes to resilient infrastructures. And it's not kind of building something like this now in response to all of these crises that are there, you know? It's already there and it's operating for many years. So, that's, one could argue, quite ahead in terms of...

title: [CORDiALL Conference] 16th April 2026 - Leanne Townsend
transcription: Okay, here we go. All right. So, next up, we're going to hear about the costs and benefits of digitalization on small-scale and diversified farms. And these insights are coming from our Living Lab in Scotland. And I should introduce myself, so I'm Leanne Townsend from the James Hutton Institute, and I've done this work with my colleague, Christina Noble, who's also here today, also from James Hutton. Okay, I thought I'd figured out which button it was, but... Okay, all right. Closer, okay. All right. So, just a little bit of background, then, first about small farms in Europe. So, small farms across different European regions face a number of similar challenges, including geographical remoteness, aging, increasingly aging populations, and outmigration of young people, uh, scales of production, and access to markets. And we know that these challenges can also have a wider impact on the resilience of the rural communities to which they belong, uh, partly because, of course, small farms are important sources of local employment, especially in regions where there are a lot of small farms, and they also contribute more broadly to their local communities and their local economies. And small farms across these regions are facing urban-rural but also intra-rural and agricultural digital divides. And by this, I mean that the benefits of digitalization are not realized in the same way by all different types of farms, uh, for example, small farms versus large farms. So, for many years now, I'm sure that those of you who have been working in digitalization for some time are familiar with these, uh, promises of digitalization, that smart farming technologies will, uh, such as variable rate precision farming, smart sensors, drones, increasingly AI applications, will be revolutionizing agriculture. And we have seen some evidence of better productivity, yield, and cost savings. Obviously, we've heard about that over the last few days, as well as evidence that these technologies can support environmental sustainability on farms as well, but the evidence does tend to be mixed. And we've already heard some nice examples of that this morning from, uh, Alexia and Germán.

title: Our Teams at DATE 2026
transcription: Hello from Verona, Italy. We're currently at DATE, the Design, Automation, and Test in Europe conference, one of the biggest conferences in the field of design automation, and a venue which is very relevant to our research. In this video, we are featuring the contributions we're making to this conference. Have fun. Hi, my name is Patrick, and in our work, we investigate how to compile quantum circuits for superconducting bus resonator architectures. This architecture, developed by IQM Quantum Computers, promises all-to-all connectivity. However, this comes at the cost of move operations. To address this overhead, we propose two solutions: one, an exact solution for small circuit instances, and two, a linear heuristic that scales to large circuits of practical size. Hi, I'm Ludwig, and here at DATE, I present our work on making ZX circuit extraction hardware-aware. So, we use a ZX calculus framework, and we adapt the circuit extraction step to make it more suited for certain hardware constraints. And this way, we achieve higher fidelity for our resulting circuits. Hi, I'm Damian, and in my work, I try to find ways to make quantum algorithms optimization work better and faster on real quantum computers. Hi, I'm Michael, and today I'm presenting my paper regarding logic synthesis. We've developed a methodology that can compute databases of optimal Boolean networks regarding switching characteristics. title: Ultrasound-CLIP(CVPR 2026)
transcription: Hello, everyone. I'm Jiayin Jin from Hangzhou City University. Today, I'm excited to present our CVPR 2024 paper, UltrasoundCLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding. Ultrasound is one of the most widely used imaging modalities in clinical practice. However, ultrasound vision-language learning remains under-explored because of heterogeneous diagnostic attributes and weak image-text alignment. To address this problem, we propose a semantic-aware ultrasound vision-language framework, together with a large-scale ultrasound image-text dataset. Unlike natural images, ultrasound images are highly challenging for vision-language learning. First, ultrasound diagnosis involves heterogeneous diagnostic attributes. For the same lesion, radiologists may describe multiple diagnostic attributes, such as echogenicity, margins, internal characteristics, and calcification. Second, ultrasound images from different organs often look visually similar, even though they correspond to completely different anatomical structures and diagnostic semantics. Because ultrasound image-text pairs often exhibit weak semantic alignment, directly applying conventional CLIP-style contrastive learning is insufficient for ultrasound understanding. This motivates the need for semantic-aware ultrasound representation learning. To address these challenges, we first construct US365K, the first large-scale dedicated ultrasound image-text dataset. The dataset contains over 364,000 image-text pairs collected from more than 11,000 clinical cases, spanning diverse organs and pathological findings. More importantly, we introduce UDT, which stands for Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Taxonomy. UDT standardizes both anatomical hierarchy and ultrasound diagnostic attributes, providing structured semantic knowledge for ultrasound understanding. This taxonomy serves as the semantic foundation of our framework.

She introduces herself and enthusiastically presents her team's paper for CVPR 2026, titled "Ultrasound CLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-Training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding." Her speech is articulate and well-paced, outlining the challenges of ultrasound image-text learning and presenting their dataset "US365K" and "UDT" taxonomy. A light, upbeat instrumental music track plays softly in the background, adding an engaging and polished feel to the presentation.

title: Giulia Carvalhal: I Chose Research Before I Chose the U.S. | MetaCast Cuts!
transcription:
I think that for most students research is actually just a step to go to a clinical, clinical career, right, in the United States. But for me, was actually the opposite. I choose the US due to research. So, first, I choose medicine because of research. So, during my biological classes, I was always fascinated about the discovery of new drugs, the discovery of new medications to treat new diseases, so that really resonated with me. So, that's honestly why I choose to do medicine because I could do, I could take care of my patient, but also I could discover something else, you know. I could impact so many patients that I couldn't see.
That makes sense. Yeah.
Yeah. And regarding like the struggles that I had during medical school, yeah, so I joined my medical school in 2019, and like six months after that, COVID happened and my university got full locked down, so all classes were online and I was actually very unmotivated, right? I mean, it's really different to having classes about histology through a camera, through Zoom, from Meets. So, I was very unmotivated, I almost gave up of medicine for a quite a while. But, something really stick with me, which was research.
Yeah.
And...
It motivated you to keep going.
Yeah, it motivated me to keep going. So, I started searching, what I could do right now, right, during COVID, what I could do to keep my research going, to pursue this dream. So, I did mainly two things. I, I joined an AI interest group and also I got involved in that COVID cohorts as well.
Yeah, it's interesting. There is something I want to talk about because most people who join the Meta-Analysis Academy, they join it because they've been so frustrated about research experiences and trying to do research in their medical schools and it's so hard and you don't have mentors and you don't know how to do it, no one will teach you. And, and there's then there's also a group like yourself who have actually been successful in doing other types of research, but they also want to learn how to do meta-analysis. So, before we talk about your incredible journey in meta-analysis, I want to, I want to talk a little bit more about these other projects that you've done. I mean, you were just in the beginning of medical school, maybe second or third year when, when you did this COVID cohort. Tell us how you got involved in that, you know, the types of publications that you got. What was your role in these projects? Because medical students from all over the world, they are always interest, they always want to do research, but it's tough, you know, you're from Paraíba, Brazil, and people from India, from, you know, Pakistan, from Colombia, they have the same struggles.

title: Introduction to the Optim.AI™ test
transcription: Opti-My can be captured, the workflow of Opti-My can be captured in a four step process. So, basically we first start off with sample collection where we isolate live cancer cells from different tumor types such as biopsy resections, ascites or pleural fluids and blood or bone marrow aspirates. So, we then perform an ex vivo sensitivity test on the isolated cancer cells by treating them with 12 drugs in a mix of combinations based on proprietary design. So, we then measure the cell viability and use it for Opti-My analysis which then generates a final test report that ranks the top single, two, three and four drug combinations including any relevant clinical trial references. So, the main parameter that we are using is normalized cell viability or NCV score. This NCV score quantifies cell killing from zero to one after measuring the amount of viable cells left after drug treatment. So, NCV score of zero indicates that all cancer cells are killed, highlighting increased sensitivity to the treatment and vice versa if the NCV score is closer to one. Basically, I think as long as we can get a sample of the tumor tissue, we can test all cancer types. Yes. So, I think in our experience in our lab is more than 20 plus cancer types including cancer of unknown primary and some even very rare cancers we have also processed them before. Right now, for our Opti-My test we do short-term culture of the tumor cells. So, for hematological cancers we seed and within 24 hours we will do drug treatment. So, there is no real opportunity for the cells to have to grow or whether or not for them to die off too much. So, for solid cancers, it's a bit longer.

She speaks in a professional, clear, and informative tone. She then explains the Normalized Cell Viability (NCV) score, which ranges from 0 to 1, where a score of 0 indicates maximum cell death. Next, she addresses the scope of the test, stating that any cancer type can be tested as long as a tumor tissue sample is available. Finally, she describes the short-term culture process, noting that hematological cancers are treated within 24 hours, while solid cancers take slightly longer.

title: 2nd National Convention on Medicine & Law 2016 | 4th Sept'16 | National Law for Ambulances
transcription: So, if the question is, do we need a national law for ambulances, what is your answer? Yes. Yes. My answer is yes, but with a caveat and that is any ambulance in isolation can never save lives. If you create laws, they should be not towards creating ambulances of people, it should be towards saving lives. And we have a great statistics of road traffic accidents and how lives are lost because people don't work in system, they work in isolation. Road engineering is different, Motor Vehicle Act is different, hospitals are different, ambulance services are different. So, the first point is the answer is yes, but national ambulance law by itself is never going to be adequate, that's my first point that I want to tell. And why is it... say this? Because any emergency medical service should not be becoming an ambulance transportation company. It is created to reduce the mortality and morbidity of emergency medical conditions. It should never be judged by number of trips that you've made. It should be judged by the accident mortality that you reduced, or morbidity that you reduced, if it was used for injury, or it was for MI, or for some other condition, you should find out at the end of the day, has it actually impacted. If you look at the chain of survival, there are different steps: access, care, transportation, care during that transportation, where they reached at the post... at the end of that transportation, how are they triaged at that point, how are they treated, and then how are they disposed, either in the form of transfer, transportation or a discharge from that facility. So if I look at this, ambulances form one very small piece of this chain of survival. And therefore, it's very essential to learn from what has happened historically in countries where EMS is still evolved, or emergency medical systems are evolved, that if you keep ambulances in isolation and don't link it up with the hospital-based care system, you will never attain your goals. In our country there are lots of important challenges and I just want to share what are the important things. If I look at emerge...

They had higher rates of those things that you see there, but the really characteristic feature of Gen Z is very, very high rates of psychological disorders. And it's not all psychological disorders. title: Event 201 Press Clips Johns Hopkins University Pre covid
transcription: It began in healthy-looking pigs, months, perhaps years ago. A new coronavirus spread silently within herds. Gradually, farmers started getting sick. Infected people got a respiratory illness with symptoms ranging from mild flu-like signs to severe pneumonia. The sickest required intensive care, many died. At first, the spread was limited to those with close contacts: healthcare personnel, co-workers, and families. But now it's spreading rapidly throughout local communities. International travel has turned local epidemics into a pandemic spanning the globe. One of these days, one of these epidemic events will be a pandemic, a fast-moving pandemic. And mitigating risk and impact of that pandemic will require an all-hands-on-deck approach. And we know from past responses that public-private cooperation will be essential. We're at the start of what's looking like it will be a severe pandemic. And there are problems emerging that can only be solved by global business and governments working together. Experts agree unless it is quickly controlled, it could lead to a severe pandemic, an outbreak that circles the globe and affects people everywhere. We could be looking at double the number of cases in one week, and 16 times as many in a month if we are not able to stop the spread. That would be on the order of half a million cases and it would continue to rise exponentially. In three months, we could be approaching 10 million cases. We have known about SARS-like viruses in animals and people for decades but have not been successful at developing a licensed vaccine. And sure, there are new technologies that may help. But it's going to be difficult. I am not optimistic about having a vaccine in time to be relevant during this pandemic. How should governments, business, and international organizations allocate and distribute pandemic antivirals and medical supplies to the people who need them most? People are avoiding public spaces out of fear of infection and in compliance with public health recommendations. This has had a dramatic effect on the retail and service sectors. Businesses of all kinds are struggling to operate, let alone provide basic services, as their workers have fallen sick or refuse to come to work.

transcription: Hi, my name is Laura Asfeller, I'm a patient advocate with Kidney Cancer Association. I'm here today with Dr. Precious Apurum, from the University of Utah, and Dr. Apurum, if you can share with us a little bit about your study and how it relates to what we're talking about today at IKCS. Our work for today, this poster, is basically on clear cell renal cell carcinoma, which is a very lethal disease. So, in the, in the world of kidney cancer, this is the most common one, that is also metabolically active, and right now the five years survival rates for patients with this is 14%, which we can tell is like very low because 14% of, 14 individuals out of 100 people are alive after five years, which is something we, we definitely see that we have to do better on in terms of the research in this area. And obesity happens to be the number one risk factor for clear cell renal cell carcinoma, but we don't understand how the mechanisms or how it associates to clear cell. Um, so in my lab, we study mitochondria. Mitochondria is the powerhouse of your body that makes the ATP, the energy that you need to work. So, after eating, your body metabolizes the substrates and the nutrients to make energy. And so, mitochondria is that organelle in the body, so in the cell, that is responsible for doing that. So, however, we've seen that as a common feature in cancer cells, but, and it influences, of course, energy metabolism and cell survival. title: Poster Interview (Clip) - Michael Harrison - 2025 IKCS: North America
transcription: Hi, my name is Laura Espeller and I'm a patient advocate with the Kidney Cancer Association and I'm here today with Dr. Michael Harrison uh from Duke and we're going to be discussing his study. So Dr. Harrison, please share with us a little bit about your quality of life study. Um sure, so this is the Odyssey prospective observational study. We named it Odyssey because we really wanted to focus on the patient journey. So it's a little bit unique in that the primary endpoint is actually around patient reported outcomes and so the gap that it really fills is that you know, and I have this in here, but uh in in the different pivotal clinical trials of which there are about four of approved therapies, they use different instruments, different patient-reported outcomes instruments. So these are like things like asking about pain, you know, are you having fatigue, other either symptoms from the cancer or side effects from the treatment. So we wanted to really focus on the patient experience but also in the real world because we know that clinical trial patients tend to be less sick and just kind of different overall than our real-world patients. Um so that that's the basis of the study and what this poster is really focusing on is those patients who got systemic therapy. So kind of the the commonly FDA-approved um four different regimens that are IO-based, so meaning with a PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor. And so we wanted to describe their characteristics and look at their quality of life and then and then what's a little bit unique is we have the ability to ask physicians, you know, in addition to asking patients how they were feeling and functioning, asking physicians why are you doing what you're doing? Um and then look at starting doses. Interesting. So uh so you are taking the patient report outcomes or PRO tools to make sure that uh patients were having the responses that we that you wanted to see and then influencing treatment decisions it sounds like potentially as well? Right. So this this is a baseline analysis. So we don't This is not reporting the longitudinal PROs meaning patients how how they're feeling and functioning over time. This is just looking at the baseline and some of the baseline characteristics. Um but yes, in future analyses, such as at GU ASCO which is in San Francisco next February

title: S9, Ep 12- What’s Coming For Rheumatology: Why Conferences Like EULAR Matter for Patients
transcription: Be inspired, supported, and empowered. This is the Global Healthy Living Foundation Podcast Network. Welcome to the Health Advocates, a podcast that breaks down major health news of the week to help you make sense of what's happening in the healthcare world. I'm Steven Newmark, Chief Policy Officer at the Global Healthy Living Foundation. And this week, I'm recording from London, where I'm attending one of the world's largest rheumatology conferences, EULAR, the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology. Now, if you're not in medicine or research, you might hear the word conference and picture doctors sitting through endless PowerPoint presentations and drinking too much coffee. And yes, there is definitely some of that going on here. But conferences like EULAR are actually incredibly important for patients because this is where new science gets unveiled, researchers and clinicians exchange ideas, pharmaceutical companies present emerging therapies, and patient voices increasingly shape the future of care. And for organizations like GHLF, these meetings are not just about networking, they are about making sure the patient perspective is present in rooms where important healthcare decisions and innovations are taking shape. So today, I want to pull back the curtain a little bit and explain what actually happens at conferences like EULAR, why they matter for patients, and some of the major themes already emerging this year, including artificial intelligence and the growing excitement around CAR T and cell therapies for autoimmune diseases. Let's start with the basics. One of the most important things that happens at EULAR is education. Thousands of rheumatologists from around the world gather to hear the latest research and clinical updates. And medicine changes very quickly, as we all know. New drugs emerge, new safety information develops, researchers discover new ways to diagnose and treat disease. For practicing doctors, conferences are often one of the fastest ways to stay current, and this matters directly to patients because the doctor sitting in front of you next month may change how they approach treatment based on something they learned this week at EULAR. That can mean earlier diagnoses, better disease management, more individualized treatment approaches,

title: [CVPR 2026] MoECLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-shot Anomaly Detection
transcription: Zero-shot anomaly detection, which aims to detect anomalies in unseen categories, has recently attracted significant attention. In this work, we propose MOE-CLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection. To perform zero-shot anomaly detection, existing studies primarily use pre-trained CLIP models and apply adapter fine-tuning methods to adapt them to the anomaly detection task. However, conventional approaches process all patches in a monolithic, patch-agnostic manner, without considering the unique characteristics of each patch, such as background patches or anomalous patches. To address this, we propose MOE-CLIP, a mixture-of-experts-based CLIP adaptation method that dynamically selects the most suitable expert for each patch. However, simply applying a mixture-of-experts framework leads to a functional redundancy problem among experts, where multiple experts learn highly similar representations instead of diverse knowledge. Therefore, we further propose FOFS and ETF loss, which encourage each expert to learn distinct and complementary knowledge. Here is the framework of our proposed MOE-CLIP. First, the mixture of LoRA experts module is inserted into the vision encoder layers, enabling dynamic expert selection and adaptation according to the characteristics of each image patch. The approach for achieving expert specialization, FOFS, is a technique applied at the input stage that enforces role separation among experts through the LoRA A matrices. Specifically, it decomposes the input feature space into multiple orthogonal subspaces, forcing each expert to observe only its own unique information without physical overlap with other experts.

title: Exercise Physiologists flex and grow at national conference in Adelaide
transcription: My name is Katie Linden, and I'm the CEO at Exercise and Sports Science Australia, or ESSA. We represent over 10,000 members, including the allied health profession of exercise physiology. And I'm here today at our national conference, Activate, where we have over 800 clinicians from around the country here today to discuss research, emerging practice, and innovative models of care. My name is Jackson Howie, I'm a PhD candidate from the Centre for Heart Rhythm Disorders at the Adelaide University. I presented some of our work in pacemaker patients. It was a simple clinical question looking at the relationship between pacemaker-detected physical activity and objective exercise tolerance. I tried to tailor this to the exercise physiologists here at this meeting. It's a good opportunity for me to disseminate and share some of our research among exercise physiology colleagues. I've met some colleagues, early, early career stages all the way up to some more senior colleagues. This is a perfect opportunity to share some of our work with the broader exercise physiology community. Many of the members I've been speaking with over the last few days have echoed a very strong sentiment that we're hearing across our 10,000-strong membership, and that is the frontline challenges that businesses are facing in providing care to an increasing demand of the community for health service access. When the GST legislation was first introduced, exercise physiology was an emerging discipline. Soon afterwards, we were added to the Medicare Benefits Schedule, and we are recognized as an essential health service. But unfortunately, through a mix of timing and a legacy issue, we are still not exempt from GST, which is creating an incredible barrier to access to exercise prescription and programming for Australians. Since the GST was first introduced and exercise physiology was recognized in Medicare, our profession has grown exponentially. We now have over 9,400 accredited exercise physiologists working across Australia helping communities every day. Most people don't know this, and when they find out, they are genuinely shocked. But if you are someone with a health condition, then you have to pay an extra tax to do one of the best things you can do to manage that condition. You don't have to pay this tax to see your podiatrist, your physio, your optometrist, or your dentist, and you don't have to pay this tax for your medication. But if...

title: Dr. Dutton Address to the Senate Standing Committee on Agriculture and Forestry
transcription:
Dr. Dutton, you now have the floor.
Good morning. I'm an associate professor at Dalhousie University in department called Community Health and Epidemiology. I'm also a member of a research group called PROOF, with members across Canada and the US, who have a goal of identifying policy options to reduce household food insecurity in Canada. I want to open by pointing out that household food insecurity is a specific scientific concept. It sounds like it should be the opposite of food of food security, but it isn't. Household food insecurity is the inadequate or insecure access to food due to financial constraints at the household level. Food security has been used to refer to everything from our ability to produce enough food domestically to feed our population, food supply chain, access to food banks. Food security therefore is a term inclusive of many problems that have to do with food and people sometimes conflate action on anything related to food with solutions to household food insecurity, which is not correct. This inappropriate combination of household food insecurity with issues grouped under the banner of food security complicates the language for people in government trying to grapple with the problem of household food insecurity. So some find it helpful to think about food insecurity as part of consumption poverty uh and so is related to challenges attributable to general affordability, cost of living, labor market outcome inequality, housing, like we like we just heard. Statistics Canada measures household food insecurity using a specific questionnaire that's been agreed upon by researchers to accurately measure household material circumstances. Uh that means efforts to decrease that measure will improve the lives of Canadians by improving their health and decreasing healthcare command for uh healthcare demand, excuse me. For reference, about one in four people in Canada are in food insecure households. I know this standing committee has heard from government employees from AAFC and ESDC, ESDC and others uh who have also emphasized that food insecurity is tied to income and I heard it all morning, so that's great. This is consistent with decades of research on food insecurity. Uh PHAC recently published reviews on what impacts food insecurity in Canada and came to the same conclusion. Food insecurity is improved by actions that decrease financial hardship. Those reviews identified that giving households food through in-kind mechanisms does not make much of an impact on food insecurity. The idea that giving a household food does not impact food insecurity is a major sticking point for many people, because it sounds unintuitive.

title: Ramayana Trailer REVIEW | Deeksha Sharma
transcription: इतने सारे लीक्स में रामायण का ट्रेलर देखने के बाद अब ऐसा क्या ही बाकी बचा है जो मैं आपको नया बता दूंगी? सच बोलूं, बहुत कुछ। इतना ज्यादा हाइप भी नहीं करना चाहिए था ना क्योंकि रियल ट्रेलर में कुछ वर्ल्ड क्लास है तो थोड़ा बहुत चीजों में 50-50 फील आ रहा है। तो चलो शुरुआत उसी सवाल से कर लेते हैं जिससे हर कोई बचना चाहता है। सुबह 4:00 बजे ट्रेलर कौन डालता है? नहीं-नहीं, यह वाला नहीं, इससे भी बड़ा जरूरी दूसरा सवाल। भगवान राम के बिना रामायण कैसी और राम के लिए रणबीर कपूर का ही सिलेक्शन क्यों? क्या वाकई में मजा आ रहा है रणबीर को ऐस भगवान राम के रोल में देखकर? देखो यह बात किसी से छुपी नहीं है जब से ट्रेलर के क्लिप्स वायरल होना शुरू हुए थे और अब फाइनली ऑफिशियल वीडियो भी आ गया है, हर किसी ने यश को ऐस रावण टोटली एक्सेप्ट कर लिया है। नो इफ, नो बट, किसी दूसरे एक्टर का नाम तक नहीं लिया जा रहा है जो इस फिल्म में रावण बन सकता था या फिर यश से ज्यादा बेटर तरीके से एग्रेशन, गुस्सा, घमंड, इन सारे एक्सप्रेशन को डिस्प्ले कर सकता था। सबसे बेस्ट डिसीजन था ट्रेलर को यश के सीन के साथ शुरू करना। देखते ही अलग एनर्जी सी फील होने लगती है। उनके डायलॉग्स उनके चेहरे को पूरी तरह मैच कर रहे हैं। यश और रावण मेड फॉर ईच अदर हैं। चाहे आप इस बात को कितना भी कंट्रोवर्शियल क्यों ना समझो लेकिन हां, इस ट्रेलर के बाद काफी लोग ऐसे होंगे जो रावण की वजह से रामायण देखने जाएंगे। लेकिन इस तरीके का कॉन्फिडेंस लोगों को रणबीर के ऊपर फील नहीं हो रहा है, फिर चाहे वो 144p वाला वीडियो हो या फिर 4K एचडी का ट्रेलर। दिक्कत वीडियो क्वालिटी की नहीं है, एक्टर से एक्सपेक्टेशंस की है। ऑनेस्टली ट्रेलर में रणबीर के सीन्स ऑन-ऑफ टाइप के हैं। जब वो ब्लाइंड फोल्ड वाला सीक्वेंस आया, इतनी खुशी हुई ना अंदर से। यह है वो इंडियन सिनेमा विजन जिसके आगे अंग्रेज भी अपनी नजरें नीची कर लेंगे। लेकिन जैसे ही ट्रेलर में आंखों से वो पट्टी हटी, रणबीर पे भरोसा थोड़ा डगमगा सा जाता है। वो भगवान से धीरे-धीरे इंसान जैसे लगना शुरू हो जाते हैं। नोटिस किया, ट्रेलर में जो पास वाले शॉट्स हैं, वो काफी डाले गए हैं जिनका परपज था गॉड वाइब्स लेकर आना, पब्लिक का सर रिस्पेक्ट में झुकाना। बट ईमानदारी से बोलूंगी एक बात, मैंने सोशल मीडिया पे कुछ फैन मेड पोस्टर्स, एआई जनरेटेड इमेजेस देखी हैं जो रणबीर को भगवान राम के रूप में कई ज्यादा डिवाइन तरीके से प्रेजेंट करती हैं। मैं क्या बोलना चाह रही हूं वो शायद आप सौरभ राज जैन को स्क्रीन पे देखकर जो महसूस करते हो, उसे रामायण में रणबीर से कंपेयर करके अच्छे से समझ जाओगे। देखो जैसे शूर्पणखा का रोल है, उसमें रकुल प्रीत का अचानक आना आपकी एक्सपेक्टेशंस को क्रॉस कर जाता है। प्रेजेंटेशन जितना सोचा था उससे भी ज्यादा बेटर निकला। यही सेम बात अरुण गोविल के लिए भी कही जा सकती है। बट वो सेम फार्मूला रणबीर के केस में उतना फिट नहीं बैठ रहा है, उसका उल्टा हो रहा है फिलहाल। याद रखना इस शब्द पे खास जोर दिया है मैंने, title: Ramayana Trailer Review | Yogi Bolta Hai
transcription: तो फाइनली वो दिन आ गया जिसका सब लोग वेट कर रहे थे। रामायण का, नाना, नमित मल्होत्राज़ रामायण का एक प्रॉपर ट्रेलर इज़ आउट नाउ ऑन सोशल मीडिया। वो भी ढेर सारे लीक्स के बाद। यार, आप ट्रेलर लॉन्च इवेंट एंड ट्रेलर को सोशल मीडिया पे अपलोड एक साथ करोगे तो ये लीक्स करना फिर उस लीक्स को हटाने के लिए एक एजेंसी को हायर करना ये सब नहीं होता। बट एनीवेज़, पैसा है तो करो ख़र्चा। राजामौली ने मस्त काम किया था भाई। इवेंट रखा और जिस टाइम पे इवेंट में ट्रेलर दिखाया था वाराणसी का, उसी टाइम पे सोशल मीडिया पे डाल दिया था। एनीवेज़, ट्रेलर आया है तो भाई बात करना तो बनता है। वेल, हेलो, मेरा नाम है योगी और हमारी मुलाकात बार-बार होगी। सबसे पहले अब मैं यहाँ खुल के कह सकता हूँ कि रावण का जो लुक अभी आपने ट्रेलर में देखा या लॉर्ड परशुराम का जो ग्लिम्प्स आपने अभी ट्रेलर में देखा या इवन कुंभकरण, वो हमने क्रिएटर इवेंट में मुंबई में देखा था नमित मल्होत्रा जी के घर। आई मीन इसके अलावा भी बहुत कुछ देखा था, ऐरावत वाली लड़ाई और कुछ एक कैरेक्टर्स। तो वही कुछ एक सेम कैरेक्टर्स इसमें भी दिखाए गए हैं एंड आई मस्ट से कि इस 4 मिनट के ट्रेलर में रावण के कैरेक्टर में यश बस कमाल ही करते नज़र आ रहे हैं। सी, आई एम नॉट ग्लोरिफाइंग रावण, बट आई एम टॉकिंग अबाउट यश की परफॉर्मेंस। एंड पूरा ट्रेलर देखने के बाद आई कैन प्राउडली से कि जितनी भी कास्टिंग की गई है वो एकदम ऑन पॉइंट लग रही है। अब देखो कोई बोलेगा कि रावण का कैरेक्टर इतना मस्त एक्शन वगैरह करते हुए दिखाया है, अग्रेशन में दिखाया है और रणबीर एज़ श्री राम को एकदम ठंडा सा दिखा दिया। भाई, वी आर नाउ हैबिचुअल टू सी मेनस्ट्रीम एक्टर्स इन टॉक्सिक मेल पर्सनालिटी। कबीर सिंह में शाहिद का अग्रेशन देख लो आप, रणबीर कपूर को एनिमल में पसंद किया गया था क्योंकि वो अग्रेशन से भरा हुआ था, यश को केजीएफ में पसंद किया गया था क्योंकि अगेन अल्फा मेल मस्क्युलिनिटी, मार्को में उन्नी मुकुंदन को, द बॉयज़ में होमलैंडर को, सेम विद पुष्पा, सेम विद अदर ग्रे शेड्स एंड एंटी-हीरो टाइप कैरेक्टर्स क्योंकि वो अग्रेशन एंड मार-धाड़ एंड टॉक्सिसिटी से भरे हुए थे एंड आजकल लोगों को वही पसंद भी आता है भाई। यहाँ रणबीर राम हैं भाई, वो जैसे थे वैसा ही प्रेजेंट किया गया है शांत मर्यादा वाले। एंड आई डोंट हैव एनी डाउट कि रणबीर एज़ श्री राम वैसा ही अपना कैरेक्टर को प्ले करेंगे जैसी रिक्वायरमेंट श्री राम की परफॉर्मेंस के लिए सूट करेगी। यश तो एब्सोल्यूट जेम लग ही रहे हैं। ही इज़ लाइक जैसे रामानंद सागर के रावण के बाद अगर कोई रावण सूट हुआ है तो वो यश ही हैं। इवन ईच एंड एवरी कैरेक्टर इज़ सूटेड फॉर देयर रोल। तो मैं कास्टिंग एंड उनके परफॉर्मेंस को लेकर कोई नेगेटिव पॉइंट ज़बरदस्ती नहीं रखना चाहूँगा। लेकिन जहाँ हम सबको पता है अबाउट रामायण, वहाँ हम इस फ़िल्म में बस प्रेजेंटेशन के लिए उत्साहित हैं एंड डैम, द प्रेजेंटेशन! रावण का वो पहला शॉट, वो एक लात से दरवाज़ा, आई मीन उतना बड़ा ह्यूज़ द्वार भव्य

title: Marco Rubio: We can't IGNORE the threat of Cuba
transcription: Secretary, great to have you back. Thank you so much. Glad to be back. It's been a while. Yeah. There's so much to talk about, but I want to start with Cuba. Um, this has been of particular interest to the State Department right now. You guys released a 100-page report on Cuba, calling it the capital of 21st-century communism, and this report talks about the fact that Cuba's goal, essentially, is to erase the United States from the earth. It also details a Cuban spy network that's been undermining American interests. How did we get to a place where Cuba has become so much of a threat, it feels like, again, to the United States? I think for those who have followed the issue of Cuba, this is not unfamiliar to us, but to the average American, you know, you see Cuba, small country, 90 miles off our shores, you know, 9 and a half million people population. What people forget that when it comes to things like espionage and influence operations, they actually are an influence and espionage superpower. If you look at the history of espionage in the United States, Cuba is the only country that consistently has implanted and embedded spies in our system without even paying them. We had an ambassador, a US ambassador who ended up being a Cuban spy and was recently convicted. We've had them penetrate the highest levels of the Defense Intelligence Agency. Ana Belen Montes was one of the single biggest intelligence failures on the part of the United States and one of the biggest penetrations we've ever had in our system. So, and then on the influence front, if you look all throughout Latin America, every communist, left-wing insurgency that's destabilized governments across the region, every single one of them over the last 40, 50 years has found its support, its help, in many cases its birth, from a Cuban influence operation. So, it was an important report just to highlight the role they play in our country, a very negative role. The report also links Cuban influence to the rise of Antifa, the riots that we saw in 2020, as well as the surge of radical activism that we've seen all over these college campuses. Um, to the average person, those things, I think, feel generally organic. But it turns out there are a lot of different powers, Cuba being one of them, that are influencing all of these things day to day. Absolutely. It's the same network of protesters around the country. There were the same people you saw in the streets burning things in 2020. They then flip it around and they become the pro-Hamas protesters. And they flip it around and within 48 hours of Maduro's arrest, have pre-printed signs outside the courthouse demanding his release.

How does he stack up with recent presidents at this same point here? Again, you see Trump at 41 now, 43 in 2018, and you see the others. Yeah, that's the interesting thing. Democrats did lose the House in '22, but it was only a few seats, and they actually gained a Senate seat. transcription: God, please, look at me. No, girl. Only Hulk. Savage Hulk is back and the big green rage monster might have just exposed a massive flaw in Doctor Strange's spell. Yeah, bro. Spider-Man: Brand New Day didn't just give us Spidey fighting Professor Hulk. It brought back the proper, old-school Hulk. The uncontrollable version we haven't really seen in the MCU for years. And I've got to know: What's next for Hulk? Come on, you already know we've got you covered. Let's get into it. To understand why Hulk loses control again, we got to go back to Avengers: Endgame, where Bruce revealed that he'd finally combined his intelligence with Hulk's strength, putting the brains and the brawn together to create Professor Hulk. After years of Banner and Hulk fighting for control, they'd finally found some kind of balance, and it seemed like the days of Bruce randomly transforming into a giant rage monster were over. Then, during the Shang-Chi post-credits scene, Bruce appeared in his human form again while wearing a device around his wrist. She-Hulk later revealed that this was an inhibitor, designed to suppress his gamma radiation and keep Hulk locked away. That technology becomes massively important in Brand New Day because Peter's superpowers have started changing. So he tracks Bruce down at his university looking for answers. Obviously, Bruce doesn't remember Peter thanks to Doctor Strange's spell, meaning Peter has to speak in code while asking how somebody might control powers that have suddenly become unpredictable. Bruce tells him about the inhibitor, and Peter then does what Peter Parker always does by casually building his own version of technology created by one of the smartest men on the planet. Peter creates an inhibitor designed to suppress his arachnid DNA and control the changes happening to his powers. He also builds a universal inhibitor that could theoretically suppress somebody else's powers, planning to use it against Jean Grey and stop her.

title: PE Fund Journal Entry Bible | Private Equity Accounting Interview Guide
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Most candidates memorize PE journal entries and still fail the interview. Why? Because the interviewer is not testing debit and credit only. They are testing cash, NAV, investor capital and LP reporting. Take one private equity fund case: commitment $100 million, capital called $20 million, investment made $15 million, fund expense $1 million, management fee $2 million, fair value $18 million, exit $18 million, distribution to LPs $5 million. Here is the scoreboard. After every entry, ask: did cash move? Did NAV move? Capital activity or performance? What reaches LP reporting? First, capital call. The fund calls 20 million from LPs. Debit cash 20 million, credit investor capital 20 million. Cash increases, investor capital increases, but performance has not improved. This is capital activity, not income. Capital call brings cash, it does not create profit. Second, investment made. The fund invests 15 million into a portfolio company or SPV. Debit investment 15 million, credit cash 15 million. Cash goes down, investment asset goes up, but there is no immediate gain. Cash became investment, that is the trap. Investment made is not an expense and it does not automatically increase NAV. Third, fund expense. Assume 1 million of audit, legal or admin expense. Debit fund expense 1 million, credit expense payable or cash 1 million. This hits P&L, so NAV reduces. LP reporting shows fund level expense impact. The trap: fund expense is not capital activity. It reduces NAV because it hits P&L.

He presents a case study involving a fund with a $100 million commitment, walking through different scenarios such as capital calls, investments, and fund expenses. title: Journal Your Best Reality ✨ How to Manifest Your Dream Life Through Writing.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever felt like you were just one step away from the life you actually want to live, but you just cannot seem to grab it? We have all been there. You have these big dreams and deep desires, but they feel like they are stuck in some alternate reality that you can only see from a distance. Well today, I want to share something with you that completely shifted everything for me. It is not magic and it is not just wishful thinking. It is the intentional practice of journaling to attract your best reality. I used to think journaling was just for recording what happened during my day like a diary, but once I realized it could be a tool for creation, my whole world changed. First, let us talk about why this actually works. When you put pen to paper, you are doing more than just writing words. You are focusing your energy, and giving your subconscious mind a clear roadmap. Most of the time our brains are cluttered with thousands of random thoughts, but journaling forces you to slow down and get specific. It is like sending a clear signal to the universe saying, 'this is exactly what I am ready for.' Your brain has a filtering system called the reticular activating system, and when you write down your desires, you are essentially telling that system what to look for in the real world. The first thing I always do before I start writing is get into a state of gratitude. You cannot manifest from a place of lack because the energy of wanting something often carries the heavy feeling of not having it. So, I start by listing three things I am genuinely thankful for right now. It could be as simple as a good cup of coffee, a supportive friend, or even just the fact that I have a quiet moment to myself. This shifts your vibration from 'I need' to 'I appreciate' which is the perfect foundation for attracting more. Now, let us get into the most powerful part of my routine, which is called scripting. Scripting is basically writing about your future as if it is happening right now, in the present tense. Instead of saying, 'I want to have my dream job,' you would write, 'I am so incredibly happy and fulfilled in my new career.' You have to get detailed. What does your office smell like? How does it feel when you see your name on that door? Who are you celebrating with at dinner tonight? The key is to involve all your senses. When you write these details, your brain starts to believe it is a memory rather than a distant hope. This bridge between your current reality and your desired one is where

title: Apple’s Journal App Helped Me Organize My Entire Life
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Most of us have thoughts we don't want to keep floating around in our heads all day. Ideas, reminders, things we need to do tomorrow, things we're worried about, things we don't want to forget. For a long time, I tried keeping all that in paper journals. I actually loved them, I probably bought way too many of them over the years. But eventually, I ran into one problem: I didn't always have them with me when I needed them. And that's when something interesting started happening. Over the past few months, Apple's Journal app has quietly turned into something different for me. It's not just a journaling app anymore, it's basically become my digital notebook. The place where I organize my thoughts, capture ideas, and keep different parts of my life in one place. So, in this video, I want to show you how I set it up, how I organize my journals inside the app, and why it's slowly replacing paper notebooks for me. But I'm curious about something first. Has Apple's Journal app replaced your paper notebook yet? Or are there things still holding you back? Let me know in the comments. And if you enjoy calm tech videos about productivity and intentional living, hit that like button and subscribe. It really helps the channel. All right, let's get into it. I've always liked paper journals. There's something satisfying about finishing one and keeping it on a shelf. It feels like you actually own it. It's not locked away inside an app somewhere. And writing with a pen just feels natural. You can jot something down quickly, cross things out, draw arrows, sketch little ideas. Things that don't always feel as fluid when you're typing. In the past, I tried using digital journaling apps, but I usually ended up going back to paper. But paper journals eventually started becoming inconvenient for one simple reason: I didn't always have them with me. If I had an idea while I was out somewhere, on the train, traveling, or just away from home, I couldn't write it down unless the notebook happened to be nearby. Another issue was organization. At one point, I tried using a bullet journal system with calendars, indexes, and sections, but maintaining all that just started to feel like a chore. Searching for something I wrote weeks earlier could be frustrating unless everything was perfectly indexed, which I usually didn't keep up with. With the Journal app, that problem basically disappears. Everything is automatically dated, everything is searchable. And most importantly, it's always with me. I always have my phone nearby, and most of the time, my iPad is within reach, too. And once Apple brought the Journal app to the iPad with Apple Pencil support, it started giving me many of the same benefits that the paper journals had. I can still jot things down by hand, sketch quick ideas, or cross things out. But now, it lives everywhere I go. Over time, I started organizing the app into different journals. Right now, I have five journals, but three of them are the ones I use the most. I have separate places for different parts of my life, so I know where things belong. The first one is called Personal Log. This works like a traditional journal. I write about my life, things that are on my mind, things that make me happy, things that bothered me,
