title: Moving Forward | My Anxiety Story (Part 7)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: What if understanding anxiety and panic attacks is not enough to beat it? For a long time, I believed that if I just learned enough about anxiety, if I became aware of its existence and its causes, it would eventually disappear. But knowledge alone didn't change much. The real change started only when I began taking action. Welcome back, or just welcome if this is your first time here. My name is Luka, and this is part seven of my anxiety story. In this video, I'll talk about the moment when I realized something important: it is not enough to simply learn a lot about our enemy, although that is certainly the first and essential step. To ultimately defeat it, or to overpower it to the point where there is no battle at all, we must create a solid plan and strategy, and then truly begin with active preparations. So, how do I stand on my own two feet again? How do I run freely without fear? All of us secretly hope that our problems will solve themselves, that someone will appear with a magic wand and make everything disappear. We just need to be patient, and it will happen. And yes, sometimes life really does work that way. Sometimes, someone unexpectedly helps you, sometimes a problem gets resolved by someone else. Sometimes, time slowly erases things. But the truth is, situations that get solved like that are actually very rare. When it comes to anxiety and panic attacks, you can be 100% sure of one thing: they will not disappear on their own. And if you do nothing, the situation will most likely only get worse. So, if we want to win the lottery, we first have to buy a ticket. That's when the first steps of self-help begin. And that's exactly what I did. My psychiatrist gave me advice and guidance on how to live with anxiety and panic attacks, how to slowly expose myself to the things that scared me, how to face those fears step by step. And I actually put many of those tips into practice. When my mind finally felt free enough to move forward, my real self-help journey began.

transcription: क्या आपके साथ कभी ऐसा हुआ है कि आप बिल्कुल ठीक बैठे हैं और अचानक आपका शरीर आपका साथ छोड़ दे? अचानक ऐसा लगे कि आपके पास आखिरी कुछ मिनट बचे हैं बस। आज मैं आपके साथ कुछ ऐसी ही बातें शेयर अटैक आया। और उसके बाद जो है, एक अजीब सी घबराहट होने लगी, अजीब सा टेंशन लगने लगा। लेकिन, वो एक दिन था, लेकिन उसके बाद ये मुझे कई बार और हुआ। तब तक मैं श्योर नहीं था कि मुझे एंग्जायटी ही है, पैनिक अटैक ही हैं या हार्ट से रिलेटेड कोई समस्या है। अब ये पैनिक अटैक ना इतनी डरावनी होती है कि ऐसा आपको लग रहा होता है कि शायद ये हार्ट अटैक है। क्योंकि इसके सिम्टम्स और हार्ट अटैक के सिम्टम्स बहुत हद तक एक जैसे ही होते हैं। तो अचानक मुझे ऐसा लगने लगा कि शायद ये हार्ट अटैक है। मैं उस दिन तो किसी तरीके से डॉक्टर के पास गया और उन्होंने मुझे मेडिसिन दी और मैं उस दिन कुछ नहीं हुआ नॉर्मल हो गया। लेकिन फिर सेम यही चीजें नेक्स्ट वीक या फिर उससे 15 दिन बाद मेरे साथ हुआ। उस दिन मुझे ये काफी लंबे समय तक रहा, मतलब मैंने मेडिसिन ले ली उसके बाद भी ये मेरे साथ चलता रहा। रात का ही टाइम था, सेम वही टाइम के आसपास। और फिर मुझे एहसास हुआ कि ये डेफिनेटली कुछ ना कुछ समस्या है। एक तरफ माइंड कह रहा था हार्ट से रिलेटेड कोई इशूज हैं, एक तरफ माइंड कह रहा था नहीं हार्ट का रिलेटेड इशूज नहीं हो सकता शायद कुछ ऐसी कोई चीज होगी, गैस बन रहा होगा कुछ और होगा। लेकिन उसके बाद जो कुछ हुआ ना, वो शायद मैं आपको क्लीयरली ऐसे बोलूँगा ना तो आप शायद समझ नहीं पाएंगे। अगर आप एंग्जायटी में हैं या आपको पैनिक अटैक आते हैं, तो आप उसको फील कर सकते हैं, आप समझ सकते हैं कि हाँ क्या हो रहा होगा। क्योंकि आपके हाथ पैरों पर पसीना आने लगता है, आपको घबराहट होने लगती है, ऐसा लगता है जैसे कि बस आपके पास कुछ आखिरी पल बचे हुए हैं और आपके साथ आज ही कुछ ना कुछ हो जाएगा और शायद आपका आखिरी दिन है, अजीब अजीब तरीके के थॉट्स चलते हैं और आपका माइंड ना बहुत ही अजीब सा हो जाता है। तो दिमाग में ना एक बात आया कि अगर मान लो, आखिरी दिन हुआ तो आपको ऐसा लगेगा कि title: How to Stop Panic Attacks: 5 Tools for Anxiety Recovery (My Story as a Single Mum)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hi. Today I want to tell you about the day I realized something was very wrong. For months, my daughter had been waiting to go to a big Disney show in Rome, and she was so excited. Really counting down the hours and the days. But when the moment came, as we were getting ready to leave, my body just stopped. I started to feel like I was going to faint, I was sweating, I felt sick to my stomach, and honestly, I thought I had a virus because I didn't even know what a panic attack was yet. I just knew that I didn't have the energy to drive for an hour, find parking, find dinner, deal with the crowds, deal with the loud music, and then drive us both back home. So, eventually my dad ended up taking her to the show so she wouldn't miss it, thank God. But I still remember sitting at home and feeling so much guilt. I felt like a failure because I couldn't be there for her. I felt sad that my dad had to do it on my behalf when he had work the next morning. And if you have ever felt that mom guilt because your anxiety is stopping you from being the parent you want to be, please listen to me. You're not a bad mother. You're just a person whose nervous system is overwhelmed and there is a way back. When I was at my lowest point as a single mother, I had to find ways to heal that were simple, fast, and free because I couldn't afford to pay for therapy. And these are the five things that saved me at the very beginning. First of all, I stopped fighting the panic. I learned that when a panic attack starts, if I fight it, if I resist it, it just stays longer. So I started saying to my body, "Okay, I feel you. You can go through." And I just imagined this kind of wave of electricity going through me. And when I stopped resisting, the attacks started coming less often. Second, Bach Flower Rescue Remedy. This was my safety net. I kept it in my bag everywhere I went. At grocery store, train, social situations. And it helped me feel like I had an escape because the moment I could feel a panic attack arising, I knew I could rely on the remedy to stop it then and there. Third, I had to remove the triggers. So I had to stop putting things in my body that made my heart race

title: I Had 85+ Anxiety Symptoms || My Anxiety Recovery Story ||
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: If you're watching this right now, I already know something about you. You didn't just stumble across this video. You searched for it. Or maybe you've been watching video after video, late at night, trying to figure out what the hell is wrong with you, and nothing is giving you answers. Nothing is making you feel better. Yeah, I know that feeling because I lived it. And honestly, at my worst, I was probably in a darker place than you are right now. So, if you can give me a few minutes, I want to tell you my story. Not the cleaned up version, the real one, because I think it might be exactly what you need to hear today. Back in 2019, life was actually pretty solid for me. I was that sports guy, always outside, playing every single day, super active, full of energy. Sure, there was normal stress like anyone else, but nothing that felt overwhelming. I thought I was living the good life. Then, February 18th, 2019 hit, and everything just flipped. That morning, I woke up and my whole body felt hot, like I had a fever, but when I checked my temperature three different times, it was completely normal. My energy just crashed out of nowhere. I told myself, "It's probably just tiredness, it'll pass by tomorrow." So, I still dragged myself to the ground and played for a couple of hours trying to act normal. But deep down, something felt seriously off. It was like my body was warning me that something bad was coming. That same night, my brother's friend was throwing a party just a mile away. I wasn't feeling it at all, but my older brother convinced me to come along. "We'll eat quick and head straight back home." The second we walked in, everything started looking blurry and weird, like I was in a dream. I turned to my brother and said, "Man, something is really not right. I'm getting super anxious." He told me to just sit down, eat with everyone, and we'd leave soon. But I could barely hold myself together. 10 minutes later, my heart exploded. It started pounding so hard I could feel

title: The Anxiety Trick No One Talks About (True Student Story)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever caught yourself trapped in a loop of your own thoughts, lying awake at 2:00 a.m., replaying a conversation from years ago, convinced everyone secretly hates you? If you have, know this: you are not broken, you are not weak. Alex felt exactly what you're feeling right now. Alex was a first-year student. Good grades, tight friend group, a hard-earned scholarship, but underneath, his mind was a battlefield. Picture it: 6:00 a.m., Alex on the dorm floor, heart hammering like it might crack a rib. No fire, no danger, just a presentation due at nine. Here's what nobody tells you about panic: it doesn't need a reason, it just needs a nervous system running on empty. Alex missed that presentation. Then three more. Isolation crept in slowly, the way it always does. Skipped classes became skipped meals. Let that sink in. One of the sharpest minds in his program was disappearing, not from lack of ability, but from a mind stuck in survival mode. Stay with me, because the breakthrough in phase three is a tool most people ignore completely, and the quiet decision Alex made in the final month decides whether any of us can break free from our own mental traps today. One, naming the enemy. Alex thought something was medically wrong. Racing heart, shaking hands, walls closing in during lectures. The amygdala, the brain's alarm system, can't tell a tiger from a test. It floods the body with adrenaline and waits for you to run. Alex wasn't losing his mind; his mind was just aimed at the wrong target. The turning point? A counselor gave him one sentence: "Name it, don't become it." Instead of "I am anxious," he learned to say, "Anxiety is visiting." The fight wasn't in the classroom; it was between his ears. Two, rebuilding from the ground up. Naming it didn't erase it. Isolation is where anxiety thrives, and Alex knew it. So he built tiny, deliberate acts of discomfort: sitting in the library instead of his room, speaking one sentence in class, texting a friend back with shaking hands. This is behavioral activation.

title: Why You Still Feel Like a Child Pretending to Be an Adult
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
You are sitting in a meeting, or maybe you're just paying your electricity bill. On the outside, you look like a fully functioning adult, but on the inside, you feel like a scared 12-year-old wearing oversized clothes, like you think, "it just feels like I was in my school," and you can't believe it. See, when a crisis happens, uh maybe a flat tire, a mistake at work, a medical issue, your first instinct is to look around the room for a real adult to come and fix it. And then, you get a terrifying uh realization, "I'm supposed to be the real adult, right?" Now you feel deeply embarrassed. Uh you look at your friends and coworkers and assume they all have life figured out, while you are just wondering how you got this old, because inside, you haven't aged a day over 12. In this video, we are going to talk about exactly why you are feeling like this and what the way out is.

Hi, I'm Gayatri Arvind, founder of Abasa Rehab and Wellness. We offer residential rehabilitation for people struggling with addiction, mental health disorders, eating disorders, and chronic conditions. Over the past six years, we have helped over thousands of people reclaim their lives through personalized care. Through this channel, we share practical wisdom to empower your mental health.

Clinical psychology says that your brain operates in different modes. Think of them as different versions of your personality that take over depending on your stress levels. For example, you have the demanding parent mode that constantly criticize you, the detached protector mode that numbs your feelings, the healthy adult mode that handles life rationally, and the vulnerable child mode. See, when you feel like a terrified kid pretending to be grown up, you are not imagining things. You have actually slipped into what we call the vulnerable child mode. Uh when you were growing up, if you didn't feel safe, or if your feelings were constantly ignored, your brain did something to protect you, right? It hits the pause button on your emotional growth. That part of your mind froze, and it got stuck at the exact age where you felt the most hurt or scared. So today, when your boss criticizes you, or when you face financial stress, you do not react with the brain of a capable 30-year-old. Your brain time travels, and that frozen, scared inner child grabs the steering wheel of your 30

title: Anxious About The New - Addiction Recovery Daily Reflection
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hello, and welcome to another Daily Reflections video. I'm Dr. Anastasia Hronis, clinical psychologist, author of the book, The Dopamine Brain, and I work in the field of addictions. And pretty frequently, I try to jump on here and provide you guys with a daily reflection in the context of addiction recovery. I'm currently coming to you from a hotel room in Hobart—not Hobart, in Tasmania, in Launceston, um, where I am doing some work over the next few days with the Royal Flying Doctors Service out here. Um, one of my hats and one of the roles that I have is to provide training to services, um, on the therapy of DBT, dialectical behavior therapy, which can be incredibly useful for people who are going through addiction recovery. But that is beside the point. Today, I have another daily reflection for you. Um, and this one is on the theme of anxiety. We haven't yet touched the theme of anxiety, but it is one that shows up quite commonly. If you're new here, I like to jump on and provide daily reflection videos. Yes, there's lots of daily reflection books out there that exist, um, for the purpose of helping people reflect on a particular theme each day in the context of addiction recovery. I like to write my own. And the reason for this is, I like to write them based on the themes that I'm hearing from the clients that I work with in the clinic who are going through the process of addiction recovery, um, but also based on the work of research that I do, as well, um, so based on what I'm hearing, what I'm thinking about, um, and the information that clients, um, who have experiences of addictions are telling me. I like to go on, way, think about those, um, marinate in those thoughts, and then write some daily reflections for you guys to think about and listen to. So, today's daily reflection is called, "Feeling anxious about the new." This is something I hear a lot of. So, I'm going to read it out, and then I'm going to share some thoughts with you. Change. Even good change can feel unsettling. When we leave behind what's familiar, substances, routines, or identities attached to the substances, we lose our old reference points. The new can sometimes feel too quiet, too predictable, too boring, or simply unknown. But that anxiety doesn't mean that you're doing something wrong. It actually means that you're growing. Recovery asks us to step into spaces that we haven't yet learned to trust. It takes time for that feeling of safety to catch up with the progress that you're making. The body and the mind need repetition to believe that the peace that you're experiencing won't just suddenly disappear. You don't have to rush into feelings of comfort. Just keep showing up for the life that you're building, even if your hands are shaking while you're doing it.

Anxiety is probably the most common thing that brings people into my office. Uh, it's actually anxiety disorders are the most common of all mental health disorders. So, this is like our bread and butter. I think of anxiety as being a close cousin of fear, right? Like fear is that sensation that you have when you are like staring down a threat, whether that's a rogue tiger or an enemy combatant or an oncoming vehicle, right? Fear is that in the moment, something is wrong, my life is in danger. Anxiety is, is that feeling, but it's future-oriented. So, it's sort of the anticipation that something bad could happen in the future, um, and it takes lots of different forms, and this is why there are so many different anxiety disorders. They all are distinguished by what the person is anxious about. And it doesn't necessarily, it doesn't necessarily mean that you're anticipating, uh, your life being threatened, but I mean, it, it could be an interview for a job or anything like that, right? Right. For, for somebody with social anxiety, it might be public speaking, you know, the fear of being evaluated or judged by someone else. title: How to Manage Anxiety and Depression Without Fighting Yourself | A Healing Story.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Every morning, Daniel woke up tired. Not the kind of tired sleep fixes, but the heavy one, the kind that sat on his chest like a stone and whispered, 'What's the point?' Before his eyes even opened, his mind was already running. Bills, expectations, old conversations replaying themselves like punishment, future disasters that hadn't happened yet, but felt certain. Anxiety arrived first, loud and demanding. Depression followed quietly, like a shadow that refused to leave. For a long time, Daniel fought them both. He read articles with titles like 'Beat Anxiety in Seven Days' and 'How to Eliminate Depression Forever'. He forced smiles, forced productivity, forced prayer, forced gratitude. When none of it worked, he blamed himself. 'Other people are strong, why can't I just fix this?' One evening, after another day of pretending he was okay, Daniel sat alone on his bedroom floor. His phone buzzed with unanswered messages. The room felt too quiet, yet his mind was unbearably loud. That night, he didn't pray for healing, he prayed for permission. 'God,' he whispered, 'I don't know how to make this stop, but I'm tired of running.' Nothing dramatic happened, no sudden peace, no miracle, but something subtle shifted. The next day, Daniel decided to stop declaring war on his mind. Instead of saying, 'I must not feel anxious,' he tried something new. 'I am anxious, and I'm still here.' When the familiar tightness rose in his chest, he didn't immediately distract himself or criticize it. He sat down, placed a hand on his chest, breathed slowly, not to make the feeling disappear, but to stay with it. 'This is anxiety,' he told himself gently. 'It's uncomfortable, but it's not dangerous.' The feeling didn't vanish, but it softened just a little. Depression was harder. Depression didn't shout, it drained. title: I Drank Alcohol During Anxiety DPDR Recovery
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I drank caffeine the entire time that I was actually overcoming anxiety DPDR. I stopped caffeine, however, in the earlier stages, and believe it or not, it made me worse. Now, when I bring up the topic of caffeine, a lot of the times, people ask me about alcohol. And during my anxiety DPDR recovery, I did actually drink alcohol from time to time. And believe it or not, it was actually my family doctor who knew my whole situation, who knew that I was dealing with anxiety, depersonalization, derealization, and gave me the go-ahead if I wanted to drink caffeine, or if I wanted to drink alcohol, and even if I wanted to consume nicotine, he said it was fine, just to be aware that it might create sensations, and to be prepared to respond correctly. He understood the framework that I was trying to use in my recovery process, and he said that this aligned with it, just to be prepared in case symptoms should show up, to know that you will have to respond correctly. And at that point, I had already started drinking caffeine again as my normal routine, and told him it actually made me feel a bit better. I was just a bit skeptical and scared about having a drink of alcohol from time to time. And as far as nicotine goes, after I fell into the cycle, I've never consumed it since, not out of fear of the symptoms, but just for health purposes. And that's a huge distinction, because once you fully overcome anxiety DPDR, the symptoms have no bearing over your decisions whatsoever. However, when I did start drinking alcohol again from time to time, I noticed that it didn't calm me down the same way it really used to, and it didn't give me that euphoric feeling that it normally would, so I didn't really enjoy it the same way at first. When I did drink alcohol, I noticed I was a little bit more alert, and I was constantly still trying to focus on whether or not I felt the effects, and in turn, would analyze my symptoms a bit. But it just never seemed to give me that same relaxed, you know, euphoric feeling that it used to before falling into the cycle. But, I did still drink occasionally, because that's what normal me would be doing. And I tried my best to not focus on the sensations, and if sensations did come up because of it, then I would just redirect my attention the same way, and treat it like any other trigger. But, what I did do, was manage the amount of alcohol I would drink. Typically, back in the day, I could drink three to five drinks and have a great time and, you know, not feel the effects too much the next day. But, because I was aware that my nervous system was sensitized, I would only have one, two, and sometimes maybe three drinks at most, all while staying hydrated and drinking water or Gatorade alongside it. As I proceeded through recovery and gained confidence,

title: Meghan's Recovery from POTs, Chronic Fatigue, Anxiety, Self-Worth, and Body Image Issues
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: It is so just absolutely profound, the change and how much it works so quickly by working with you. Like, it was just, I was like, oh my gosh. This is just amazing how fast this works. And it is the difference between working on it with somebody who is caring and you trust, and creates a safe space, and you just feel like, okay, I can do this. I've had a lot of improvement from just our three sessions together. It worked really quickly for me. Like, I went from super anxious to just down to this calm feeling of like, I was safe and I'm okay. It just really, absolutely took my anxiety from like, very high to all of a sudden, I'm like way down here. And began to see how much my emotional state was influencing everything where I didn't see that before. I had this mental block about it because I had been told by so many doctors that, "No, you do have these infections," and I had been, I think in a sense, brainwashed to believe that I didn't have that kind of power over my own body, that I wasn't able to do anything about it. And now, I absolutely, 150% believe that I can, and I can thrive, and I can play with my kids, and I can exert, and I can do all of these things that before, I think I was just so stuck on what the doctors were telling me. I just thought that, "Well, I've got to cure the infection." And now, I have proof that I'm doing better without having any of that stuff involved. So, you used to have thoughts like worst-case scenarios for your health, or maybe some like, self-critical thought or something like that, and you would just spiral, right? It would just go on and on. Mm-hmm, and I would feel it in my body and the sensations, and now I know when I'm having a thought like that, the feeling that I have in my body, it had nothing to do with like, the infections. It just had to do with the way that I was clinging to these memories like they were my truth, and they were not my truth. Yes, so if you think about one of those memories now that we rewired, what happens inside you?

title: Dear Anyone Whose Anxiety Never Fully Goes Away...
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Dear anyone. You know that feeling when you wake up and for one second, just one, everything feels okay? And then it comes back. That quiet tightness in your chest. That feeling that something is wrong even when nothing actually is. You didn't even do anything. You just woke up and it was already waiting. If that's your life, not just bad days, not just stressful weeks, but this thing that just never fully leaves, stay with me because I don't think you're weak. I think you've been carrying something most people don't even know exists. Let me describe your day. Before you even check your phone, your body is already on alert. Not panic, not a breakdown. Just that background tightness that never fully turns off. You go through your day, you function, you talk to people, you laugh at the right moments, like a tab open in the background that you can never fully close. And the exhausting part? It's not the big moments. It's the small ones. The phone ringing unexpectedly, the slight change in someone's tone that sends your whole nervous system into high alert, and you think, "Why am I like this? Everyone else seems fine." Sound familiar? Here's what people around you don't get. They think anxiety is just worrying, just overthinking, just being a little nervous. They don't understand that for you, it's not occasional. It's waking up at 3:00 a.m. for no reason, heart already racing. It's replaying a conversation from three days ago and still finding new things to feel bad about. It's canceling plans not because you don't want to go, but because your body said no before your brain could argue. And when you try to explain this, they say, "Just breathe," or "Stop overthinking," as if you wouldn't choose calm if calm were that simple.

title: I FULLY Recovered from Anxiety DPDR Without Changing Much
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I suffered with anxiety DPDR for two years straight and honestly, I didn't change that much about me, if anything at all, really. I have a pretty bad sleep schedule, meaning I go to bed very late and I also wake up late. Didn't change that, not even once throughout my recovery. I like to drink caffeine, I drank caffeine throughout my entire recovery. I like to occasionally have alcohol, I drank alcohol during my recovery. I didn't have an extremely strict routine and ultimately, I really did not change anything about my core self or personality or the typical behaviors I would engage in. What I did change, I didn't drink extreme amounts of caffeine because before I fell into anxiety DPDR, I would drink like, and I'm saying insane amounts of caffeine, not just, you know, a few cups of coffee. I would pound pre-workout, like three scoops, which led to like, I think like 500 to 700 milligrams at a time before working out, not to mention the caffeine I'd have throughout the day. And I only stopped that because it was just generally unhealthy. Outside of that, I didn't change any actual things regarding my personality or regarding my behaviors at large. What I did change, however, is my understanding of anxiety, depersonalization, derealization, and nervous system sensitization. I suffered for two years because I didn't actually understand these concepts wholeheartedly. And a part of me kept wondering, "Maybe it's something worse," and that worry, in and of itself, kept it alive. Once I fully understood these concepts, and how they're intertwined, and how our nervous system operates, and the reason it produces these types of symptoms, I was able to change my relationship with the symptoms, which inevitably reduced the fear of the symptoms, which allowed me to let them exist alongside me while I lived life normally, still doing the, quote unquote, "crappy" things I would do in my behaviors. And despite my nervous system being incredibly sensitized for two years straight, and I mean like, terrible symptoms for two years straight, I actually recovered pretty quickly after I stopped caring about it. The hardest part is just reaching the point where you don't care. And truthfully, that just comes from going into the symptoms, and living life as normally as you possibly can, allowing them to come with you, labeling them as what they are, as just products of sensitization, and allowing them to take their time, take as much time as they need to. Not putting timelines on yourself, and not putting this extra stress on yourself, and just focus on responding properly to the symptoms, and not on the symptoms themselves. And I'm sure there'll be people that will say, "Oh, well, your case is different," or "maybe you didn't have it that bad." I had it for two years, and that was two years of constant 24/7 suffering, and I'm not exaggerating when I say, two years straight.
caption: A man's voice is heard in this recording, speaking clearly and directly to the listener as he shares his personal journey of recovering from anxiety and DPDR (Depersonalization-Derealization Disorder) over a two-year period. His tone is conversational and reflective, conveying a sense of authenticity as he explains that he did not make drastic changes to his lifestyle or habits during his recovery, but rather shifted his understanding and relationship with his symptoms. The audio quality is clean and focused, with no significant background noise, allowing his message of acceptance and patience in the recovery process to be heard with clarity.

title: Preparing For Therapy? What To Do? | Mental Health Awareness

transcription:
0:00 - 0:04
Hi, welcome back to my channel. And in this video, I was going to talk to you a little bit about how I prepare for, oh. It's a bit windy. A little bit how I prepare and, yeah, preparing for therapy sessions. I am in therapy. I have mental health issues like a lot of people. A lot of people have mental health issues. But I just want to talk about my preparation process and stuff for therapy sessions. So, there's many things I prepare for therapy, do for therapy before, during and after therapy sessions. So, we'll start with before and then we'll go through it, through the whole process. So, before therapy session, I keep a journal. And I have a page in my journal for each therapy session. And I keep this, my page in my journal. So, my therapy sessions are every other week. So, for two weeks, I have this page in my journal for things I want to talk about with my therapist. So, things that come up, things that happen, things that I'm thinking about. I'm like, "Oh, I want to talk about that with my therapist." So, I'll write it down. And during my therapy session, I'll bring out my notebook and I'll go through the list and we'll talk about those things. That's one thing. And I keep this journal with me like almost 24/7. Like everywhere I go, I have a bag with me that I put my journal in. Everywhere I go, I keep this journal with me. That's one thing I do to keep my or to prepare for therapy sessions. Another thing is I arrive maybe 15 to 20 minutes early for my therapy sessions and I sit in my car. And what I do is some exercises. I do some breathing exercises like square breathing, I do box breathing and then I do some muscle relaxation. And I also do some mindfulness, just to kind of get my mind into the mood of talking and just getting my my head into that.

I've gone to plug in my SD card, plugged it into the laptop, nothing's there, other than like, eight videos from this camera here. title: Why Your Future Therapy Clients Aren’t Searching for What You Think (SEO for Therapists)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: So most therapists and coaches I work with aren't struggling because they're bad at their work. They're usually struggling because the people who need them can't actually find them. And usually, it's not because they're bad at marketing or selling. It's because clients don't search for help the way we've been trained to talk about it. Before I dive in, just a little context, especially if you're new here. I work with therapists and coaches and heart-centered practitioners who want to be visible without becoming someone that they're not. Uh usually, people who care deeply about ethics and depth and how their words land and what they bring to their clients land, and who still want the right clients to find them. So a lot of what I share here sits at that intersection of psychology, lived experience, and a very practical question. How do we meet people where they actually are and not where we wish they were? And today's topic sits right in the middle of all of that. A potential client doesn't sit down and type: trauma-informed integrative psychotherapist specializing in nervous system regulation. As much as we might wish they would. So, what they actually type looks more like this: Why do I feel on edge all the time? I can't stop overthinking everything. Is something wrong with me or am I just exhausted? I feel fine, but also not fine at all. Those aren't neat keywords, you know, that hit on the spot of what we do. They're more emotional signals and half-formed thoughts like, like late night questions. We all know those. So, they are moments where someone is circling the idea of help without being ready to say the word therapy yet. So, most advice about SEO or visibility focuses on taking or talking about services you already offer, but that completely misses the moment before someone knows what they are actually looking for.

She explains that clients do not search for services using clinical terms, but rather through emotional, raw queries reflecting their feelings of anxiety, confusion, or exhaustion. She shares her focus on helping heart-centered practitioners achieve visibility while maintaining their values, stressing the importance of understanding the client's search journey.

title: Fitness Isn’t Wrong, It’s Just Incomplete
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I wanted to share a few reflections around this post because I think some of the ideas can be a bit unfamiliar at first, specifically when trying to understand what we mean by these big ambiguous terms: movement, movement practice, or movement-oriented approach. I chose to start with fitness as a reference because it's the main cultural lens that many of us have inherited when thinking about the body or when thinking about physicality. One of the more important distinctions that I wanted to start with is that movement is not something that we can push or force back into fitness. It's actually the other way around: fitness ends up being nestled inside of movement. And this is something that I see regularly when I look out in the world and I see how movement is being represented. It's represented as movements, things that we do that are isolated in skill or meant to represent some particular outcome, yet it's not encapsulating this unique wholeness that movement is meant to offer. It doesn't mean that fitness is wrong when we think about this nestling or this being smaller than movement, it just means that it's incomplete. And like I said, fitness culture tends to narrow the conversation of the body towards isolated outcomes: strength, flexibility, aesthetics, performance, body comp, and so on. None of these are bad and they can all be valuable, but they don't represent the whole picture. And what we're calling the whole picture in this case is movement, this larger perspective, this larger ongoing study. Implicitly, the question fitness often asks is how can I improve the look or performance of the parts? What we're more interested in through a movement lens is how do these parts participate in the use of the whole? This shift in this way of viewing changes everything.
caption: An adult male speaks in a reflective and articulate tone, sharing thoughts on the conceptual differences between "fitness" and a "movement-oriented approach." The recording has high clarity with virtually no background interference, allowing his gentle, measured cadence to be heard clearly. He posits that movement is not something to be forced into fitness, but rather that fitness is nested within the broader concept of movement. He critiques how fitness culture often narrows the focus to isolated outcomes like strength, aesthetics, and flexibility, asking "how can I improve the look or performance of the parts?" In contrast, a movement lens invites a more holistic perspective, asking "how do these parts participate in the use of the whole?" He concludes that this shift in viewing the body and physicality changes everything.

title: Glimpse of the PC Space: JA JAYS EDITION
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hi, I'm Chelsea. Hi, I'm Gabby. Hi, my name is Kaylin. Hello, my name's Koey. Hi, I'm Sam. Hi, I'm Amelia. Hi, I'm Jen. Hi, I'm Katrina. Hi, I'm Luke. Hi, I'm Mar. What's up? My name is Aldwin. Hi, I'm Ari. Hi, I'm Danielle. Hi, my name is Hazel. Hello, my name is Caitlin. What's up, y'all? I'm John. And I'm a PC! If you could describe the PC Counseling space in one word, what would it be? And why? Is that a word? Useful. Open. Safe. Intentional. Authentic. Home. Impactful. I would describe it as community. This space has a way of bringing people together, inside and out. The space is very special because it brings a unique perspective, not only on your own life and your own experiences, but on other people as well, and how you want to change, and how you want to build your life moving forward from your situations and your prior experiences. And it's a really great space for reflection. I used to think to myself so much that nobody understands what I'm going through or nobody gets this emotion or feeling I'm getting. But when I entered this space and hearing all the experiences, even though like people haven't gone through the exact situations I've been through, it's that like shared emotion or that shared feeling, and that helped me realize that like, wow, I do have such a support system around me. How has the PC space helped you grow as a mentor towards your students? Just seeing the impact I have on them. All my students are very different, have different personalities, but I love that. Being a mentor isn't all about being perfect. At the end of the day, it's mostly about just being real and being someone that people can authentically look up to. Being someone that gives others a comfortable space to just be. What would you want to say to someone who's hesitant on joining the PC space? Like what Miles Morales says in, like, Into the Spider-Verse, you have to take a leap of faith. You really do. You can definitely go in with a lot of fear. But it's one of those spaces that you definitely grow into and you realize that you're not growing alone. Your presence alone is more than valued in the PC space. To apply as a PC, to get a PC, to come to open practicum, to befriend a PC, you just have to be open. Whether it's open to conversation, open to listening, open to learning, your perspective still matters even if you don't think it does. I, I was in the experience where I was really scared. I was not involved in KP anymore. I knew that it meant doing the commute like twice a week for me. But when you, when you take that first dip in and it's your choice of like if you're going to pull back or if you're going to fully go in, and I think the best choice you can do is just fully go in. What do you love most about the PC space? Oh, no! 100%

title: I Stopped Fearing Anxiety And This Happened
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Sunny days are overrated. That's what I just kept thinking about in this moment. Chasing sun was only a part of a program they gave us. And maybe that's where we get it wrong. Anxiety is not that bad. But, like all things, complexity seems to creep in. The human mind is quite complex. Deals with many things, calculates many decisions, and makes judgments every moment. It is said that mental pain is less dramatic than physical pain. Both are hard to carry, but mental pain seems to stay a little longer. This message hit harder when I landed in South Africa. I didn't really understand it, but at that point, when I reflect on it now as I edit this video, it really hit me. This was a place I always wondered about, place I imagined, place I only saw in pictures and videos, and then I actually was here. And all I can see is the small things that I've never seen before. Different air, different sky, different road in front of me. And you would think at a moment like this, it would be perfect. But then I felt it, that little tiny itch of anxiety. Not some big panic attack, no heavy breathing, just a feeling inside like something was still trying to get my attention. I started asking myself, why is this even here? I'm in the place I always wanted to see, across the ocean, took the longest plane ride of my life, and I'm standing inside something I used to only imagine. So why am I still feeling a little unsettled, uneasy? And maybe that's what anxiety does. It follows you into beautiful places, not always to ruin them. Maybe sometimes, and just sometimes, to ask you what you've been ignoring.

His slow pace, characterized by thoughtful pauses, is accompanied by a gentle, ambient, and slightly melancholic synth soundtrack playing softly in the background. He speaks about the nature of anxiety, comparing mental and physical pain, and shares his personal experience of feeling anxious despite traveling to a long-desired destination in South Africa. The overall atmosphere of the recording is contemplative, poetic, and deeply emotional.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 Review, but I Respect Your Time..
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: So you clicked this video to see if the new Z Fold 5 is all hype, or maybe you want to buy it so you've watched 54 videos already. Either way, my day starts off turning this tiny ass phone into a massive tablet, literally because I can, and realizing I forgot to charge it last night after all my scumbag activities. Luckily, the new silicon carbon battery is fat, giving solid screen on time. Likewise, Samsung decided to cook with this form factor, being that it's short and fat, but also absurdly thin all at the same time. Well done, Samsung. Still, for me, the Z Fold 5 can blast music hella loud with stereo speakers while I clean my disgusting mouth, and yet, somehow, they fit dual speakers into this wildly thin frame. Right now, I'm hyper-fixated on music from the '60s. Maybe it's because I'm a geriatric ass millennial, or maybe it's just having a tablet for a phone. Regardless, the speakers on here do sound excellent. Not as good as the 23 Ultra, but definitely solid. Turning on the bright ass cover screen to see what's going on for my day, I'm realizing I have no friends, but at least I can still watch Saturday morning cartoons and count all my internet points at the same time, and just marvel at the fact that I can put this whole thing in my pocket. Call it multitasking, call it generational brain rot. Just imagine an iPad mini folding in half and putting it in your pocket. Enjoying some more of my morning though, I'm making some performative pour over coffee while watching some more cartoons and catching up on all your lovely comments. Shout out to TimK4861 for tapping in. You, sir, are a gangster. And would you look at that, somehow we're just about to hit 125k subs. I have no idea what's wrong with any of you or myself. I guess people really dig when their time is both wasted and respected at the same time. Holding this thing though, it's hard not to appreciate the passport size and marvel at how good this feels in hand. Thin and light while folded, and even thinner when opened, yet still well balanced. Comfortably holding this in one hand is almost a non-issue, and I can dramatically silhouette in front of my window while sipping coffee. I mean, it's not too much different than the Fold 4, but there is something special about having a shorter form factor. Seemingly the love child between a BlackBerry and 13 Mini, I can say the camera is surprisingly good. Sure, you're not getting the telephoto lens you'd get on the Ultra, but both the main and ultrawide 50-megapixel lenses give you enough resolution to crop where you need to. And yeah, as a photographer, I'm straight booty cheeks, but this camera holds up marvelously and does a lot of the heavy lifting. Where it actually shines for me though is the fact that this does get Samsung Log, similar to both the Ultras, which allows me to edit and color grade more professional-looking content, even...

title: 2 - I Had ACL Reconstruction Surgery Today – Full Update
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Well, it's D-day. I've been waiting for this one. Very anxious, didn't sleep brilliantly last night. My wife's now driving me to Winchester so I can get into that hospital and have the reconstruction surgery using the hamstring and uh, yeah, reconstructing the uh, the ACL tendon in my left knee. Um, so yeah, I'm going to take you with, with me as much as I can. I hope I'll be able to film in hospital. Obviously, I won't be able to film in the theater, um, but yeah, I'll see you there. Well, it's just before the procedure. I've had six people visit me so far. I've had someone take my menu, I've had a physiotherapist in here, I've had a nurse in here. Who else we had? The surgeon, two nurses, yeah, the anesthetist, and the anesthetist. So, it's uh, been a busy old time, it's barely stopped, but I just wanted to do a quick update. My wife Sam's here to support me throughout this, this journey, which is great. Um, and uh, the surgeon's in, I've just met him, um, just gone through everything and uh, they'll take me through soon to be anesthetized and uh, then it's time for the operation, which I won't know anything about. So, uh, next update, see you on the other side. So, that's it, I'm out the other side. They've given me fentanyl, they've given me morphine. My knee feels like it's been hit with a sledgehammer, but it's not a sharp pain, it's a dull pain, and I'm, I'm not going to lie to you, a little bit out of it. But it's done, it was a success. I think less than an hour ago, I was, was in it. Um, keen to get the PhysioLab thing on as quickly as possible. But yeah, it's not, it's not that bad. I guess the drugs are doing their job. So, yeah, I'll do another update in a little bit and see how I'm getting on, but at the moment, I just think, I think I'm just going to have a nice little sleep now. Yeah. Well, I'm about three hours out of surgery now. I won't lie to you, still feeling a little bit woozy. I'm on fentanyl and, and morphine. And uh, that's starting to fade off now, so I'm going to have a little bit of dinner in a minute. But, interestingly, they've already put the PhysioLab on me and that cold compression feels absolutely glorious, probably the fentanyl as well at this stage. But so far, so good.
caption: A British male voice is featured in this audio, narrating his experience of undergoing ACL reconstruction surgery. The audio has four distinct segments. In the first segment, he speaks in a clear, excited, yet anxious tone while in a car, with upbeat instrumental music playing in the background. In the second segment, he is in a hospital room, his voice still clear and energetic as he describes meeting various hospital staff before the operation. In the third segment, immediately post-surgery, his voice becomes very groggy, quiet, and slow as he describes the effects of painkillers like fentanyl and morphine and the dull pain in his knee. In the final segment, three hours post-surgery, his voice is slightly more alert but still relaxed, and the upbeat music returns as he talks about the cold compression therapy he is receiving.

title: Besremi dose 43 - Reflux, digestion🩸My Polycythemia Vera Journey @MatthewMesler
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hey everybody, it's Matt. We are back again for the 43rd dose of Bezremi. Today is May 29th, 2026. We'll be doing the left thigh at 100 micrograms. It is the 9th time dosing at the monthly dosing for me, so I've been doing it for the past 9 months. I feel very stable right now. A couple videos ago, I shared some of my, you know, blood panel results. Doctors seem pleased with where I'm at. A couple numbers are low, but nothing is out of the, out of bounds really. And so we're going to keep doing that. Hopefully being able to, maybe spread it out from four weeks to five weeks and stay at that 100 micrograms and just continue to kind of wean and check results. But what I want to touch on in this video today is something I've been dealing with. I've talked again about it in some of the videos. I think most of it pertains to the portal vein thrombosis, which happened about 2 years ago, for anyone who's just tuning in. I had a portal vein thrombosis, which led to the polycythemia vera diagnosis, so blood clots in the stomach. Lost a lot of weight. Lost my appetite for a little bit. But as I'm improving over these past 2 years, I have noticed that I'm back to kind of eating normal. And really reflecting on what is causing this acid reflux that I keep getting. Obviously, there's a change in my mechanics, my system has changed forever. But, you know, I can eat healthy, I can have broccoli and cauliflower and sweet potatoes and chicken, everything kind of lean and mean, and I'm getting reflux. And so I'm wondering, what is going on? Diving a little deeper, there is, there's a thing called mechanical, basically again, the mechanics have changed in here, so mechanical reflux. What I, what I've determined is that I have always overeaten. Like, I love to eat, I don't gain weight easily, so I fill my plate more than I need, usually go back for seconds. title: Why A Psalm for the Wild-Built Feels Like Therapy for the Soul.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Becky Chambers' A Psalm for the Wild-Built is a thoughtful, calming story that blends hope, philosophy, and adventure into a deeply human journey. Here's a friendly, engaging audiobook summary style script designed for around 10 to 11 minutes of narration. In a world where people often feel exhausted, disconnected, and overwhelmed by the pressure to constantly do more, imagine a future where humanity actually chose a different path. A future where society stepped away from endless consumption and rebuilt itself around balance, sustainability, and peace. Now, imagine that, one day, after centuries of silence, a robot walks out of the wilderness and asks a simple but life-changing question. "What do people need?" That's the heart of A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a beautifully quiet yet powerful novella by Becky Chambers. This isn't a story packed with giant battles or dramatic twists. Instead, it's the kind of story that gently sits beside you and asks you to think about your own life, your purpose, and what truly makes you happy. And by the end, it leaves you feeling strangely comforted, like someone finally gave you permission to breathe. The story takes place on the moon of Panga where humans once lived alongside robots, but long ago, the robots gained self-awareness and decided they no longer wanted to serve humanity. Instead of fighting, the robots peacefully walked away into the wilderness and humans let them go. Over time, people adapted. Society became slower, greener, and more community focused. Technology still exists, but it no longer controls people's lives. The world Becky Chambers creates feels hopeful because it imagines humanity learning from its mistakes instead of repeating them forever. At the center of this story is a character named Sibling Dex, a tea monk. In this world, monks don't simply live in temples. They travel around offering tea and emotional support to anyone who needs comfort. Dex spends their days listening to people's worries, helping them process emotions, and giving them a brief moment of peace in a busy life. On the surface, it sounds meaningful and fulfilling, but despite helping everyone else, Dex feels restless inside. There's an emptiness they can't explain. A quiet voice keeps asking, "Is this really all there is?" That question becomes the emotional engine of the story.

title: The Psychology of the Self-Doubt Loop: Why Reassurance Never Works
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In 2016, Casey Neistat ended the most-watched daily vlog on the internet at the exact moment it was still growing. 5 million subscribers, over a billion views, revenue climbing every month. He stopped anyway, telling his audience there was nothing left to say through the format. The metrics were screaming reassurance at him. He ignored them. Seth Godin has published something close to 8,000 blog posts. On his own site, he's written that focus groups and informal feedback are a trap. The people you ask are rarely the ones your work is actually for. He built one of the most cited marketing platforms alive by refusing to let outside opinion gate what got published. Jason Fried co-founded Basecamp on the same refusal. In Rework, he and David Heinemeier Hansson call waiting for perfect information a trap with no exit. Decisions don't get safer the longer you sit on them, they just pile up. Basecamp shipped early and often, without waiting for a chorus of yeses first. Three different fields, same move. All three stopped asking if it was okay and started reading the actual result instead. There's a name for what they refused to do. It comes out of three separate, unconnected corners of clinical research that landed on the same finding without meaning to. Paul Salkovskis' 1985 model of health anxiety, James Coyne's 1976 theory of depression, Adam Radomsky's research on what's called checking by proxy in OCD. Different disorders, different decades, same mechanism. Reassurance lowers anxiety immediately, then the anxiety comes back, often stronger, because the uncertainty underneath it was never actually resolved, just rented for a few hours. I call this the certainty debt loop. Every time you ask for reassurance instead of letting the uncertainty sit, you're not paying off the doubt

title: Stress, Conflict, Justice The Human Architecture of Stress, Conflict, and Justice
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You know that feeling. Picture this: a quiet terrace, an overcast sky, and two colleagues, Mira and Aarav, just sitting down with a thermos of warm water. The air feels heavy. And then Mira says something that I think absolutely every single one of us has felt at some point in our careers. She says, "I've been feeling stretched. Not just tired. Like I'm being pulled in too many directions." Man, that right there, that is the very real, very heavy feeling of workplace overwhelm. Welcome to today's explainer where we're going to unpack exactly what Mira is feeling. Today, we are exploring the human architecture of stress, conflict, and justice. We'll be looking at how your individual strain, interpersonal friction, and systemic fairness all come together to build your fundamental experience at work. It's a truly fascinating framework drawn from Mira and Aarav's terrace reflections, and I am so thrilled to guide you through it. Okay, let's look at our roadmap for today. We're going to start with the anatomy of work stress, then look at coping and interventions, understand the dynamics of conflict, and discuss how to actually resolve that conflict. After that, we'll explore the three pillars of justice, and we'll wrap up with why justice is a daily choice. Let's dive right into section one, the anatomy of work stress. This is all about the individual experience. Now, Aarav defines stress in a very specific way. He says it's the physical and emotional strain that arises when job demands literally exceed a person's capacity to cope. Notice that it isn't just about having a heavy workload. It's really about a lack of control, clarity, support, and meaning. And Mira adds another crucial layer to this. She says stress can be totally silent. It doesn't always look like panic or tears at your desk. Sometimes, you know, it is simply a slow erosion of joy. So, what actually causes this erosion? Well, the major culprits range from role ambiguity and role conflict to work overload, lack of autonomy, poor relationships, and organizational change. Let's ground this with a real example. Mira shared this story about an internship where she was handed tasks with absolutely zero context. I mean, she didn't know who to report to, what the metrics for success even looked like, or how to ask for help. That is classic role ambiguity, and let me tell you, it causes severe, silent stress. And the consequences of this, they ripple outward.

title: Arrive - One morning at a time
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Maya wrote in a gratitude journal every morning for 19 days. Then three mornings in a row, she didn't. Most habit apps would have shamed her back. Arrive doesn't. This is Arrive, one minute a day, the gentler the accountability, the higher the return rate. Arrive opens with one question. How do you arrive today? 38 named emotions grouped by weight. From the moment Maya picks one, the rest of the screen tunes to what she chose. Because she picked anxious, the mindfulness agent runs first, a short breathing or grounding exercise. The user can skip, most don't. Then, the reflection agent writes a paragraph of witness shaped to her mood, and the journal opens. Three things make Arrive genuinely agentic, not a journal with a chatbot bolted on. First, adaptive strategies. The insight agent receives the last seven entries: emotion streak, average length, missed days, dominant feeling. After three anxious mornings, the reply shortens and softens. The gold chip is the system telling the user in plain language what it noticed, before responding to today. That's adapt based on what the user is actually carrying, not on paper. Second, agent coordination. When Maya wrote anxious, the mindfulness agent had already switched from breathing to grounding, because breathwork on entrenched anxiety can worsen it. The reflection agent shortened its paragraph, the insight agent kept its reply under 12 words. Three agents, one shared context object, one voice rulebook. Nobody is repeating themselves at the user. Nobody is congratulating them, either. When she misses a day, the grace agent writes the re-entry: one soft sentence, no guilt. Grace days are pure math, one per month, automatic. title: Marketing for Physiotherapists: Get More Bookings Today
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You could be the best physiotherapist in your area, but if your calendar still has gaps, there is a problem. And most of the time, that problem is marketing. When someone searches "physio near me", your clinic doesn't show up, or it doesn't give them enough reason to book. That's what we're fixing today. Hey there, I'm Svetlana from Cuey, and we make digital marketing simple for small businesses. Today, I'll share the best practices for marketing your physiotherapy clinic, starting with what matters most. So, what does actually count as marketing for a physio clinic? Basically, everything that helps someone find you, decide you're right for them, and then book. That's your Google profile, your website, your reviews, the relationship you've got with the GP down the road, or the Pilates studio, or the local running club. Get this right, and patients show up already trusting you. Before any of that, decide who you actually want to treat. You could have the best-looking website in your city, but if it's trying to talk to everyone, runners, office workers, post-op patients, retirees, all at once, it lands with nobody. Pick one or two groups. Runners with knee pain, desk workers with a stiff neck, whatever fits what you are genuinely good at. The goal is simple: someone lands on your site and thinks, "They treat people like me." Once you've picked your focus, back it up with your specific experience. Your actual training is what makes someone choose you over the clinic two streets over. Now to the things that move the needle. Step one, get found locally. Type "physio near me" into Google right now. See who comes up. Want to be one of them? Start with your Google Business Profile. Fill in every field, address, phone, hours, your full list of services. Add real photos, outside the building so people can actually find your door, inside the clinic, the treatment room. Google's own data says that profiles with photos get 42% more requests for directions and 35% more clicks through to the website. A handful of decent photos and you're already ahead of half the clinics in your area. Get your category right, too. Physiotherapist as your primary category, and then add sports medicine clinic or rehabilitation center if that's genuinely what you do. Then, reviews. Check how many the top clinics near you have got. That number is your target. After every patient finishes a course or a treatment, send a quick message with a direct link.

title: The Morning After I K*ll Myself
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The morning after I killed myself, will I still wake to my mother's prayer, her voice trembling softly between incense and faith, as if God still listens to tired women before sunrise? Will I still hear my father's familiar scolding for not waking up early enough, those small ordinary rants I once mistook for irritation, never realizing they were love wearing a rough voice? Will I still receive those annoying texts from my manager, those weekend meetings I hate with all my heart, and still secretly laugh at how life never asks whether we are tired before demanding more? Will my best friend still wait outside her house for me, ready to pull me away from this suffocating city life, just for an hour, just to remind me that breathing is still possible? Will my mother still save strawberries for me because she remembers what I like, even when I forget what it feels like to be loved? Will my father still stand outside the main gate of our house if I come home late from work, pretending he was just walking outside after having dinner, when really he was waiting to make sure I returned safely? Will those annoying relatives still ask those annoying questions about my marriage, my future, my life, as if they know anything about the storms a quiet person survives without making a sound? No. The day after I leave, none of it will reach me. Not the daily noises that make me frustrated every day. Not the love hidden inside that noise. Not my loved ones waiting for me to reach home safely. Not my parents worrying about my safety. Not the ordinary little things that look so small until I imagined a world without them. And maybe that is the tragedy of hopelessness. It does not always come because life has no love in it. Sometimes it comes because pain grows so loud that it drowns out the love that was there all along. While I was losing hope, everyone around me was still quietly holding hope for me.

The narrative contrasts the mundane, sometimes annoying aspects of daily life—such as her father's scolding, her manager's texts, and relatives' questions—with the realization that these were actually expressions of love and care. The performance ends on a powerful note, reflecting on how pain can drown out the love that was always present.

title: Just Do It - Spoken Word by Paul Harris Steward ft Ansel King
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Thank God I don't look like what I've been through. Tell you the truth, I'm lucky that I'm even standing right here in front of all of you. I was 14 years old the first time, the first time those thoughts crossed my mind, but see, I was too worried about leaving my mother and my little brother behind. In high school, it was bad. No, in college, it was worse. Shit, I don't even know how I made it through my 20s and 30s because those thoughts used to float through my mind, but I used to be able to push them out right in time. Tell you the truth, I did not know that anything was wrong. I'm from Chicago. I was raised to be strong, never show any weakness. What happens in this house stays in this house. My mom said, "Boy, you better always keep your business to yourself." So, I thought that meant even if it jeopardized my mental health. See, I've come to the conclusion that my happy moments, my happy moments in my life, they're like waves, they never stand still. I've been in denial and hurting for 32 years and it hasn't been easy to heal. But it seems like the older I got, the thoughts stopped floating. In my mind, those demons would stay and play every day, got me going through it. They're no longer whispering, now every day they're screaming, telling me to just do it. I can't outrun it. I read the books, took the meds, sat in therapy trying to understand my head, but some nights the darkness wins, and I'm exhausted from fighting it. I tell my family I'm fine, but I don't know how to explain. Someone said, "Paul, don't worry, they're just passive, intrusive thoughts. It's only dangerous if you make a plan." Well, I remember the day I held that pen in my hand. On my calendar, I circled October 14th, 2021, and I wrote, "just do it." And this time, it wasn't just a cry for help. This time, it wasn't just words of my mouth, I swear to God, y'all, this time I wouldn't chicken out. I had already been in the house for two weeks by myself. I look at my clock, and I realize I only had eight minutes left. I pick up my phone one last time, and then I saw her. She was on The Breakfast Club doing an interview, and she said, "Come out of those dark rooms and get some help." It felt like she was talking to me. It felt like she understood my pain. So, for the rest of my life, I'll say her name. Jenifer Lewis, Jenifer Lewis, Jenifer Lewis saved me because her words stayed in my head to the point where I started seeing my mom at the edge of my bed. My mom said, "I miss you baby, but I'm not ready to see you yet." Bro, that night my mom fought for me. Dog, my mom fought for me. She took me out of his hands. She gave me enough strength. The next morning, I checked myself in because my heart was dark, and so was my soul.

title: From Anxiety to Alignment: A Spoken Word Healing Journey
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: This is me in my 20s. A mind too loud, out pacing my breath. Running in circles with anxiety's depth. Depression would sit like a weight on my chest, a body on edge that never found rest. Irritated, agitated, out of place, wearing a calm but losing the race. Unbalanced steps on a thin tightline, losing my body while chasing my mind. I ate what I knew, what I thought was right. Meats on my plate and dairy at night. Ice cream melting to soften the day, gallons of milk as years slipped away. Feeding the habit and quieting the ache, numbing the signals my body would make. Chasing a comfort that would never stay, holding me gently then drifting away. But something inside was trying to speak. A truth in my body steady but weak. A whisper beneath all the noise and the fear calling me closer, I couldn't yet hear. I didn't know then what I know today, that the mind can lead you further and further astray. When it grips too tight, when it won't unwind, you lose the body, ah, you lose the divine. Now, this is me nearing my 50s. Breath more steady, movements more free. Vegan, mostly raw, alive in the skin, feeding my body, woo, from deep within. Vegetables and fruits and nuts and seeds, with light fueling my days, restoring my night.

title: Quiet Desperation
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You ever notice how some people look completely fine on the outside? But something about them feels tired? Not physically tired. Soul tired. They wake up, go to work, answer texts, laugh at the right moments, pay bills, scroll their phone at night, and repeat the same cycle over and over again like a machine pretending to be a human being. And nobody notices because nothing is technically wrong. That's the terrifying part. Quiet desperation doesn't always look like a breakdown. Sometimes it looks like functioning perfectly while slowly dying inside. Henry David Thoreau once wrote that most men live lives of quiet desperation, and the older I get, the more disturbing that sentence becomes. Because desperation is easy to recognize when it's loud. When someone's screaming, spiraling, crashing out, everybody sees it. But quiet desperation, that hides behind routines, behind careers, behind relationships, behind smiling photos, and "I'm good" responses. It's the kind of suffering that learns how to behave, and I think a lot of people fall into it without even realizing it. It starts with tiny compromises, tiny betrayals of yourself. "I'll chase my dream later." "I'll settle for this job for now." "I'll stay in this relationship because at least it's familiar." And at first, it feels temporary, but temporary has a way of becoming permanent when fear gets comfortable. Years pass. Your responsibilities grow roots around you, and one day you wake up realizing you built an entire life around survival, but forgot to include yourself in it. That's why some people feel empty even after getting everything they thought they wanted. Because achievement without alignment creates exhaustion. You can win the game and still hate waking up in the morning. You can make money and still feel spiritually bankrupt. You can be surrounded by people and still feel emotionally isolated. Quiet desperation is the gap between the life you're living and the life your soul knows you were meant for. And social media makes it worse. Now everybody performs happiness like it's a full-time job. People don't even ask, "Am I fulfilled anymore?" They ask, "Do I look fulfilled?"

title: The Truth About Recovering From Depression (That Changed Me)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: People often ask me when I finally got better, as if there was one magical morning when I opened my eyes and everything felt different. As if healing arrived all at once, like flipping a switch. Darkness one moment, light the next. But that's not how it happened, and honestly, that's not how healing usually works. My depression didn't leave overnight. It left quietly, slowly, almost invisibly, like the tide pulling away from the shore. One day, the water would retreat and I'd catch a glimpse of the beach beneath it. I'd laugh at a video, reply to a message, cook a simple meal, take a walk outside. For a few hours, life felt manageable. Then the tide would return. Not violently, not dramatically, just enough to make me wonder if I'd imagined those better moments. For a long time, that cycle frustrated me. Whenever I felt better, I expected it to stay. Whenever I felt worse, I assumed I was back at the beginning. I didn't realize healing was happening underneath it all. I remember mornings when getting out of bed felt impossible. Not because I was physically tired, because mentally, everything felt heavy. Simple tasks felt enormous: brushing my teeth, taking a shower, answering a text. Things that seemed effortless for everyone else felt like climbing a mountain. And the hardest part was knowing what I was supposed to do. I knew exercise could help, I knew fresh air could help, I knew routines could help. But depression has a way of turning simple actions into impossible missions. Knowing and doing become two completely different things. It's like having a map but no energy to start the journey. Then one day, something happened, something that would seem completely insignificant to most people. I got up and took a shower.

title: Senior Depression Doesn't Look Like Sadness—Watch for This Instead
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: If your mom or dad has seemed more worn out lately, more on edge, or just kind of distant, most of us chalk it up to getting older. That's just what happens, right? But honestly, a lot of the time, that's not what's going on at all. And missing what's actually happening can make things so much harder down the road. So today, I want to walk you through five signs that your parent might be struggling with depression, not just aging, and what you can realistically do to help. Here's the thing about depression in older adults. It's one of the most missed diagnoses in the country. And the reason it keeps getting overlooked, it doesn't look the way we expect it to. There's usually no breakdown, no "I think I'm depressed." It disguises itself as stuff that just looks like normal aging. That's exactly how it slips by everyone, including doctors. So let's go through the signs, one at a time. Sign number one: fatigue and low energy. The first sign is a kind of bone-deep exhaustion. Not "I didn't sleep great" tired, more like a heaviness that just follows them around, no matter how much rest they get. Maybe they're sleeping in more than usual, napping constantly, or they just seem completely drained by the smallest things. Now, yes, some tiredness comes with age. That's real. But when it shows up out of nowhere, or keeps getting worse week after week, that's not something to brush off. It's the change you want to pay attention to, not just the tiredness itself. Sign number two: irritability, not sadness. This one catches families completely off guard. When most of us picture depression, we picture someone crying, shutting down, saying they feel hopeless. But in older adults, it often comes out as irritability, snapping over little things, getting frustrated way faster than usual, seeming angry for reasons nobody can quite figure out. So if your parent has gotten noticeably more short-tempered lately, and that's just not like them, please don't write it off as them being grumpy. There may be a lot more going on underneath that. Sign number three: losing interest in the things they love. Think about what your parent used to love doing. Maybe it was tending to their garden, watching their shows, cooking a big Sunday dinner for whoever could make it. And now, they just don't. They're not interested. title: Stuck Already? Why Your 2026 Resolutions Are Slipping Away | Wrightly Depressed
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: As the final days of January 2026 slip through our fingers like the last grains of sand in an hourglass, I find myself enveloped in a familiar sense of malaise. The champagne is long since gone flat, the confetti swept away, and the echoes of Auld Lang Syne have faded into the ether. We stand now at the precipice of a new year, yet I, like so many others, feel inexplicably stuck. The dawn of 2026 was heralded with such promise, such optimism. The arbitrary flip of the calendar's page seemed to offer a tabula rasa, a chance to shed the skin of years past and emerge, phoenix-like, into the new. We scribbled resolutions on scraps of paper, whispered promises to the universe, and clinked glasses to the future. Yet here we are, mere weeks later, watching as our best-laid plans begin to list precariously, like a ship taking on water. Old habits, it seems, have die-hard convictions. They creep back into our lives like ivy, their tendrils insidiously wrapping around our good intentions, threatening to strangle them before they can bear fruit. I had sworn to eschew the snooze button, to embrace the dawn with the vigor of a Benedictine monk. Yet my alarm clock and I remain locked in our eternal pas de deux, those nine tantalizing minutes of stolen slumber too sweet a temptation. The gym membership card, once a badge of honor, a testament to my commitment to physical renewal, now languishes in the dark recesses of my wallet. The meditation app, downloaded with such gusto, has been relegated to a distant corner of my smartphone's home screen, its daily reminders met with increasing indifference.

title: Depression Starts in the Gut? The Hidden Truth Nobody Tells You
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever felt heavy without knowing why? Have you ever woken up tired, even after a full night of sleep? Have you ever felt sadness, but there was no clear reason? What if the answer is not in your thoughts, but in your stomach? Yes, you heard that right. Your gut, your digestive system, may be deeply connected to your emotions, your mood, and even depression. Welcome to Universal Wisdom. Today, we explore a powerful truth that most people never notice: the secret link between your gut and your mind. This is not just motivation; this is science, awareness, and deep understanding. Take a slow breath, and listen carefully, because what you are about to hear may change how you see your body forever. The second brain inside you. Inside your body, there is a system so intelligent that scientists call it the second brain. This system lives in your gut. It controls digestion, but it also communicates constantly with your brain. Every second, signals travel between your stomach and your mind. If your gut is healthy, your mind feels calm. If your gut is disturbed, your emotions become unstable. Think about this: when you feel nervous, your stomach tightens. When you feel fear, digestion slows down. When you feel stress, your appetite changes. This is not coincidence. Your gut and brain are in constant conversation. And when this communication breaks, emotional imbalance begins. The hidden cause people ignore. Many people try to fix depression by changing thoughts only. They try positive thinking, motivation, distraction, but they ignore the physical root. Imagine trying to fix a tree's leaves while the roots are weak. Real healing begins at the root. Your gut contains trillions of microorganisms. These tiny life forms help control mood, energy, and mental clarity. When these microorganisms are balanced, you feel light, focused, and emotionally stable.
