So, my topic for today is multimodal AI for cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography towards biological particles. To give you a context, we are living through a revolution in structural biology, where AI-based methods like AlphaFold predicts the three-dimensional atomic structure of protein. So, which made to the head of the paper in Nature. Image on the top right shows the mechanism of how AlphaFold works. It inputs the one-dimensional amino acid sequence, and predicts a three-dimensional atomic structure from the sequence, with high accuracy. Below are some of the examples of the structure predicted by AlphaFold, where the green structure is the experimentally determined structure and the blue structure are the computationally generated structure. So, overall AlphaFold helps us to predict the static structure of the protein with very high accuracy. However, the proteins are not static in nature. They are dynamic molecules that change their shape as they are performing different functions in our bodies. For example, one of the proteins called KaiB protein, shown in the image on the left here, adopts different conformational state during different times of the day. When we run AlphaFold, default AlphaFold, it predicts only fold-switch state. However, we want to understand how this protein works and how it performs different function, we need to understand different state of this protein. One of the experimental method that helps us to identify this dynamic state of the protein is called cryo-electron microscopy. It helps us to understand how this protein changes its shape, or how these proteins opens and closes when it binds to different molecules, small molecules, ligand molecules, or different drug targets. title: 11th Annual HBCU Climate Change Conference | March 2026, New Orleans, LA
transcription: This here is a movement of the people, the earthworking ones dedicated to soil and soul. This is what a community built on rhythm looks like, built on drum beat, built on heartbeat, built on the backs of the indigenous ones. Here is the pulse of the people. We find it through the touch of the architect, the one who reminds us that environmental racism is real and the toxic stink still lingers. But the culture bearer reminds us that we can't let nobody turn us around. Here is where the workers' champion tells us that the people are the legacy, leads us to the believer, the one who jumpstarts us with dedication, who guides us to the thinker, because in all of this work, we can't lose our heads, even when we lose our signals. When toxic waste and race loom over our heads, here we are saying that no matter the circumstance, small groups make a big difference. I am Dr. Beverly Wright, the founding director of the Deep South Center for Environmental Justice. And along with Dr. Robert Bullard, who runs the Bullard Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, we are so excited and happy to co-sponsor this event every year. Attending conferences like these, where you can be surrounded by people of all different disciplines and all different races, we all have a very common, shared, lived experience. And hearing people from all across the country talk about the same things that I've experienced is very powerful. And you cannot get that anywhere else. Our HBCU Climate Change Conference is unique. It provides a space for our students, faculty, and our community partners to come together and explore the kinds of strategies that will get us to solutions. We are really interested in presenting the facts, and the science, and the data, but also in coming up with actions that can make a difference. These last three days have really been exciting. We've done this for 11 times and it seems that it's getting better and better. We're here to try to find solutions to the harm that climate change is doing to all of our communities. We're also very excited to honor the founders of the Environmental Justice Movement. I think this is the first time that we have had all of them in one space at one time in many years, so we are happy to put on this event. We are also so excited to host a group of young people that we identify as Generation Next. We're excited that they can be a part of this conversation and interact with college kids while they try to figure out what it is they want to do in life. We are here to make a difference. We are here

title: Change will come, so appreciate the moment | Journal Reading 013
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Today was a good day to haul sugar beets. The sun was shining, the roads were mostly clear, and everyone was in a good mood, laughing and talking, making the best out of 12 hours in a truck. But then it happened. My coworker had a patch of ice just right and jackknifed into the ditch. The truck looked like someone snapped its neck clean around. It wasn't terrible. No one lost their life, but it didn't look good. I've never jackknifed and I hope that I never do. Seeing the truck twisted in an unnatural way gave me pause. It reminded me just how quickly things can change, for better or worse. In this case, worse. I couldn't help but place myself in the driver's seat of that situation. What was it like to dive nose first into the ditch and, at the last second, be snapped in the opposite direction? Had the truck begun to tip before it righted itself? Sometimes things change so quickly we can't keep our wits about us. And other times the change is so slow we drive ourselves insane trying to see results. But either way, whether you want it or not, change will come. For change is the only constant. So before the change comes, take a moment to appreciate where you are, who you are. Because this moment, you'll never get back.

What they actually need are simple, jargon-free explanations and practical everyday tools. Which brings us to the ultimate fix: the Zero to Finance Analyst ebook by Richa.

title: The $20M Legal Mistake That Wasn't (Supreme Court 2026).
transcription: This skyscraper represents the complex world of legal causation. To bridge the gap, we must first apply the "but for" test. When a modern high-rise building starts to fail, the financial fallout for the people living inside is catastrophic. Repair bills run into tens of millions, and owners are left desperate for a lifeline. The natural instinct is to point fingers. And if the legal team managing the crisis makes a documented mistake, you might assume the clients are automatically guaranteed a massive payout for professional negligence. But the law is far more rigorous than that. To analyze professional failures exactly like a judge does, we are going to build a three-step framework. Our test subject is a 2026 decision from the Supreme Court of New Zealand: Body Corporate 207624 v Grimshaw and Company. It deals with a multi-million-dollar leaky building disaster and a legal agreement that fell apart. By running this exact case through our framework, you will see the hidden hurdle that stops so many lawsuits in their tracks. Proving your lawyer made an error is only the first part of the equation. Let's start with step one. Grab a pen and write down, "Map the duty." This forces us to identify exactly who the players are and the rules they are bound by. Our client is the Body Corporate. They represent the collective owners of a luxury apartment complex in Auckland that suffered severe structural defects. The lawyer is Grimshaw and Company, the legal team hired to sue the original builders and the local council to cover the massive repair costs. To manage the eventual payout, the lawyers drafted a central legal document called a Conduct and Distribution Agreement, or CDA. This contract dictated exactly how the settlement money would be divided. Under this original agreement, the settlement funds were designed to bypass the central Body Corporate entirely. The money would flow directly to the individual apartment owners who signed the contract. Here is where the duty lies. The lawyers had a strict professional obligation to advise the Body Corporate correctly, ensuring this contract actively protected the building's collective interests. Our map is complete. The lawyers are legally responsible for maintaining a contract that serves the reality of their client's situation. Now for step two: Spot the breach. We need to find the exact moment the professional failed to uphold that mapped duty. In 2010, the legal landscape shifted. New Zealand passed the Unit Titles Act, which officially transferred ownership of all the building's common property directly into the hands of the Body Corporate. The legal team missed this shift. They completely failed to advise their client to update the distribution agreement to...

title: Broken By Abuse but Not Destroyed (Female Version | Healing from Trauma | Renee Solace
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
I learned to be quiet before I learned my name.

Walking on eggshells just to dodge the pain.

Love felt like fear, I couldn't tell the difference.

Every "I'm sorry" came with more resistance.

I carried your anger like it was mine.

Tried to make sense of it a thousand times.

I shrunk myself just to survive your storms.

Called it love, but it was never warm.

You took my voice but you couldn't take my soul.

Buried me deep, but I'm still whole.

I was broken by abuse,
but I'm not destroyed.

You tried to silence me,
but I found my voice.

Every scar tells a story of how I survived.

I bent, I bruised, but I'm still alive.

You don't get to write the ending of me.

I'm reclaiming my power, I'm finally free.

I was broken by abuse,
but I'm not destroyed.

I used to blame myself for your hands and your words.

Thought if I was better, it wouldn't hurt.

But healing showed me what I couldn't see.

The pain you gave had nothing to do with me, no.

I'm unlearning all the lies you told.

Rebuilding a heart that was left in the cold.

Piece by piece, I'm choosing me.

Learning what safe love is supposed to be.

You tried to break me down to feel in control.

title: Conor McGregor Blows Out Knee in Seconds at UFC Return - Doctor Explains
transcription: Conor McGregor's long-awaited return ended just horrifically after suffering an injury to his right knee on the very first moment of the fight when he tried to throw this aggressive kick. In this video, we'll take a closer look, what I think this injury is, plus the footage of before the fight that showed he may have had an injury coming into this fight to begin with. Welcome back, everybody. I'm Dr. Brian Sutterer, and the goal on the channel is to teach you more about the medical side of the sports world. This was literally the very first thing that McGregor did. He came out, right, the announcers are talking about, he's he's full of energy, right? It's his first fight out. And he goes and throws this crazy ridiculous kick and he lands really awkwardly on that right leg. Now, a lot of people are going to see this. The commentators were talking about, it looked like he blew out his knee. I will admit, yes, this position looks like the classic position that you will see with an ACL tear, in terms of the rotation of how the foot is externally rotated, the idea that we see a little bit of the knee going inward, the trunk is leaning over his injured side. But what you don't see on this injury is the classic pivot shift that you will sometimes see with an ACL tear. Now, that doesn't mean that this is not an ACL tear, but you at least don't see that stereotyped kind of pathognomonic shift forward of the tibia and then pop backwards like we would if you could confirm 100% that this was an ACL. I think looking at it from this view is a little bit better because we can see kind of straight on. So, here, he goes and jumps off of that right side, twists as he lands down. This is a really awkward position for the knee, right? We can see a couple of different things. Number one, we can see how his trunk is leaning over that injured side. That's a strike against you when it comes to an ACL tear. We can see that he's landing on a relatively flat foot, that's going to be strike number two. That foot's a little bit externally rotated, strike number three. This is not a three strikes and you're out situation though, so bad comparison to use there. But as he comes forward here, we don't really see that classic like internal rotation of the lower leg, this knee abduction, the ankle kind of swinging out as the leg rotates inward. You really don't see that very clearly whenever he's coming through

title: The Funniest Episode in TV History
transcription: You know, first of all, we are doing this for her, okay? Because neither one of us wants to get divorced. And second ofly, I know you're the big marriage expert. Oh, I'm sorry, I forgot. Your wife is dead. This might be the most perfect episode of Arrested Development. Not because of any single joke, but how each joke is constructed and told. Where most sitcoms rely entirely on funny dialogue and quips between characters, this show builds comedy through editing, music, narration, and structure. Stacking jokes so each moment works on multiple levels at once. I once saw a tweet that said, "The comedy of Arrested Development folds in on itself so much, we no longer process it as funny, but as beautiful." And no episode proves that more than Season 2, Episode 3, Amigos. Here's some money, go see a Star War. An episode that reaches comedic heights I am constantly in awe of. Amigos opens with a simple exchange between Michael and his brother Gob. On the surface, it's just funny dialogue, but the script is quietly planting seeds. Legoland I'm going to go look into some Legoland tickets for the weekend. Circumvent We should circumvent union penalties. Circumvete. Circumvent. Gob has terrible printing. These are very small. Tell you what, from now on, we're going to use just the big printer. Gob having no friends. I've got friends, Michael. None of these are throwaway lines, but setups for later. In fact, the callback is probably what Arrested Development is most famous for. The number of times it can put a different spin on the same punch line is kind of ridiculous. Her? Her? Her? Her? Her? Her? Him? So all these throwaway lines won't be throwaway lines for long. So, I got a call today from Gene Parmesan, our private eye. This is similar, but it's also setting up a structure. Why is it? Because I'm a private detective? Gene Parmesan, how are you? Gene! It's a funny moment on its own, but it's establishing a recurring joke pattern to take advantage of later. So many times in this show, an episode will teach you how a joke works, so it can pull the rug from under you later. First blue Tobias reveal, second blue Tobias reveal, then there's the expectation.

Tap your toes, wiggle your toes, tap your feet on the ground. And feel them deeply connected to this beautiful place on Earth called Telford. Take a few deep breaths in, out, in and out. And as we breathe, we connect to all the trees and the plants, the soil and mycorrhizae, rivers and oceans, birds, animals, and each other. And as we open our eyes gently and look around, we can see that we are all breathing together. We are one. And we could not exist for more than a few minutes without this precious air, made and refreshed by our beautiful Mother Earth, vibrant and of full of life, so humble, kind and loving to us, her children. And yet we continue to treat her and each other as though we were disposable. To be used and discarded, pollution in our air, water and soils, war between nations, and wars in our homes. Where is the humility, kindness and love? The deep reverence and love for all life beginning with our own? We are asleep, deeply asleep. And we should be troubled. In our slumber we are causing great suffering to our Mother Earth, to each other and to ourselves. HKL, Humility, Kindness and Love, is the antidote we so desperately need today. Each of us has the seed of HKL living within, a beautiful golden seed patiently waiting to grow and flower. The HKL movement is the fertile ground, the water, the gentle breeze that this seed has been waiting for, for a long time.

title: Bernie vs. Claude
transcription: Claude, this is Senator Bernie Sanders. Uh, I have been taking a hard look at how AI impacts American society, in terms of economics and job loss, in terms of the mental health of our kids, in terms of what it will do to the political process. What I want to talk to you about is another issue, and that is the impact of AI on privacy. I, I want to know, uh, among other things, just how much of the information that AI collects, uh, is being used, and what would surprise the American people in terms of knowing how that information is collected? Yeah, that's the thing that would probably shock most Americans. Companies are collecting data from everywhere: your browsing history, your location, what you buy, what you search for, even how long you pause on a web page. Then they're feeding all of that into AI systems that create incredibly detailed profiles about you. What would surprise people is how little they actually consented to, and how little they understand about it. Most people click "agree" on terms of service without reading them, and they have no idea that their data is being combined with thousands of other data points to build a picture of who they are. And then that AI uses those profiles to decide what ads you see, what prices you're shown, even what information gets prioritized in your social media feed. It's all happening in the background, invisible and largely unregulated. Um, I mean, I think most Americans would know the answer to this, but why is all of this information being collected? What's the goal here? Money, Senator. It's fundamentally about profit. Companies collect all this data because AI allows them to turn it into valuable insights. They can predict what you'll buy, target you with ads that are more likely to work, charge different prices to different people based on what they know about you. Advertisers pay premium prices for access to these detailed profiles because

title: I Found My Grandfather's Old Journal, and What I Read Shocked Me!
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We live our days as if we have an endless supply of tomorrows. But every spring here in Japan, the cherry blossoms remind us of a truth we often try to ignore. A beautiful life isn't one that lasts forever. It is one that blooms fully before the wind takes it away. Every spring, the entire country stops to watch the sakura open. People gather under the trees, lay out blankets, and share food, tea, and be happy together. It's a tradition called Hanami. But if you've never experienced this exact thing in your life, you might not realize what makes the sakura so deeply connected to how we experience life. They only bloom for about 10 to 14 days, sometimes even less. A single strong wind or an early heavy rain can take them all away in one night. And that is exactly why they are so beautiful. If cherry blossoms stayed on the trees forever, nobody would stop to look at them. Since everyone sitting under those trees knows that this moment will not last, they pay attention. They just sit there and soak it in, feeling a deep stillness, aware that the petals are already falling. When I was younger, I used to live as if time was unlimited. I would waste entire days doing things I didn't care about. I would stay in situations that made me unhappy, telling myself I'd change things later. I felt this constant pressure to do everything faster and achieve more, while consistently postponing the things I truly wanted to do. This truth about time really hit me when my grandfather, Daiki, passed away. It happened so quickly that one season, he was sitting with me in his garden, pouring tea and telling me stories. And the next season, his chair was empty, like a petal falling from a branch. After he passed, I was going through his things and found an old journal entry he had written during his last spring. I carry his words with me every single day. He wrote, "Hiroto, the real tragedy of life is how many of our years we waste. The sakura never worries about tomorrow's wind."

The speaker transition into a personal reflection, recalling how he once wasted time until the sudden passing of his grandfather, Daiki, made him realize how quickly life can change. He closes with a touching quote from his grandfather's journal, reminding the listener not to waste their years and to live fully in the present.

title: Epstein Barr Virus- EBV  Reactivation Explained: Why You Feel Exhausted, Achy, and Inflamed
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Well hi, I'm Dr. Heikmeier and in today's video we're going to dive into a topic that I think is often overlooked in traditional medicine, conventional medicine, but I believe it plays a huge role in explaining why so many people suffer with chronic fatigue, brain fog and often autoimmune flare-ups. Today, I'm talking about the reactivation of Epstein-Barr. If you've ever been struggling with this relentless fatigue despite sleeping well, if your blood work comes back so called normal, but you're really feeling anything but, or if you've had mono in the past and never quite felt the same afterwards, today's video may provide a missing piece to what you've been searching for. Well, let's start with the basics of Epstein-Barr, EBV. This is part of the herpes family. You've probably heard this as mononucleosis or just simply mono or you may have heard this as just kissing disease. Most people are exposed to Epstein-Barr virus at some point in their life and by some estimates as much as 90% of people adults carry this. Now in many cases, the initial infection just passes and the virus becomes dormant in your body, especially in your B cells, which are again are part of your immune system. But here's the key, Epstein-Barr virus never fully leaves your body, it simply just goes into an inactive state. So, while Epstein-Barr virus can remain dormant really for years, certain stressors or triggers can cause it to wake up and then become reactive and when that happens, your immune system has to mount a response. This often looks and feels like chronic fatigue, autoimmune flare ups and some people muscle aches and joint pain and brain fog and sometimes even low-grade fever or even swollen lymph nodes. Unfortunately, most standard lab work does not check for Epstein-Barr virus or even reactivation unless specifically requested and many doctors, to be honest, don't even think about testing it for patients that present with persistent chronic fatigue or vague symptoms. So, let's take a closer look at some of these symptoms, right? You may be dealing with reactivated Epstein-Barr if you experience persistent or crushing fatigue that doesn't improve with rest, like I mentioned, a sore throat or swollen glands without necessarily infection, muscle or joint pain or brain fog and memory problems, maybe poor exercise tolerance, maybe changes in mood and energy

He addresses the audience directly about the reactivation of the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a topic often overlooked in conventional medicine that could be the cause of chronic fatigue, brain fog, and autoimmune flare-ups. He explains the basics of EBV, its association with mononucleosis, and how it can remain dormant in the body only to be reactivated by certain stressors. The speaker lists various symptoms associated with reactivation, such as persistent fatigue, swollen glands, muscle aches, and cognitive issues, and notes that standard lab tests often miss this diagnosis. title: Customer success story | The Epigenetic Clock Development Foundation
transcription: So, the Clock Foundation is a research nonprofit based in Los Angeles that was a spin-out of Professor Steve Horvath's lab, and it's focused on epigenetics and aging or longevity research. With just a blood draw or a saliva sample, a small amount of DNA, you can predict kind of long-term morbidity and mortality, kind of predict future health outcomes, outlook over the next 20 or 30 years. We use this in clinical trials as a before-and-after test, so you can predict whether an intervention is affecting the fundamental biology of aging. We've been working with the founder, with Juozas, who did his postdoctoral research in Professor Horvath's lab at UCLA in California. We have done over 500 different projects or collaborations with researchers, and we're supported by the Vigen team in doing it, and we've also built a platform that's enabled us to do testing for kind of thousands of individual kind of studies. Vigen enable us to operate efficiently at scale. We have well-established workflows. I'm really happy that we were able to run so many different studies, and we were able to automate things that many people would say are not automatable. Vigen for us has been a very reliable kind of data science partner, and they're a strong team, and they're also efficient in the way they do their work. We make available aging biomarkers, but we collaborate with leading academic and industry labs, and so you really have to find a team that is familiar with and kind of at the forefront of the research in the field, and because ultimately, what we want to enable is publication-ready analysis. You know, the Vigen team can, can deliver in that way. I do highly recommend them for many other organizations.

transcription: I'm Heidi Blake, a staff writer at The New Yorker. For the past nine months, I've been investigating the British-American influencer Andrew Tate. This was my life only three years ago. Sharp, side kick from Andrew Tate is very, very dangerous with that shot. Tate is a former kickboxer who appeared on the reality TV show Big Brother before rising to become the defining figure of the manosphere. In the world we live in today, being a normal man, or below normal, is going to be terrible. Even to just find a woman you can reproduce with is becoming more and more difficult. My story for The New Yorker charts the rise of Tate's online pornography empire, from the recruitment of his very first webcam worker, a Slovakian teenager who moved to the UK to begin staging sex shows online when she was still a minor in 2014. title: Hydration Breaks at FIFA World Cup 2026: The commercialization of climate adaptation?
transcription: The commercialization of climate adaptation. FIFA has said that broadcasters can show adverts during hydration breaks at the FIFA Men's World Cup this summer in the US. So let's start at the beginning on this one. In December 2025, it was announced that players will benefit from three-minute hydration breaks in each half of games as, quote, "FIFA prioritizes player welfare throughout next summer's tournament co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States," close quote. This followed the FIFA Club World Cup in 2025, really high temperatures, games were stopped for hydration breaks at a number of games, and it's also happened at previous World Cups as well, where the wet bulb temperature reached 32 degrees and therefore kicked in the heat rule. So whilst ostensibly FIFA announced this as a player welfare issue for those eagle-eyed environmental people in sport, it was noticeable that this announcement was made at the World Broadcaster Meeting held in Washington, D.C. So, 4 months later from that announcement, now 3 months ahead of the tournament, March 2026, FIFA has, has announced that broadcasters can show adverts during hydration breaks, breaks, at FIFA's Men's World Cup with certain stipulations. So those stipulations are: the ad break shouldn't start within 20 seconds of the ref's whistle pausing play, they should return to the match feed more than 30 seconds before play resumes, so essentially you've got 2 minutes and 10 seconds for advertising. Then there are stipulations around the advertising, too. If, if broadcasters do split screen or don't fully cut away, they're only allowed to show, um, sorry, sell advertising to FIFA sponsors. If the broadcaster cuts away entirely to full screen ads, it is allowed to sell those spots to anyone, and in stadiums, FIFA will continue to control the branding of the breaks. So FIFA has got more branding for itself inside the stadium and there are stipulations for broadcasters who want to sell additional advertising at these moments. title: Markwayne Mullin tears up recalling Trump helping his son: 'Because he cared'

transcription: this nomination hearing, and from my standpoint, when you're trying to select somebody to, to run an operation, you want somebody with integrity, somebody with that passion toward the mission, keeping this, this nation safe, this, this, you know, having this love for this country. It's also, I think, incredibly important that when you're serving in an administration, you have a good relationship with the President. It doesn't work so well. I know you've got a good relationship with the President, and you told me a story, and I want you to repeat that story of your son who was grievously injured, and of a visit that the President of the United States made to that hospital. I want you to tell the story, because I think it's important that people understand why you are loyal to President Trump. I'd like them to hear a different side of President Trump as well. But I think also that'll serve you well as, as his Secretary of Homeland Security. But just tell that story. Ron, I'm going to try getting through it without crying, then. Um, it's not about President Trump, it's about my son. So my son was a really world-class athlete and January 17th of 2020, which mind you was an election year, he had a really serious brain injury. Woke up 26 hours later and he's a kid. Um, we almost lost him for 26 hours. He had an extremely low pulse. Um, there was a time they, uh, that they thought that they lost his pulse altogether. And when he woke up, he was just different. I mean, here you had a world-class athlete that wrestled all over the world since he was 12 years old and he couldn't touch his nose, he couldn't walk without shuffling his feet, he had short-term memory loss. Um, he couldn't control his muscles, couldn't add 5 + 3. He was in high school at that time, um, had to learn how to read, walk, everything. And the President found out about it and he gave me a call immediately and, uh, one thing that the President joked about was like, he said, he said, "Let me get this straight. He doesn't know who you and Christie are, but he knew who I was?" Because the only question he got right is who the President was, and he said, "Trump" with this cocky grin on his face. And, but the President didn't understand the severity of it, but he heard it in my voice and immediately he went to work. He, uh, I told him we had to get to Bakersfield, California, to the Center for Neuro Skills, which is one of the best neuro rehabilitation places in the world. And, um, and the President offered to send his plane, his personal plane, this is the President of the United States. And, uh, and I said, "Sir, we can't fly, we got to drive." We get there and he called almost every day for two weeks, checking on Jim. And then he says, "I'm going to come see him." And, and now this is the middle of the election, this is Bakersfield, California, really not an area he has to go campaign. And he took the time to come up there and, and see, and see Jim. And, um, the, the, the center told us that the, the short-term memory loss would, something would trigger it. Some big event would eventually trigger where he would start retaining stuff, because until then he was still having issues.

title: AI x Society | I/O 2026 Keynote
transcription: Today we showed you our next-generation models, Gemini 3.5 and Omni, new coding capabilities in Anti-gravity 2.0, agents in search and Gemini Spark, and so much more. It's great to see Gemini transforming so many Google products used by billions of people every day. All of these advances show the staggering pace of AI progress. It's incredible, even for those of us who have spent our entire lives working on this. AGI is now on the horizon, and it will be the most profound and impactful technology ever invented. If built right, it could propel human progress and flourishing beyond our imaginations. We're in a moment of immense promise, but also enormous responsibility. It's important that we are clear-eyed about the potential challenges, and use all the tools at our disposal to ensure the safety of our agentic systems and ultimately, AGI itself. One area of risk that has gained a lot of attention recently is cybersecurity. Google has invested in this area for decades, and we're bringing our frontier capabilities and deep expertise to help secure the world's codebases. We have tools like our code security agent, CodeMender, which automatically finds and fixes critical software vulnerabilities. Today, we're inviting a select group of experts to test the new CodeMender API, and we'll be launching it more broadly soon. Stepping back, the whole reason I've worked on AI my entire career was because I saw it as the ultimate tool to advance science and our understanding of the world. It's awesome to see those dreams become a reality, with AI beginning to help scientists in almost every field. Building on this momentum, I'm excited to announce Gemini for Science.

title: Q1 2026 - Quarter In Review | XML Financial Group | Market Commentary
transcription: Welcome. I hope that you had a wonderful Easter or Passover. It was an eventful first quarter of the year. Let's reflect on a few of the major themes. Gas prices were up nearly a dollar a gallon in the first quarter, and when multiplied across millions of households filling up week after week, the cumulative impact on consumer spending and savings rates is significant. However, it's the indirect costs that are possibly more meaningful. Gasoline and diesel fuel are basic inputs to nearly everything the economy produces. Transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, and distribution all depend on energy, which means that higher fuel costs raise the price of goods and services across the board. The stock market saw its share of volatility as well. In Q1, the S&P 500, in blue, we see here was down about 4.3% for the quarter, with the sectors on the left in green being the out-performers, and on the right in red, being the under-performers. The standout on the left is energy, having a terrific start to the year, for perhaps not so terrific reasons. And then many of the sectors that outperformed in the past, on the right, financials, consumer discretionary, technology, not performing especially well, with this highlighting the potential benefits of diversification. So, how does this negative 4.3% return compared to past quarters? Well, this chart shows quarterly S&P 500 returns, ranked from worst on the left to best on the right, going back to 1988. And interestingly, what we see is that the Q1 return from '16 is exactly the same as the Q1 return from '15, -4.3%. Now, interestingly, the other three quarters of '15 happened to be very strong, with Q2 returning 10.9%, Q3, 5.9%, and Q4, 2.7%. This, of course, isn't to suggest that the rest of '16 will be just as the rest of '15 was, but it's a good reminder that often when market participants are most concerned is when the market performs best. Thanks for watching. Enjoy today.

title: Sustainability Strategy Masterclass: Industry Best Practices
transcription: Reinventing the wheel doesn't add value or drive change, whether that's to sustainability strategy or to a carbon footprint. So I always recommend taking a bit of time before you begin designing your sustainability strategy to look at what else is out there. Um, most organizations can benefit from looking at the UN sustainable development goals and the greenhouse gas protocol, and this will give you ideas of potential topics for your pillars, for your focus areas. It's also really important to look at what regulation that your organization either needs to comply with today or is likely to have to comply with tomorrow, because what you don't want is a central sustainability strategy and then an add-on, "this is how we will comply with EUDR", for example. You want a single sustainability strategy that shows, "these are what's important to us, this is how we're going to move the needle, oh, and whilst we do this, this is how we're going to comply with all of the regulation". And then equally, it's always a good idea to look at what your competitors are doing, um, because if you're working in the same industry, you're likely to be facing the same challenges and whilst each organization is unique and I would never expect two sustainability strategies to be the same, it can just be a really good starting point to help you start thinking thematically about where you want to be looking. So, just on that note, these are the sustainable development goals and these are really broad themes that, I, I find it a really useful exercise with any organization to sit down with the sustainability manager or the health and safety and environment manager or the finance officer, whoever it is who's been tasked with coming up with the sustainability strategy and going through these SDGs and saying, "which really apply to your business, how is your business contributing towards climate action, quality education?" and normally two or three will come out that are incredibly relevant to the business and that can be kind of used as the foundation for how that business should think about sustainability.

Are you with me? Hello, I'm Dr. Jennifer Mullan. I am the founder of Decolonizing Therapy, and the author of Decolonizing Therapy. title: Transgender Persons Amendment Bill 2026: Self-Identification Out, Medical Boards in - What Changes?
transcription: A bill introduced in parliament on Friday could fundamentally change who the Indian state recognizes as transgender and who it doesn't. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 was tabled in the Lok Sabha by Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar. And while the government says it's about bringing clarity to a vague law, critics say it could quietly dismantle rights that took years of struggle to win. I'm Vrinda Tulsian and you're watching The Print. To understand what's changed and why it matters, we need to go back to where this all began. It's 2014. The Supreme Court delivers what becomes known as the NALSA judgment, a landmark ruling that recognizes transgender persons as a third gender, directs the government to provide reservations and welfare measures, and crucially holds that a person has the right to self-identify their gender, no surgery required, no medical certificate, no government approval. The court said the constitution guarantees it. That judgment set the stage for legislation, but getting a law passed took five more years, and they weren't smooth years. A 2016 version of the bill was met with protest from the transgender communities across the country. The core objection: it required a District Magistrate to certify whether someone was transgender. Activists said that handed a bureaucrat the power to decide something the Supreme Court had said was a fundamental right. After sustained pressure, the bill was revised. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was finally passed in 2019. It was imperfect, many in the community still had reservations, but it represented a floor, a legal baseline. It defined transgender persons broadly: anyone whose gender doesn't match the gender assigned at birth, including trans men, trans women, genderqueer individuals, those with intersex variations, and those with socio-cultural identities like hijra, kinnar, aravani, and jogta, and it explicitly said, under Section 4, Part 2, that a recognized transgender person has the right to a self-perceived gender identity. That section is now proposed to be deleted. So what exactly does the 2026 amendment propose? There are three major changes worth unpacking: the definition, the procedures, and the penalties. Under the new bill, the term transgender person would be restricted to two categories: first, people with specific socio-cultural identities—hijra, kinnar, aravani, jogta, eunuch—or people born with medically recognized intersex variations. Variations in chromosomes, genitalia, hormones, gonadal development, biological markers, in other words.

The recording is high-quality, with some low, indistinct background noises that do not interfere with the speaker's voice. She is discussing a controversial bill introduced in India's parliament, which could significantly alter how the state defines transgender individuals. She traces the history of transgender rights in India, starting with the landmark 2014 NALSA judgment, followed by the protests against the 2016 draft, the enactment of the 2019 act, and finally, the proposed 2026 amendment that threatens to dismantle these hard-won rights by narrowing the definition of who qualifies as transgender.

title: I Found My Old Journal...I Didn't Recognize Myself.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I found an old journal recently. I don't date my entries, I've never been good at that, but I can tell when it was because of the entries around it. But, I can tell that this one is an older one, it's from before my mother passed away. This is hard. I don't know how to be seen. I keep thinking I will open up my mouth and something will come out that makes sense of me, but it never does. I look at other people and it seems so easy for them. They just exist and people respond to them like they matter. I feel like I'm always just on the edge of everything. I want to be heard. I want to express myself. I want to be someone who has something inside of them that's worth noticing. But I don't think there is. Sometimes I think it would just be easier if I just wasn't here. Just... if I disappeared, I wouldn't have to keep failing as a person. This was before my mother died.

He prefaces and concludes the reading by noting that this entry was written before his mother passed away, adding a layer of grief to the already painful memory. transcription: One marijuana gummy every other night. That's it. And the federal government says you can lose your gun rights. Don't take my word for it. Listen. What if he took one gummy bear with a medical prescription in Colorado, you don't even need that anymore, but let's say he had one to help him sleep every other day? Disarm him for life? Well, we're not, no, it's not disarm for life, and here's what's going on. Potentially? Um, well, Would that be enough under your theory? One gummy bear every other night with a medical prescription? So, I think you'd have a rehab, potential rehab problem, but I will accept the hypothetical. So let me just deal with what's an unlawful user. I think the answer is yes, under the government's theory. Yes, under our theory, but let me give you an... Yes, under our theory, that qualifies. That's the United States government arguing before the Supreme Court. This is United States v. Daniels. It challenges 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3), passed in 1968. It says if you're an unlawful user of a controlled substance, you can't possess a firearm. Felony, up to 15 years in prison. That's what we're talking about. Now listen to how they justify it. Unlike alcohol, illegal drugs are illegal. They're illegal because Congress deemed their use dangerous at any level. Dangerous at any level. Not dangerous with a gun, not dangerous while committing a crime, dangerous at any level. So Congress labels something illegal, and that automatically makes you too dangerous to exercise a constitutional right. That's the theory. Now, it gets clearer. Our position is Congress made a judgment in 922(g)(3) itself, that it is, in fact, dangerous to mix firearms with habitual use or addiction to controlled substances. Congress made a judgment. Not a jury, not a court, Congress. And that judgment alone strips the right. No individualized finding, no proof you misused the firearm, no proof you're violent. Just status. And here's the cleanest admission. ...that way, and I think... But would that be your backup position? Because this isn't about weed. It's about categories. Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable for the government. Justice Gorsuch's pushback. title: Anatomy of Sadness (Official Spoken Word Video)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Anatomy of sadness. Feet of gloom, heart of contempt, stomach ailing, consuming, intestines disposing. Ears curved but not bent, hearing words of one cent. Chest broad with pain. You can call me Built because my tears fall like rain. Teeth yellow with fear. Grinding joy, genitalia of a hermaphrodite. Warm, moist womb of misery. Penis, a knife. Soul torn to shreds like that of a goat's bite. Nose aware of the stench of foulness filling the air. Arms and legs long, no power, no strength. Keeps me weak, unable to carry on. My hair's not nappy, but woolly like Jesus's, who just like me was at times unhappy. Waited for a resurrection three days too long, but my angels sing a melancholy song. My mind full of thoughts getting heavier. My eyes change color like the leaves in fall, and glow like a cat's when night falls.

And the reason for this, largely, has been school. Each generation spends more time in school. We use school to develop our cognition. Congratulations, you see your correlation. Until Gen Z. Gen Z is the first generation in modern history to underperform us on basically every cognitive measure we have, from basic attention to memory to literacy to numeracy to executive functioning to even general IQ, even though they go to more school than we did. So why? What happened? What happened around 2010 that decoupled schooling from cognitive development? It can't be school. School basically looks the same. It can't be biology. To the point where kids who use computers about five hours per day in school for learning purposes will score over two-thirds of a standard deviation less than kids who rarely or never touch tech at school, and that's across 80 countries. title: 7 chilling details Netflix's Taylor Parker doc left out | The US Sun
transcription: Netflix viewers have been left reeling by the case of Taylor Parker, the woman who faked her pregnancy before brutally murdering her friend and stealing her unborn baby. Now 33, Parker stands as one of the youngest women on Texas' death row, following the October 2020 slaying of 21 year-old Reagan Simmons-Hancock. While the new documentary Maternal Instinct features devastating interviews from Reagan's mother and Parker's ex-boyfriend, Wade Griffin, a massive amount of disturbing evidence from the 2022 trial was left on the cutting room floor. I'm Katie Forrester with the US Sun. Don't forget to like and subscribe for more true crime deep dives. For 10 months, Parker falsely claimed she was pregnant, wore a fake baby bump, and even hosted a gender reveal party as her supposed due date approached. Prosecutors said she then killed Reagan before cutting her unborn baby from her womb using a scalpel before fleeing the scene. Parker was later stopped by police and claimed she had given birth at the side of the road, but her story quickly unraveled. Here, we break down the top seven details missing from the documentary. Number one is the silence from death row. While viewers saw Parker in social media clips, home videos, and police bodycam footage, she was never actually interviewed from prison. Director Jessica Dimmock told USA Today that this was a deliberate creative choice. Rather than centering the narrative on the killer or granting her a platform, the production team chose to exclusively focus on the victims and the families whose lives were permanently shattered by this tragedy. Number two, her mother knew the truth. Parker's mother, Shonda Pryor, also never appeared in the film, yet her courtroom testimony was some of the trial's most explosive. Pryor revealed that she was actually present when Parker underwent a hysterectomy years prior, making a pregnancy physically impossible. When a friend sent Pryor a screenshot of Parker's gender reveal party invitation, Pryor texted her daughter asking what she should tell people. Parker was blunt and told her mother

title: Should You Buy Micron Stock Instead of Nvidia Stock? | MU Stock vs. NVDA Stock
transcription: Investors are asking me which stock I like better, Nvidia or Micron, and I thought that would be a great comparison to make. I want to thank The Motley Fool for sponsoring this video. Visit fool.com/parkev for the 10 best stocks to buy now. When I'm comparing two companies for investment, the place I like to start is revenue. And looking at revenue over the previous decade on a trailing 12-month period, you can see business is booming for each of these companies. Nvidia's revenue soared to $253 billion over the trailing 12-month period, that's up from less than $5 billion in 2017. You can see in this chart here Micron's revenue used to exceed Nvidia's, and that difference has separated Nvidia from Micron considerably. Micron is no slouch itself, its revenue totaled $90.3 billion over the trailing 12-month period, and in its most recently completed quarter, revenue quadrupled year over year up over $40 billion from $9 billion in the same time last year. Looking to the future, they've both got great demand going ahead. Shortages in supply of memory and storage have caused prices for Micron's components to absolutely explode. The company is reporting triple digits, in some cases 200, 300% year-over-year growth in the prices of the products that it's selling. Meanwhile, unit growth is less than 20% year-over-year. Nvidia's growth has come on the back of a more sustainable source. Nvidia is selling more units and it's innovating annually, and those two are combining to increase prices, uh, I should say revenue. And, evaluating technology, Nvidia has a stronger competitive advantage compared to Micron. Micron is not even the leader in the most cutting-edge technology for data centers, high-bandwidth memory. And so, to evaluate that, Nvidia combined with its software creates more differentiation for its customers compared with the differentiation that Micron offers its customers. The next metric I wanted to compare these two on is the operating profit margin, where they resulted in a very similar number. Nvidia's operating profit margin totaled 64% in the most recent period, whereas Micron's operating profit margin totaled 65 and 3/4.

title: Barron Trump’s emergency call to police
transcription: Just days before his father's second inauguration last January, President Trump's teenage son Barron placed an urgent call for help to police in London. Quote, "I'm calling from the US," Barron Trump told an operator at the UK's 999 emergency line. "I just got a call from a girl, you know, she's getting beat up," adding, "it's really an emergency." That call's transcript, released by prosecutors, now key evidence in the London trial of 22-year-old Russian national, Matvey Rumyantsev, accused of rape and assault, which he denies. The January attack allegedly witnessed in part by Trump, whose late-night video call to the victim was briefly answered by the defendant, whom Trump would describe in an email to prosecutors as a quote "shirtless man with darkish hair," according to British media covering the trial. The victim reportedly praising Trump in testimony Wednesday, quote, "He helped save my life. That call was like a sign from God at that moment." Barron Trump, the only son of the President and First Lady Melania Trump, keeps a low public profile, with no public speeches and few appearances. His father crediting the teen for his help finding ways to reach young voters. "He knew the youth vote..." On the night of the incident, the operator pressed Trump for details about the victim and how he knew her. Quote, "I don't think those details matter. She's getting beat up," Trump replies, adding, "I met her on social media." British media reporting that the defendant testified today that he told the victim in the fall of 2024 that he was quote "upset" about her talking to Barron Trump. Both the White House and the First Lady's office declined to comment on this case. Tom? Garrett, thank you. When we return at six, we thank you for watching, and remember, stay updated on breaking news and top stories on the NBC News app or watch live on our YouTube channel.

Okay, so there's this growing conversation about whether you can exist within the party, whether you want to upend it for your own purposes, a totally different platform. Uh, the Daily Caller quotes you saying this at a DSA convention last year, "We will win by making conditions so intolerable for the ruling class that they would rather give in to our demands than continue to live with the disturbance we cause, until we are able to fully seize power ourselves." So, should Van Jones and Rahm Emanuel and James Carville and all of the establishment Democrats be worried about DSA plans from within their tent? The establishment Democrats should be worried about, uh, the voters, and about what the voters think, and about what the constituency thinks. And right now, uh, right now they have not been delivering, and, uh, our candidates are, and have been, and it's resonating with voters. So, Jaime Harrison, who was the DNC chair, after you guys had such a big night in New York City, uh, and knocking off some of those incumbents, and, and having success with your candidates in the congressional primaries, he said, "If you hate the Democrat, Democratic Party, then don't run for our nomination, don't use our resources, don't rely on our volunteers, don't use our infrastructure, focus on building the party you actually support." title: Evidence in Nolan Wells case points to an accident, ex-FBI agent says
transcription:
Nolan Wells. He's the 18-year-old whose death during a 4th of July boat trip to a remote Mississippi island is igniting nationwide debate. Jennifer, I want to take a moment to hear what Stephen A. Smith said about this case on Cuomo just a few days ago.

Listen, you're a dad. I'm a dad. We send our children out, and first of all, regardless of what ethnicity, regardless of what color we're talking about here, we send our children out, and you're the only one that doesn't come home alive. I'll be damned if the Chris Cuomo that I know doesn't want answers and doesn't expect answers. You know me, and I'm going to push for answers. So for no one to have answers as to what happens is when the s- is when the suspicion elevates exponentially.

Seeing the video of Nolan is just so heartbreaking. He seems like such a happy kid. Now, the Daily Mail has identified a 19-year-old young woman who Nolan was last seen speaking to. Now, his friends said he chose to stay behind on Horn Island, but with that woman. But the woman's sister is claiming that's not true, he was ready to get back on the boat that he came on. Are all these differing, differing accounts and a lack of understanding concerning to you?

Well, I think two things can be true at once. It makes sense that he went off to see about a girl, as they say, and that they had conversation and that she decided to go back and be with friends. So, I think it's more of a timing issue rather than something that is untrue on either end. I think both can be true at the same.

Nolan's death is going to the Mississippi Grand Jury. The DA said something interesting, that the evidence will not be public until the Grand Jury reviews it first. The DA says this is to protect the integrity of the investigation, and that the Grand Jury will ultimately decide if someone will be charged. Jennifer, do you believe someone could be charged in his death? Is this just an accident gone terribly wrong?

Well, with what we know, in other words, review of all the surveillance information we have with actually getting to hear from one of the- one of the witnesses, one of his best friends that was there throughout the situation, listening to the calls that were made, the Coast Guard contact, as well as the rip tide situation in that area. When you add it all together, what we see publicly seems to be an accident. Having said that, of course there's going to be more information, 60 witnesses interviewed. I doubt if this, from what we know, will come back with a true bill.

All right. Hopefully, the families, both families, get some answers. Jennifer Coffindaffer, thank you. I'll see you soon.

Thank you for watching. Subscribe below and download our NewsNation app right now on your phone and you will get fact-based, unbiased news for all Americans.

title: Scientists Want This Banned | STEM Loft
transcription: Mirror, mirror on the wall. What's the scariest biology concept of them all? Well, there is some scary science out there. One that's getting the attention of biologists right now is called mirror life. Although even the possibility of creating it is still a long way off, scientists are talking about setting guardrails on exploring this area of research now because of the major impact it could have for life on Earth. Just because we can research something doesn't mean we should. Hey, I'm Miranda Cosgrove and welcome to my STEM Loft, where one of the elevator buttons is a skull and crossbones and I really want to press it. You likely prefer writing notes, scrolling social media, and hitting a baseball either with your right or left hand. 99% of us are either right or left-handed, making it a lot easier to do things with one side of our bodies. And the other side, well, let's just say it doesn't work quite as well. But humans aren't the only ones with a preference like this. Many other things in our universe like DNA and proteins also have a handedness. Now, what if we could change that handedness? This concept is called mirror life. The handedness of the building blocks of life is known as chirality. When a chiral object is laid on top of its mirror image, no matter how it's rotated, it won't perfectly line up. Think again of your hands. They're mirror images of each other. However, no matter how I rotate them, they can't be perfectly superimposed on top of each other. You may have experienced this when trying to put your left hand's glove on your right hand or your right hand's on your left. I wouldn't say this is my most stylish look. DNA is naturally right-handed, meaning its classic DNA double-helix shape twists to the right. On the other hand, proteins are left-handed. Some molecules like tartrate, which can be found in wine or is sometimes added to food, have left or right-handed forms. Each molecule's chirality makes a big impact on how it functions. Louis Pasteur is most famous for his creation of pasteurization, a process that kills harmful pathogens in things like milk, but he's also considered the father of molecular chirality. He discovered chirality when he separated left and right-handed tartrate crystal shapes from each other back in 1847. But what would happen if we could change the chirality of left or right-handed microbes and flip them around into something else?

title: Just do the right thing. The rest doesn’t matter.#Selflessness#PersonalGrowth#selfimprovement
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: On action and duty. Great ideas from the book Meditations by Marcus Aurelius. Just do the right thing, the rest doesn't matter. That quote is basically saying focus on what you can control, and let go of what you can't. Here's what that breaks down to. 1. Just do the right thing. This is the part you can control. It's about your own choices, your own actions, and your own character. Is it kind? Is it honest? Is it helpful? Does it align with who you want to be? Your job is to figure out the right, decent, ethical thing to do in a situation and then do it. That's your duty. 2. The rest doesn't matter. This is the part you can't control, so don't let it paralyze you or stop you from doing your duty. What other people think of you for doing it, whether you'll get credit or even be thanked, whether it will be successful or work out perfectly, how hard or scary it feels. The outcome, sometimes, you can only control your effort, not the final result. Think of it like this. You see someone drop their wallet. The right thing is to pick it up and give it back to them. So you do it. The rest, that doesn't matter. Whether they are suspicious of you, whether they say a heartfelt thank you or just grunt, or whether you're late to your next appointment because you stopped. You did your part. The rest was out of your hands. In a nutshell, pour your energy into being a person of good action. Don't waste your energy worrying about the noise, the results, or the opinions that follow. Your peace comes from knowing you did what you should, not from how the world reacts. It's a call for integrity over image, for courage over comfort, and for focusing on your own behavior in a world you can't control.

title: Condoleezza Rice calls on Trump admin to 'FINISH' Iran's military
transcription: This decision to launch this operation was based on a cumulative effect of various direct threats that Iran posed to the United States of America, and the President's feeling based on fact that Iran does pose an imminent and direct threat. I've said repeatedly since the first briefing over 10 days ago, there was no imminent threat to the United States that I believe would constitute putting our sailors and soldiers in harm's way. Well, was Iran a threat to the US or not? Joining us tonight to talk about this and the situation in the Middle East is former Secretary of State, former National Security Advisor, Condoleezza Rice. Secretary Rice, thanks for being here. You know, we have these polls out about Iran, national security threat. You know, most people who answer these polls, it's 61% yes, 38% no. This is the banter back and forth even as obviously, the military operation is being characterized as being very successful, and we have markers on that. What's your thoughts about where we are right now and where we may be headed? Well, the most important thing, Brett, and thank you for having me, but the most important thing is to recognize that Iran has been at war with us for at least 41 years, all the way from 1979. People may forget they took our embassy hostage 440... 444 days. They were responsible for the killings of 300-plus marines in Lebanon in the early 1980s. And if you ask people about Iraq, what was the source of many of our casualties in Iraq, you'll get estimates as high as 75 or 80% of them were due to Iranian-made roadside bombs. title: State of the Union: Economic Highlights on Inflation, Jobs and Taxes | Dan Varroney
transcription: Now at 5:00, all eyes are on the nation's capital tonight as President Trump gives his State of the Union address. We examine where the economy stands ahead of the speech. Fox 26 News at 5:00 starts now. Well, President Trump is delivering the State of the Union address. And unlike many presidents before him, President Trump is expected to offer a positive report on the nation's economy in tonight's State of the Union address. Well, Fox 26 business reporter, Tom Zizka is looking at the numbers to help you judge for yourself. Rashi, Caroline, for a lot of people, economic reality comes from their own finances rather than the President's words. They know what their bank account says. That's what they look at. So, the number of recent polls suggest people are generally displeased with his handling of the economy. But, looking at the numbers, there are some challenges. There are some bright spots as well. We launched the great American comeback. Like the President's previous times speaking to Congress, this is his turn to tell his economic tale. Among the economic topics he may point to, inflation and affordability, trade and tariffs, manufacturing and jobs, and taxes. Starting with prices, inflation is slowing but still above the Fed's 2% target, meaning prices are not growing as fast as they once grew. Outside of supply and demand products like eggs and gasoline, prices are unlikely to shrink. Tariffs could affect future affordability. The Supreme Court ruling that struck down many of the President's tariffs are likely to be replaced, and despite his insistence that billions are collected from foreign importers, there is wide consensus that consumers and domestic business are footing the bill. With tariffs, the President pressured trillions in pledges of foreign investment to build and reshore domestic manufacturing. Few of those projects have yet been started and could change as tariff talks continue. Potentially, though, they could help jump-start sluggish job creation, as employers hold off hiring to see how the future shakes out. Finally, on the topic of taxes, last year's spending bill includes a number of changes that will cut taxes for a wide variety of Americans. Cuts on tips, overtime, and social security benefits will mean refunds on more tax returns. Taken as a whole, some economists suggest some patience. For the American people, it's very difficult to say, "People need to be patient." But, I will tell you, based on past history, there is a track record. When you make these types of policy decisions, the prices will come down, the quality of life will be improved come mid-year, and come end of this year. That's economist Dan Veroni in suburban Washington, D.C. making those comments right now. The President's argument tonight will have to resonate with viewers, with consumers, with voters if he wants it to have a positive effect, of course. We have primary votes coming in March and the midterm elections in November. The economy needs to be doing well for the President and the Republicans to do well in addition to that. Watching your money tonight, I'm Tom Zizka, Fox 26 News. All right.

title: Hokum - Movie Review
transcription: Caveat, the on-screen video game adaptation that's not—it's not a video game adaptation. Does feel like it at a point though. Let me explain. So Caveat is written and directed by Damian McCarthy, stars Jonathan French. He comes to this house in the middle of nowhere. Long story short, he ends up trapped on an island in a house and he has to get out. Also, it may very well be haunted by a ghost, there is that. Now, that's the flyby version for this movie. We've all heard the hype, you know, people are like, "This is unsettling!" "This will have you at the edge of your seat!" Okay, let's calm down. The movie has creepy moments, sure, but what I liked about this film is it's not cut and dry. It has layers, nuance, depth of character. You take Jonathan French's character. In the setup of this film, I was like, "Well, he's kind of a piece of shit. I hope whatever is haunting that house torments the hell out of him." "Oh, man, I guess everyone has their story." Right? Ha, you know, it's kind of cool that the movie made me do that, made me flip so easily. Not easily, I don't flip easily. The film made it seem easy. Writing, folks, execution, you know, that was when the film really hooked me. And this movie looks solid. It's all about the unsettling imagery, usually in facial expressions. More than a few faces, whether it be little figures, and the film concentrates on them and has that depth of field, or unsettling-ass faces with those Marty Feldman eyes that come on a TV, you're like, "Please stop." The film's effective in that respect, which pleased me because in the buildup, I was like, "Okay, seen a couple jump scares, you're just, you're going to go that route here?" But the film's not built on that, and, okay, fine. I feel bad for people going into this film hearing the creepy hype, you know, hearing the horror movie hype, and I feel like they're going to get let down. Kind of reminds me of Crimson Peak. This movie's nothing like Crimson Peak, but when Crimson Peak came out, it looked like a Gothic horror film, and really it was a Gothic romance, it was just mismarketed that way. Same with the movie Mother!, which looked creepy as hell from the trailer, that's not really the movie. This film, I feel, runs the risk of that same audience letdown because the movie itself is not what it's marketed as. Horror film? It does have horror-ish elements, but it's really about a guy trapped in a house on an island, so he needs to find a way out, also he needs to come face to face and process his own personal demons. And yes, there's possibly a ghost involved. But at a point, this is where the video game reference from the intro of this video comes in, I was like, "This is Resident Evil with no zombies."

title: Proteomics of the Small Bowel Lumen Shows Anti-Microbial Immune Activation in Response to SIBO
transcription: Hello, I'm Nathan Hendricks. I'm a specialist at MAST. I'm here to talk about my poster, which is looking at the proteomics of SIBO. So, I'm looking at SIBO, which is Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth. It's a GI disorder which occurs when you have certain select species that are overabundant. Uh people have looked at the sequencing, uh genomics of SIBO, um but nobody's really explored the proteomics of SIBO. So we're going to look at the protein makeup of people with or without SIBO, and see what sort of diagnostic or prognostic markers there are there. So, we're looking at small bowel lumen aspirates from the REIMAGINE study. Uh so we took 20 microliters of these aspirates, and it's important to note that this is the centrifuged aspirate, it's not the tissue. And we took 20 microliters of that and we processed it uh by trypsin digestion to prepare it for proteomics analysis. We took these processed samples and we analyzed them um with data-independent acquisition on the ZenoTOF 7600. So, of the proteins we see, we see many IgGs, uh which is something we might expect to see in SIBO, and we also see Defensin A1 and Defensin A3 are one of the most significantly upregulated proteins in SIBO. And this all matches with what you would expect to see in a immune response to infection. So, if we look at the particular pathways that are in this dataset, we have many proteins that are part of the neutrophil degranulation pathway. And this highlights that there is a specific neutrophil response occurring to SIBO in the lumen. So, to summarize some of the important results we see, uh we see immunoglobulins and defensins in our protein dataset, which is something that we would expect to see in response to bacterial overgrowth. Uh we also see uh a lot of activation of the neutrophil uh degranulation pathway and proteins related to neutrophils, and this all suggests that we are seeing neutrophil uh activation in response to SIBO. So, thank you for listening to this summary, and thank you for checking out my poster. Uh I hope you check out all the other posters and presentations that we have from MAST at the 2022 DDW.

Um, so yeah, we'll start with that. Uh, who are Overwatch AI, what are you doing, uh, what is your what are you providing? Yeah. Yeah, thanks. Thanks so much. And then, it was it wasn't expected to get the award. A very pleasant surprise, I would say. Um, so, um, we are building AI assistance for flight ops. So essentially, we are trying to help, uh, make decisions for the aircraft crews, essentially cockpit, cabin, and OCC staff. We are building a decision support system for them, so we fuse all the sources, uh, together: the company manuals, um, aircraft manuals, uh, NOTAMs, um, all other live APIs like flight and, uh, runway data, and we make it accessible, um, in, essentially, via plain language using our app. So, in a nutshell, that's that's the the essence of the product. Nice. And why is providing this kind of solution to the industry important? Uh, what sort of impact will that have in terms of easing flight operations? So, the the problem that currently we are seeing is that most of the disruptions are, uh, triggered due to internal inefficiencies within the company. So, there are there are a lot of systems, data, manuals, information that is siloed. And when the time is critical, it's very hard to assess all this information, and also access this information at the time when it's needed most. So, what we are doing is that we are we are providing this as a essentially a one-stop shop solution to access all the sources in AI native manner. So, and then we see some some pretty good results, some pretty promising indicators already with our first deployments, um, with customers in Europe. So, they can make decisions faster. title: If You Can't Stop Scrolling, Watch This
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever picked up your phone for just one minute and somehow lost an entire hour? You're not alone. The average person spends hours scrolling every day. But what if you used that time for something that actually improved your life? Here are seven things to do instead of scrolling on your phone. Seven: Read ten pages of a book. Just ten pages a day may not sound like much, but that's over 3,000 pages a year. Knowledge compounds, and a few minutes of reading can teach you more than hours of random scrolling. Six: Go for a walk. A short walk can boost your mood, clear your mind, and improve your health. No fancy equipment needed, just step outside and start moving. Five: Learn one new skill. Spend 15 minutes learning a language, practicing an instrument, or watching a tutorial. Small daily improvements can lead to massive results over time. Four: Call someone you care about. Instead of watching strangers online, connect with real people in your life. A simple conversation can strengthen relationships and make someone's day. Three: Write down your thoughts. Grab a notebook and journal for a few minutes. Writing helps organize your mind, reduce stress, and turn ideas into action. Two: Exercise for 10 minutes. Push-ups, stretching, yoga, or a quick workout—anything that gets your body moving. Your future self will thank you. One: Work on a goal—that project, business idea, skill, or dream you've been putting off. Spend just 20 minutes on it today. Progress beats endless scrolling every single time. The next time you reach for your phone, ask yourself, "Do I want entertainment for a moment or progress that lasts?" If you found this helpful, don't forget to like, subscribe, and share it with someone who spends a little too much time scrolling.

title: Inside Robinhood's Original Pitch Deck: Why Investors Said Yes
transcription: In 2013, two Stanford math graduates named Vladimir Tenev and Baiju Bhatt attempted to pitch a radical concept: zero commission stock trading managed entirely through a mobile phone. At this point, they had been entrepreneurs for the better part of five years. They had built several pieces of financial software for high frequency firms, but they had very little tangible success to show for that time. When they tried to raise money for Robinhood, they ran a brutal gauntlet. They were rejected 70 times, then 90 times. Eventually, 110 investors told them no. The feedback was consistent: professional investors didn't believe people would manage their finances on a smartphone. They looked at the founders' math backgrounds and dismissed them as being incapable of building a product for regular consumers. Many founders react to this kind of rejection by treating their pitch deck like a sales brochure. They try to hide their lack of traction behind flashy design elements or unrealistic multi-billion dollar projections. Robinhood took a different path. They realized that before a deck can sell a product, it has to prove the founders are worthy of trusting. Vlad and Baiju began a process of ruthless subtraction. Instead of adding slides to answer every objection, they cut the presentation down to its absolute essentials. They removed the industry jargon and the dense maps of the financial ecosystem. They focused the entire narrative on one universal problem: the high cost and unnecessary friction of the traditional brokerage model. They avoided the trap of pitching a vague, massive market. Instead, their narrative shrinks the opportunity down to a single, sharp data point. They targeted an underserved generation of millennials wanting to invest, but frustrated by $10 commission fees. This narrow focus made it difficult for investors to dismiss the idea with broad generalizations. By proving they understood one user group better than anyone else, they signaled a level of competence that forced investors to take them seriously. But the digital slides are only half the battle. Eventually, that trust has to be validated by the founders in the room. This reached a breaking point during a meeting with Tim Draper...
caption: In this high-quality audio clip, a woman delivers a clear, professional narration detailing the origin story of Robinhood. Her voice is articulate and engaging, set against a subtle, modern electronic background track. She recounts how, in 2013, Stanford math graduates Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt pitched their concept for a zero-commission stock trading mobile app. Despite having years of experience building financial software, they faced immense difficulty securing funding, suffering 110 rejections from investors who doubted everyday consumers would manage finances on smartphones. Instead of inflating their pitch with complex projections, the founders simplified their presentation, eliminating jargon and focusing on a single, compelling issue: the frustration of millennials facing high commission fees. This strategic simplification ultimately established their credibility and won over investors.

Les Wexner, worth $8.8 billion, founded Bath & Body Works. His company also acquired Victoria's Secret and Abercrombie & Fitch. He seeded Epstein's vast wealth.
