title: Why We Will Never "Cure" Cancer
transcription: In 1971, Richard Nixon signed the National Cancer Act and declared war on cancer. The language was deliberate: a war with a target date, the way you'd talk about landing on the moon. 55 years later, cancer still kills about 10 million people a year worldwide. We didn't lose that war through lack of funding. The United States alone has poured well over $100 billion into cancer research since that signature. We lost it because the enemy was never a single enemy. That's the part the fundraising campaigns skip. Cancer isn't a disease. It's a category closer to infection than flu. Breast cancer alone splits into at least four molecularly distinct diseases that happen to grow in the same organ. Lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, leukemia: different biology, different mutations, different behavior, filed under one word because they share a symptom: cells that won't stop dividing. Asking for a cure for cancer is a little like asking for a cure for infection. Which infection? Which mechanism? Which host? Point one: The enemy evolves faster than you can aim. Here's the detail oncologists live with and rarely get to explain on camera: a tumor isn't one clone of identical cells. Peter Nowell described this back in 1976 in a paper called "The Clonal Evolution of Tumor Cell Populations," and the idea has only gotten scarier with better sequencing. A single tumor is a population: genetically diverse, competing internally, mutating with every division. Give it a drug, and you're not killing the tumor. You're running a selection experiment. The cells sensitive to the drug die. The handful that happened to carry a resistance mutation before treatment even started now have the whole tumor to themselves, no competition left. Six months later, the cancer comes back, and it comes back immune to the exact drug that shrank it. This is why remission and cure are different words. Oncologists know the difference intimately.

title: How Jumping Rope Changes the Human Body.
transcription: The 5-minute jump rope will help you burn fat, create strong and powerful legs, and have you feeling younger than you actually are. This jump rope right here cost me about $5 on Amazon. Cheap, simple tools can have the greatest effect on your body. There's a study that shows jump rope is just as good at improving cardiovascular fitness as running. I am not here to argue that jump rope is any better than running, but there are some unique benefits to jump rope. Number one, you can plainly see on the screen right now. I can't go jogging down the street leaving my boys here to fend for themselves, but I can get 5 to 10 minutes of jump rope in while they play on their scooters around me. It can be the non-runner or parents' weapon to getting into incredible shape in the comfort of your backyard. Now, I assume that jumping rope originated with boxing, but that was only when it was popularized in America. Jump rope started as a fun game for kids way back in ancient Egypt, China, and Greece and Rome. It was brought to America by the Dutch, and eventually turned into an exercise that athletes, especially boxers, still utilize today. Why? Well, it comes down to one quality: rhythm. Boxers have found that the rhythmic, quick feet required to jump rope translates great to their sport. This is a lost quality in modern-day fitness. Many people sit on machines, lay on benches, losing that rhythmic quality that most of us had when we were younger. Here's a few things you probably didn't know about rhythm. Number one is that our brains crave it. It's why we love music. It's why dancers are the most embodied athletes. Rhythmic movement increases coordination, triggers the parasympathetic nervous system, and even increases heart rate variability. Rhythm, combined with bouncing on your feet, strengthens the vestibular system. This improves balance, coordination, and spatial awareness, all things that we slowly lose as we age. And a benefit that you won't find listed on Google is that all these qualities combined result in somewhat of a natural high. And the more competent you become with the rope, the more you experience these elevated feelings. But we also lose muscle and bone density as we age, and the less that we physically train, the easier it is to deteriorate. Most people know to do some resistance training and some cardio, but 90-something percent of the population are missing out on the benefits of plyometrics. Plyometrics are quick, explosive movements that involve lengthening the muscle and then quickly shortening it. And every time you land and rebound, it's three times your body weight in that moment. This has incredible effects on strengthening muscles, connective tissue, and bones. It's a quality that can literally keep you younger, and I think jump rope is the easiest way to safely maintain it. These small doses of impact result in a very strong frame. Skipping rope strengthens your whole lower body structure, and specifically your quads, glutes, and calves. You develop legs that are good at being active, translating well to activities like hiking, cycling, and running. And ask any orthopedic doctor. title: Trump's 15% Tariff Shock: What the US Supreme Court Ruling Means for India
transcription: Okay, let's get right into it. We're talking about an absolutely wild 48 hours where a single Supreme Court decision triggered a presidential move that sent a massive shockwave through global commerce. This is the story of a huge legal showdown and the chaotic trade policy that came out of it. And it all kicked off with this, a bombshell announcement on a Saturday. Just one day after he introduced a brand new 10% global tariff, the president cranked it up by 50%. You can just imagine the uncertainty this threw international markets into. So how did we get here so fast? I mean, a court ruling on Friday and a massive global tariff on Saturday? To really get what happened, we need to rewind the clock by just 24 hours to the verdict that changed everything. Right. So the whole story starts at the Supreme Court. A decision that came down on Friday morning is what set this entire chain of events in motion. And this wasn't just any ruling. It was a major constitutional showdown over the power to tax. You see, through 2025, President Trump had been using this act, the IEEPA, as his main tool for imposing these really broad tariffs. He declared national emergencies over things like trade deficits or drug trafficking, and that was the justification for these new taxes on imports. The case, which was Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, really boiled down to this one fundamental disagreement. On one side, the majority said, "Look, the Constitution is crystal clear. The power of the purse, the power to tax, belongs to Congress. Period." But the dissent shot back saying, "Hold on. Tariffs are a classic way to regulate trade, and that falls right under the president's emergency powers." And wow, the way the chief justice framed the court's 6-3 decision was pretty striking. He basically said you can't hang this enormous multi-billion dollar power on just two little words buried in a statute. So, in the end, the court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, calling them a huge overreach of executive power. So you might think that's the end of it, right? The president's main tool for tariffs is now illegal. But nope, he didn't retreat. Instead, he pivoted incredibly fast to a different, much older law. The speed here was just breathtaking. Think about it. Friday morning, the old tariffs are dead. By Friday evening, a whole new 10% tariff is announced, and then by Saturday, it's already jacked up to 15%. A true whirlwind. So the administration's new weapon of choice was this thing called Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. It's a provision that's hardly ever used, and it has some very specific rules. It lets the president slap on a temporary tariff for what are called balance of payment reasons, but, and this part is absolutely key, it comes with a 150-day expiration date. As you can probably guess, this super fast and dramatic policy change sent huge shockwaves of confusion and uncertainty through the global economy. We're talking about massive disruptions to supply chains all over the world.

title: 0110 Podcast – Episode 1: The Reality of Always Being Liquid
transcription: Hey everyone. Welcome to episode one of the 0110 podcast. The reality of always being liquid. I'm Star, your host. And if you're an entrepreneur, founder, or just hustling through business and finance, this is the raw, no-fluff space where we tackle the real challenges, ones that keep you up at night, like cashflow crunches, debt ditches, and building that buffer so you can actually breathe. If you caught the teaser, you know we're diving into getting out of debt, splitting your money smartly, and why liquidity is your lifeline. Today, we're going deeper. Aggressive debt payoff strategies, how to build and use savings without guilt, the mental tune-up that comes with it, daily traps that sabotage you, and the key lifestyle shifts to set yourself in a better, healthier environment. We'll touch on friends, boundaries, and even handling work spaces, with more networking vibes in future episodes. Let's keep this around 10 minutes, so buckle up. For 0 to 1, let's build this. First off, aggressive debt payoff. Look, if you're sitting in debt right now, loans, credit cards, whatever, that's a normal entrepreneur life. But that's a ditch that's killing your options. Drains your cash, spikes your stress, and locks you into bad decisions like taking crappy clients just to pay bills. The truth, you've got to attack it head-on. Start here, list all your debts by interest rate, highest first, that's the avalanche method. Or, if you need quick wins for motivation, go snowball, smallest balance first. Either way, throw everything extra at it. Cut the non-essentials ruthlessly. Downgrade that streaming bundle, cook at home, skip the impulse buys. Aim to pay 20 to 30 percent above minimums if you can, and automate it. Set up auto payments so you don't forget and spend elsewhere. But mindset matters. Treat debt like a fire. Extinguish it before it spreads. Celebrate small wins like paying off one card, but don't reward with spending. That's a trap. Instead, visualize the freedom. No more interest eating your profits, more cash for your opportunities. I've seen founders go from 10k USD in debt to zero in 18 months by treating payoff like a side hustle. You can too. Just commit. As you climb out, split your money three ways like we teased. Aggressive payoff, which we've covered, saving, and investing. Investing is for later episodes, think stocks, real estate basics. Today, saving. As a founder, cash is your lifeline. Business is unpredictable. Clients ghost, expenses pop up,

title: Dax – “My Silence Was Crying for Help” (2026 Lyrics Video)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The loudest cry ever made, was the one nobody heard. Stopped asking for help, and everybody thought I was healing. And everybody thought I was healing. I became the friend everybody leaned upon. The one who stayed steady when everything went wrong. Always saying, "I'm good" with a practiced smile. Even though I've been breaking for a long, long while. I mastered the art of hiding in plain sight. Laughing in daylight, unraveling at night. Every "I'm okay" felt heavier to say. Because the truth kept begging me, not to look away. I answered every message, returned every call, but nobody noticed I was disappearing through it all. Not because they didn't care, maybe because I became too good at pretending I wasn't hurting. How do you explain a wound nobody can see? How do you ask for rescue, when you've convinced everyone you're free? My silence was crying for help. Every quiet moment said my name. I smiled so nobody would worry, while carrying invisible pain. My silence was crying for help, but nobody knew what to hear. Sometimes the strongest disguise is looking like you're doing fine. The hardest conversations that ever left my chest, I rehearsed them a thousand times, then buried every sense. I wasn't afraid of being judged, I was afraid of becoming a burden, so I carried everything myself until my own heart began to feel too heavy to lift. People celebrated the version of me they could see, nobody met the exhausted soul trying to survive behind closed doors. There were nights I stared at the ceiling not asking for answers, just hoping.

title: The Foundry Pitch Competition Informational Video
transcription: Before starting Amplab, I definitely was the type of person to not go outside the box and kind of just do what was asked of me. But then coming to Amplab and having my brother be here before, I kind of saw how important it is to step outside the box to get something out of Amplab. You have access to so many connections and like a huge network here, it's crazy. So using that network to really help set your business apart was a big thing for me. So here at Amplab, they focus on problem-solving a lot. You need to have a problem to be able to come up with solutions. So I looked into my own life and kind of took my love for animals a part of that and saw my dog was having issues with nutrition and saw how big of a role nutrition actually plays in pets' lives. So I saw his food allergies and his skin issues and how they were connected, so I wanted to create a pet food business that focused on the customization of nutrition and showed how high-quality ingredients can really help with that. So preparing for the Foundry was a lot, but it was very empowering. We spent a couple weeks working on our pitch, which was five minutes long, and then we also prepared for the Q&A that the judges did. And with that, we just asked each other questions and prepared that way. My business, Tailored Bites, that me and my business partner worked on, we also competed in Innovate WithIn, so we used a lot of our Foundry prize money towards that competition. So a lot of it went to ingredients so we created a bunch of food to sell at the Fort Wayne Farmers Market that is right here by Amplab. So a lot of it was ingredients to make the meals. We had a human-grade chicken dog food. We also prepped the judges' food for the Innovate WithIn contest and created custom lunch boxes with our food in it. So anyways, without further ado, the winner of the first-ever Foundry pitch competition, Tailored Bites. I would say really put your best effort. It is really rewarding to see it all come together at the competition like seeing the months of preparation come out and to be able to show it to your family and friends and also community members is really impactful.

title: Investigation uncovers sexual abuse allegations against Cesar Chavez
transcription: There are new revelations and allegations of sexual abuse and rape of women and minors by one of America's iconic civil rights and labor leaders, the late Cesar Chavez. A new investigation by the New York Times included the accounts of two women who are now 66 years old, who allege that Chavez abused them during his time leading the union he co-founded in the late 1970s, the United Farm Workers. Civil rights leader and the co-founder of that union, Dolores Huerta, also said today that Chavez raped her back in the '60s. Our William Brangham has more. Jeff, in a public statement today, Dolores Huerta alleged that Chavez assaulted her in a vehicle. She said she stayed silent then, and for decades after, because, quote, "I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farm worker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for. I have kept this secret long enough." She says she was impregnated by Chavez, and that those children were then raised by other families. The two other women who spoke to the Times were daughters of longtime organizers for the union. Both said Chavez's abuse went on for several years, starting at the ages of 12 and 13. Both suffered depression, panic attacks, and one attempted to end her life multiple times. At least a dozen other women told the Times that they had also been harassed by Chavez over many years. The reactions to all of this has been swift. A number of cities and organizations are now canceling upcoming celebrations or events that are tied to Cesar Chavez Day. And so, for more on the impact of this stunning story, I am joined by historian Miriam Pawel. She is author of "The Crusades of Cesar Chavez: A Biography." Miriam, thank you so much for talking with us. As someone who has written extensively about this man, what is your reaction to these allegations? I mean, the Times did indicate that there had been whispers about this going on. Had you heard about any of this? I mean, what do you make of this reporting? Oh, and the reporting is obviously quite stunning in its level of detail, very shocking and disturbing. There were, the issue of Chavez's adultery was well known. I wrote about that, others have written about that as well. There was a well-known incident when his wife left him after intercepting a love letter from an 18-year-old. title: Report: Donald Trump told Florida police chief ‘everyone’ knew about Jeffrey Epstein
transcription: There is brand new reporting from Julie K. Brown of the Miami Herald. She's been a trailblazer on the Epstein story. Once again, calls into question every single statement Trump puts forward when it comes to the central issue. What did Donald Trump know, and when did he know it, about Jeffrey Epstein's child sex trafficking? From that reporting, quote, "In July 2006, just as Jeffrey Epstein's criminal sex charge became public, Donald Trump called then Palm Beach Police Chief Michael Reiter to tell him that Epstein's activities with teenage girls were well-known in both New York and Palm Beach." Reiter recalled his conversation with Trump in a 2019 interview with the FBI. More from the reporting, quote, "Thank goodness you're stopping him, everyone has known he's been doing this," Trump told Reiter. Reiter told FBI agents that Donald Trump revealed that Epstein's associate Ghislaine Maxwell was Epstein's, quote, "operative," and that Donald Trump said, quote, "She is evil," and to focus on her, according to the reporting. Trump told Reiter that, quote, "He was around Epstein once when teenagers were present, and Trump got the hell out of there," the report said. Donald Trump also told Reiter that he threw Epstein out of his Mar-a-Lago club. A Justice Department official tells us that, quote, "We are not aware of any corroborating evidence that the president contacted law enforcement 20 years ago." Well, this squares with something the White House has said in the past, it does not square with what Trump has said himself about the past. This is from 2019, the days after Jeffrey Epstein's arrest. Did you have any suspicions that he was molesting young women? Underaged women. No, I had no idea. I had no idea. I haven't spoken to him in many, many years. If, quote, "everyone has known he's been doing this," as Trump reportedly put it, and Trump himself was with Epstein when there were teenagers present and, quote, "got the hell out of there," as he said, why didn't he contact authorities? Why didn't he contact authorities when Epstein, quote, "stole," Trump's words, not ours, survivor Virginia Roberts Giuffre from her job at the spa at Mar-a-Lago in the year 2000? Trump did say this, though, about all that back in July of this year, last year. Yeah, he took people, and because he took people, I said, "Don't do it anymore." You know, they work for me, and he took, uh, beyond that, he took some others. And once he did that, that was the end of him. I didn't like— when they steal people, I don't like it.

title: JonBenét Ramsey's Dad Responds to Claim She's in Epstein Files | E! News
transcription: John Ramsey is setting the record straight about a new rumor involving his daughter JonBenét Ramsey and Jeffrey Epstein. After a TikTok video recently circulated claiming the child beauty queen is in the Epstein files and that the millionaire convicted sex offender had a relationship with her, JonBenét's father is speaking out. Telling TMZ January 27, "Absolutely no truth to it. I haven't seen this but with AI, anything is possible. I figured one of these days I would be accused of being an Epstein pal. Hasn't happened yet. Internet people can be very cruel." The viral video also alleges that Epstein's co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell, who was found guilty on several charges, including sex trafficking of a minor, was at JonBenét's sixth birthday party. Another claim, John denies. E! News has reached out to John for comment, but hasn't yet heard back. These conspiracy theories come 30 years after JonBenét was found sexually assaulted, beaten, and strangled in the basement of her family's Boulder, Colorado home the day after Christmas. Following her death, authorities initially suspected parents John and Patsy Ramsey, however, they were never prosecuted. Patsy later died in 2006, and the case of JonBenét's mysterious murder remains unsolved.

title: This Michael Jackson Biopic Feels Off...
transcription: It's been a while since my last video. I had two weeks to give myself just a little break and it's good to be back. What's on the schedule? Oh, f- goddammit. I'll tell you the truth, I've been dreading the Michael video for weeks. I didn't know how I was going to feel about it, but I knew whatever I did say would be met with capital O opinions. Michael Jackson is just that kind of figure. He means a lot to a lot of people and people weren't being normal about this movie well before it even came out. Appropriately so, he's not a normal guy and naturally, this is not a normal movie. Michael, if you're unaware, is the long-awaited Michael Jackson biopic starring his nephew, Jaafar Jackson, which recaps the first half of Michael Jackson's career focusing mainly on his relationship with his father, Joe Jackson, played by Colman Domingo. The film has been on the radar since 2019 and after numerous setbacks, reshoots, and a lot of tinkering, it's here and you can feel all of that interference on the screen. Much of these complications stem from the fact that the script originally focused on the sexual abuse allegations towards Jackson, so much so that the film supposedly opened with that part of his life and looped back around to focusing on the scandal for the third act. But after an attorney for the Jackson Estate discovered a clause in one of the accusers' settlements with Jackson, barring the depiction or mention of him in any movie, things changed. This and some other factors ultimately pushed the film back an entire year, leading to 22 days of reshoots that occurred as recently as last June. And the result is a movie about a flawless protagonist, a really talented guy who, after overcoming some seemingly minor hurdles, became the most famous person on the planet thanks to writing some of the best songs of all time. Michael was, like any musical biopic about a beloved artist, always going to work on me just a little bit. These movies are carried on the backs of some of the best music ever written, they coat themselves in it. Watching the process of how these records came to be makes their reveal through the giant IMAX speakers unquestioningly satisfying. I enjoy listening to Michael Jackson's music, so as a result, I enjoyed listening to some of this movie. Where these films have to prove their quality is in how much they let the viewer into the lives of these icons, if that's the route they choose to go, and taking it a step further, how they let you into those lives. Better Man, for example, does not hold back and does so in a big, bold, and audacious way, capturing the excess and absurdity in a way that's both enticing and weirdly moving. A Complete Unknown, which is fine at the end of the day, purposefully leaves

title: BREAKING: Trump calls off MASSIVE Iran attack
transcription: Here's President Trump calling off a massive attack against Iran last night. The commander-in-chief says the change comes amid progress with the regime. Rebecca Castor is live in Washington with the details. Good morning, Rebecca. Good morning, Charlie. This was set to be one of the largest bombing campaigns against Iran to date, but now the President is signaling a peace deal could be close. He wrote on Truth Social, the USA is locked and loaded and ready to go against Iran. Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran and other Middle Eastern countries to hold off any attack, and that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to. This would include the immediate complete and total opening of the Hormuz Strait, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. I have agreed to cancel the attack subject to being able to rapidly make a deal. According to Axios, one of those Middle Eastern allies who asked President Trump to hold off on further strikes was the Saudi Crown Prince. The White House confirmed they spoke on the phone yesterday. And this comes after the US and Saudi Arabia launched joint strikes against Iranian militias in Iraq last week. But now the Saudis and other partners in the region are pushing the US and Iran to de-escalate. In an interview with Laura last night, Secretary of State Marco Rubio says it's because of President Trump that Tehran can no longer avoid consequences and may be ready to fold. I don't think the Iranian regime has ever faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action. You know, they got used to for 20 or 30 years, not just the US, but the broader world allowing them to get away with things like lying, breaking deals, tricking people into agreements and so forth. The regime has to change. Their view is they don't want to just govern Iran, they want to govern the region. They view them- they want to export their revolution. That does have to change. And the only way you're going to change that is if you if you make the price of it too high for them to be able to pay. Qatari mediators held separate talks with US, Iranian, and Omani officials yesterday on reopening the strait. Axios reports those talks made progress. Charlie, Laura, and Griff, back to you. All right, Rebecca. Thank you, Rebecca. Overnight, President Trump pausing the strikes on Iran, revealing a rough outline for a deal. The President writing, "The immediate complete and total opening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. I have agreed, for the future benefit of the world and likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a deal." Joining us now is former National Security Council member, retired Vice Admiral Robert Harward. Uh thank you for joining us this morning. So, um, w- w- where do you think uh things stand right now? Obviously, we have heard, uh we've seen President Trump both uh bombing Iran and then uh holding out hope that we might get a deal. Where are you on that?

title: Staying | The Cost of Choosing Loyalty Over Safety
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The hardest battles are often fought in silence. Behind polite smiles, behind tired eyes, behind voices that still say, "I'm fine." Some people carry storms so quietly that even the people closest to them never fully see the rain. And sometimes, the mind becomes heavy for so long that exhaustion starts feeling normal. Thoughts repeat themselves, doubts grow louder. The world slowly loses color and people begin believing they are far less important than they truly are. Pain has a way of shrinking perspective. It whispers things that sound permanent during temporary seasons. It tells tired hearts that nothing will change, that peace belongs to other people, that healing was never meant for them. And slowly, the weight of those thoughts begins to feel real. But thoughts are not always truth. Some people are not trying to leave life behind, they are simply trying to escape the heaviness of carrying everything alone. The pressure, the expectations, the loneliness hidden beneath functioning lives. And sometimes, the people who seem strongest are simply the ones who learned how to suffer quietly. Not because they are weak, but because they became used to surviving silently. One day at a time, sometimes one hour at a time, and occasionally, one breath at a time, there is no shame in surviving slowly. None of us truly know how deeply we are woven into the lives of others. Sometimes, we minimize our importance because pain has made us forget how much of our presence...

Her speech is slow, gentle, and whispered, conveying a sense of warmth, sadness, and profound understanding. Accompanied by a soothing and melancholic ambient background track with gentle piano chords, she speaks about the battles people fight in secret, hiding behind polite smiles and tired eyes. The message is one of validation and comfort for those carrying heavy burdens alone, emphasizing that there is no shame in surviving slowly, one day, one hour, or even one breath at a time.

title: Emerge 2026 – Empowering the Next Generation of Leaders #Emerge2026 #youthleadership #futureleaders
transcription: It is the seventh edition of the annual Youth Leadership Conference, Emerge 2026, a platform designed to break boundaries and unlock the potential of young people across Nigeria. This year's event takes place at the iconic Ade Ajayi Auditorium. At the registration point, students gather eager, expectant, and ready for what many describe as a life-changing experience. Inside the auditorium, every seat is filled. Young minds from diverse backgrounds come together, united by a shared desire to take their future to the next level. The convener, Olusegun Odufuwa, explains that the conference is designed to equip participants with the right tools to excel in their chosen careers. This conference is not just about conversations, it is about transformation. It is about equipping you to lead in your spaces, to influence your communities, and to create solutions that will outlive you. Speakers from different sectors deliver practical insights, sharing real-life experiences aimed at shaping the mindset of the next generation. The Group CEO of Red for Africa, Ayodeji Razaq, challenges participants with a thought-provoking session on "becoming the person your future requires," focusing on identity, growth, and future-proofing. In reality, what it means to emerge, if you look at the definition, is really to become someone different. Think of it like a butterfly. It goes from larva to butterfly. You have to become a new version of yourself. Representing the Lagos State Deputy Governor, the Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Mobolaji Ogunlende, emphasizes the importance of creating value and developing solutions to emerging societal challenges. There's no shortcut to the top. We are here to talk about leadership skills, or talk about leadership in general. So, I'm throwing things, nuggets at you. Because if you want to be a leader, we say the young, the youth are the leaders of tomorrow starting today. There are some key things that you must realize and understand and connect with. There's no shortcut to the top, forget about it. Organizers believe the event has equipped participants with the knowledge and confidence to navigate their paths, contribute meaningfully to society, and thrive wherever they find themselves, reminding them that the answers to many of society's challenges lie within their ideas, innovation, and determination.

title: Mayra Velasquez denies 2012 killing as attorneys challenge DNA link and suspect focus
transcription: Myra Velasquez and her attorneys continue to insist that Arlington police have used DNA evidence to go after the wrong killer. JD Miles has more on today's developments. I am Myra Velasquez. Um I did not do this. Myra Velasquez sat next to her attorney and professed her innocence now that she's free on bond while accused of murdering her friend Erasema Chavez 14 years ago inside the victim's Arlington apartment. I would never do this to no anyone. I'm a good person. She was my friend. I know God and all those people who know me they know that I could have never do something like this to anyone. Velasquez did not take questions and her attorneys had the media sign an agreement not to ask her any. She was arrested earlier this month after Arlington police used investigative genetic genealogy to connect her to a drop of blood found inside the victim's apartment. The attorney for Velasquez says an examination of security camera video of the suspected killer shows that they had a different body type. Frank Sellers also called on authorities to reinvestigate another woman who knew Chavez. There was a breakup that happened that day between Erasema and another woman. This is somebody who had passion. This is somebody who had, as the initial detective said, he thought was from a romantic fallout. Arlington police insisted during a media briefing 2 weeks ago that they have more than just DNA evidence to prove Velasquez brutally killed her friend. Um they were friends and uh Ms. Velasquez had been in the apartment before, um but we were able to obtain some information from her in the interview uh which will help in uh her prosecution. But I have faith in God that they're going to find out who did this to her, to my friend. Velasquez's short public statement was arranged by her attorneys in an attempt to show that she's not capable of being a cold-blooded killer. And I think part of the reason we wanted Myra to come and talk to everybody is, you know, she deeply cared about her friend, Erasema, and I, I think you can sense that when you're near her, when she talks about her. Velasquez posted a $450,000 bond to get out of jail while waiting to hear if a Tarrant County Grand Jury will indict her on a capital murder charge. In Fort Worth, JD Miles, CBS News, Texas.

transcription: A new Chinese lunar mission is drawing interest from an entire continent, while NASA's rover uncovers strange honeycomb patterns etched into Martian rock. This is Fascinating Frontiers, episode 149. African nations are examining hardware and science participation in China's Chang'e 8 lunar mission. The mission director has stressed openness and inclusiveness as core principles guiding international involvement. African partners are positioned as active contributors to lunar surface operations rather than passive observers. The initiative reflects growing interest among those countries in contributing instruments or joint experiments. Now, on a completely different note, here's what you may have missed across the past several days. NASA continued rolling out new data products and mission updates that keep reshaping how we picture both Earth and Mars. Fascinating Frontiers episodes tracked steady progress on international lunar plans and European formation flying tests. Meanwhile, ESA and partner agencies shared fresh results on solar wind interactions and atmospheric loss, giving clearer context for the long-term story of how planets lose their air. Curiosity rover spotted intersecting ridges that form polygonal cells in layered sedimentary rock on Mars. Scientists are weighing whether the honeycomb patterns result from ancient water activity or later erosion. Close-up images show consistent geometry across the outcrop in a region that preserves evidence of past environmental conditions. Further analysis will compare the textures with similar formations elsewhere on the planet. Precise formation flying kept the occulter aligned with the main spacecraft within millimeters over distances of hundreds of meters. title: Finding True Abundance | Journal Reading 019
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Good morning, YouTube. Today's journal reading was written on March 17th, 2026, and in this one, I kind of explore ideas of abundance, and I think that's a theme that maybe I've wrestled with a lot throughout my life. Anyway, here it goes. Abundance is found in nothing. Abundance is found in knowing enough. As I write this, I'm sitting back in our brown leather recliner we found sitting outside our dumpster when we first moved here. That probably sounds gross, but it was in good shape, and we needed some furniture. That was roughly six years ago. There was a time in my life where material abundance and worldly status mattered to me. It was something I chased. Where I was, or what I had, was never enough. I needed more. I needed to progress. But then something changed. I don't know when it happened, or why, or what triggered it. All I know is one day, all that once mattered seemed trivial. Among the spiritual community, there's a decent amount of talk about abundance, the law of attraction, and manifestation. If only we align our thoughts and energy with the life and success and the material we desire, all we imagine will be ours. Whether there's any truth to that, that doesn't really matter to me. What does matter to me is why our lives, where we are at this—where—lah, where we are at any given moment is not enough for us. I think we all have ideas in our head of what it means to be abundant and successful, and likely more often than not, those ideas are filled with lavish material items and social recognition from our fellow man. It's what I thought. It's what I chased. But I've come to understand that that's not true abundance. That's not what true success is. True success and abundance is looking around at your life just at it—just as it is right now, and seeing all that you have, all that you've accomplished this far. If you live in America, odds are you have everything you need, plus some. You have a roof over your head, food in the fridge, people who love you. Recognizing the value in all of that you already have is true abundance. Knowing enough in a world that is constantly telling you to go for more, to go for better, is a superpower. It's abundance. Knowing enough is not a lack mindset. It's peaceful sustainability. It's the mindset of the richest people on earth.

title: Company Culture | Simon Sinek
transcription: So, I think the concept of leadership is one of the most misunderstood concepts in business, quite frankly. We think about leadership as a rank or position, like "I'm in leadership." The question is, are you a leader? Leadership is the awesome responsibility to see those around us rise. It is a skill set that needs to be learned and practiced. Most of us, the way we have achieved our leadership position or rank is because we were good at the job. The problem is that's not your job anymore. You know, when we're super junior, the organizations we work for give us tons of training how to do our job. Some of us go to college and how to do our job. If you're an architect, you have to go to school to learn how to be an architect. And if you're really good at your job, they'll promote you until you reach a position where you're now responsible for the people who do the job you used to do. But they don't teach us how to do that. And so the reason we get managers and not leaders is because we don't get taught how to do our new job called leadership. When leaders take themselves on, when leaders uh become students of leadership, you'll find that all of the traditional metrics that we try and push and, you know, and drive every day, go up. Productivity goes up. Engagement goes up. Uh uh innovation goes up. Um I think it's very funny, I love uh I love organizations that when they write their values on the wall, you know, it's like, integrity, innovation, you know, honesty. By the way, if you have to write honesty on the wall, you've got bigger problems. Um But those those things are not things you can do. Those are the result of things. You can't walk into someone's office and say, "Lynn, a little more a little more innovation from you today, please." Like, what are you supposed to do? And so, it's not a value. A value is is is a behavior. And the better we understand our values and the better we incentivize to behavior, the stronger your culture. And the stronger your culture, the more innovation you get, the more integrity get, the more productivity you get, the more uh uh engagement you get. My favorite definition of culture is culture equals values plus behavior. So, values, number one, needs to be written as verbs. It's not integrity, it's do the right thing. It's not innovation, it's find a new way to solve a problem. It's not honesty, it's tell the truth. Which are which are behaviors and we can incentivize and reward to those behaviors. And the people who are best at embodying those values, those are the ones that we should promote into leadership positions because those are the ones that set the example of of how we how we work here.
caption: In a clear, engaging tone, a man discusses the concept of leadership, emphasizing that it is a responsibility to help others succeed rather than just a rank. He explains that people are often promoted because they excel at their tasks, but they aren't taught how to lead. This lack of training results in managers instead of leaders. When leaders focus on learning, productivity and engagement improve. He concludes that culture is the sum of values and behaviors, and that values should be expressed as actions (verbs) rather than nouns to encourage better leadership.

title: Broken Bone Healing Process | How Plaster Helps in Fracture? | Bone Fractures | Dr. Binocs Show
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: What are you timing, little kitty? Figuring out how quickly this plaster cast helps my broken bone heal. Ah, then let's find out how does plaster help heal fractured bones? Zoom in! You might think that a plaster cast heals a broken bone. Surprisingly, that's not the case. Plaster doesn't repair the bone itself. Instead, it provides the support and stability your body needs to heal the fracture naturally. In fact, the healing process begins the moment the bone breaks. Firstly, a blood clot forms around the fracture, helping stabilize the fracture site and causing swelling. Meanwhile, specialized white blood cells, including macrophages, remove damaged tissue and prepare the area for repair. Before applying a plaster cast, doctors examine the injury and use x-rays to assess the position of the fractured bone. If the broken pieces are out of alignment, the patient may first be given pain medication or sedation to improve comfort. The doctor then carefully moves the bone fragments back into their proper position in a procedure called a reduction. Once the bone is correctly aligned, the injured limb is wrapped in a protective layer and covered with wet plaster bandages. These bandages can be molded to fit the body shape and gradually harden

The background is filled with upbeat, playful instrumental music and a variety of cartoon-like sound effects, such as ticking clocks, whooshes, and squishing sounds, which complement the narrative. The narrator explains that the plaster cast itself does not heal the bone but provides stability for natural healing. He details the physiological process starting from blood clot formation and the role of white blood cells, followed by the medical procedure involving X-rays, bone reduction, and the application of wet plaster bandages.

title: How to Bullet Journal in 2026 (Every New Technique)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: There's a quiet rebellion happening against the algorithm life, a return to the physical world. Australia just passed a law against young people accessing social media, no-phone cafes are popping up in big cities around the world, and traditional gyms are slowly losing ground to wellness centers focused on health and community. These all address a need that can only be met in the physical world: connection. Nowhere is this need for connection more necessary than with yourself. What are you thinking, feeling, doing about your life? Hi, I'm Ryder Carroll, the creator of the Bullet Journal Method, and today, I want to show you why a paper notebook just might be the most radical productivity tool you can use this year. I'll also include specific ways that the Bullet Journal Method has evolved to help us navigate an increasingly busy, digital, and disconnected world. Let's dive in. Bullet Journal is not a notebook or a type of paper. It's a personal operating system that helps you write a better life. We use notebooks as our preferred platform to run that operating system because it helps us go offline and think with less distractions. That said, you can Bullet Journal in any app you would like. So how does this operating system actually work? Here are the four main steps. Record: This is about creating a record of your life using one-sentence journal entries to capture your notes, actions, moods, and events. Each is paired with a symbol to visually categorize them, hence, Bullet Journal. Reflect: This is about regularly reading your record. As the saying goes, "You don't learn from experience, you learn by reflecting on experience." We do this through practicing daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly reflection rituals. These help us become more aware of patterns in our thinking, feeling, and doing that are impacting our lives. Refine: This is about applying any insights we gain from reflection. It's about cutting what isn't working and cultivating what is, which brings us to the last step. Respond: Respond is the most critical step. It's the step that takes us out of our notebooks into the world by taking intentional action based on all the previous steps.

He speaks about a growing movement back to the physical world, driven by a need for genuine connection, particularly with oneself. He positions the paper notebook as a radical tool for productivity and self-awareness in a digital age. He clarifies that the Bullet Journal is not just a notebook but a personal operating system, and goes on to explain its four main steps: 'Record' (using brief entries with symbols), 'Reflect' (regularly reviewing entries), 'Refine' (acting on insights), and 'Respond' (taking intentional action in the physical world).

transcription: Final practice in Spa had a dramatic conclusion as Lewis Hamilton found the barriers at turn 13 after a steering snap took him into the gravel. Oh, was it on an upshift there as well? And it's just added maybe a slight kick of torque there for Hamilton when he's already right on the edge on the uh second lap on those tires. Yeah, I have to show you the car, mate. Sorry. No problem. Up until that moment, it had been a reasonable session for the seven-time champ, who had made a promising start to his Spa weekend, finishing P2 in first practice. His earlier laps prior to the crash were good enough for P5. Teammate Charles Leclerc finished P6 after a bit of a scruffy session, the Monegasque frequently fighting his Ferrari on his qualifying simulation runs. Having struggled for performance in FP1, Kimi Antonelli showed a marked improvement in second practice, bagging the fastest lap of the day. And he was again the quickest man on track in final practice. His best lap clocked at 1 minute 45.990. No such luck for Mercedes teammate George Russell, who languished in P8 at the flag yesterday, unable to unlock his Silver Arrow's full potential. He complained again of a lack of power on the straights, this time out finishing fourth. Lando Norris finished Friday in P2 but wasn't getting carried away with that, suggesting McLaren were probably the fourth-fastest car. He went a little wide exiting turn 14 in this session, flirting with the gravel, but he was again second quickest. A new electronics power unit fitted to his MCL38 means he'll face a 10-place grid drop on Sunday anyway, no matter where he finishes in qualifying. Oscar Piastri's Friday running was curtailed by a hydraulic issue, unable then to challenge the top times. P7 this time out, Oscar would work to do ahead of calling. Max Verstappen topped the timing tables in the first hour of Friday practice and despite falling back a little later on, felt satisfied that he'd maximized the Red Bull package. In the session, the four-time champ went very wide at turn nine, spraying some stones, but thankfully staying mostly away from the track. He was P3 at the flag. Isack Hadjar is taking new parts this weekend, enough to drop him to the back of the grid on Sunday. He's putting his shiny new RB22 through its paces, scraping the floor

title: A Prison Called My Mind
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Thud. Thump. Thud. Thump. The steady, heavy sound of a heartbeat echoes in the quiet room, looping like a ticking clock of anxiety. The beat drops in slow, heavy, mournful piano chords blended with vinyl static. Step inside the vestibule where shadows wear my face. I rent a room in ruin in a quiet crowded space. The blueprints of my sorrow were drafted in my youth, a self-inflicted torture built to barricade the truth. They think freedom is a pardon from a cell of iron bars. They've never felt the prison of beneath a million stars. My consciousness is solitary, padded with regret. Every mirror is a guard that I can't quite outrun or let go of the whispers that bleed through the drywall, predicting every stumble, orchestrating every fall. The key was swallowed years ago, dissolved in bitter acid. Now I sit in silence, paralyzed and flaccid. Trapped inside an echo chamber, spinning out of phase, navigating hallways in a permanent twilight maze. In a prison called my mind, the warden wears my eyes. He feeds me daily rations made of fabricated lies. No walls of grey concrete, just the weight of what could be. I built the cage myself and threw away the sanity. Oh, let me out. Let me face the open sky. Serving life in hard times in a prison called my mind. I pace the perimeter of all the things I never said, a graveyard of intentions resting heavy in my head. There's a library of every single look that made me shrink and a reservoir of ink from every time I dared to think that maybe I was more than just a tenant of my doubts. The fire starts to flicker every time the oxygen runs out. My heartbeat's like a metronome for grief I can't release, trading bits of sanity for moments of a fragile peace.

title: People Need Holding Before Vision | Gianpiero Petriglieri | International HR Day 2026
transcription: Caring is a lot harder than calculating. Calculating, the machine can do. But caring is something that we uniquely bring to the table. But care requires more than passion because passion is fickle, passion makes us irrational, passion sometimes erodes. Care requires courage. What are the biggest leadership mistakes companies make during periods of change? To put vision before holding. People often need holding before vision. So, people first need to say, "This is where we are, this is the truth, this is what we know, this is what we don't know, we will be okay if we stick together." And then, out of that connection, let the vision emerge. Leadership happens before a vision emerges. Once the vision has emerged, your job is done. Without goals, we're just philosophers. But without ideals, we are machines.

title: When You're Depressed and Feel Alone: A Message for Your Darkest Days
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I know you're here because it's heavy, the weight, the one no one can see, the one you can't explain. You wake up, and it's there. You go through the day, and it's there. You lie awake at night, and it's still there. But people say just be positive, as if you haven't tried. People say think happy thoughts, as if your thoughts are listening to you anymore. People say you have so much to be grateful for, and you know they're right, but knowing doesn't change the feeling, does it? And I'm not going to tell you those things today. I'm not going to tell you to cheer up, or look on the bright side, or just get over it, because I know, I know that when you're in this place, those words feel like knives, well-meaning knives, but knives nonetheless. Today, I'm going to sit with you in this darkness, not to pull you out, not to fix you, just to be here with you, because here's the truth nobody tells you about depression: It lies. It tells you you're alone. You're not. It tells you it will never end. It will. It tells you you're broken. You're not broken, you're hurting. There's a difference. Let's talk about what depression actually is. Not the dictionary definition, not the Instagram version, the real experience. Depression isn't sadness. Sadness is a feeling; depression is the absence of feeling. It's numbness, emptiness, a void where emotions used to live. Depression isn't laziness. Laziness is choosing not to do something. Depression is wanting to do something, and your body simply won't move. It's like being paralyzed from the inside out. Depression isn't weakness. Weakness is lacking strength. Depression is having strength and watching it drain away, no matter how hard you try to hold on. Depression is showering feeling like climbing Everest, answering a text feeling like writing a novel, eating feeling like running a marathon, existing feeling like too much. And here's the cruelest part: depression convinces you that you're the only one feeling this way, that everyone else has figured out life, that you're somehow broken in a way no one else is broken. Let me tell you something that might surprise you: some of the most brilliant, creative, loving people in history have sat exactly where you're sitting. Abraham Lincoln called it his melancholy, Winston Churchill called it his black dog, Vincent van Gogh painted it, Ernest Hemingway wrote
